indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Regulation 80/2019 on E-Commerce (PP 80/2019)
- Article 9(2) states that international e-commerce transactions must comply with regulations governing exports and imports, and regulations in the field of information and electronic transactions. 
- Article 15: E-commerce operators must have a clear legal identity and comply with local financial regulations, including collaborating with licensed payment system providers (typically requiring a local bank account for the processing of payments and tax compliance).
- Article 16: Foreign e-commerce providers must comply with Indonesian tax regulations, which involve using Indonesian payment gateways and banking systems for local transactions
- Article 60: This article specifies that operators of Trade Through Electronic Systems (PPMSE) are required to make transactions in Rupiah currency as a means of payment and shall be in accordance with the provisions of laws and regulations.

Regulation 50/2020 on E-Commerce implementing regulation that complements and builds upon Regulation 80/2019 specifies that the currency used for payments must comply with Indonesia’s financial regulations, implying that transactions are expected to use Rupiah (IDR) within the country unless exceptions apply to international trade.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 18/40/PBI/2016 on the Implementation of Payment Systems
indicators.impact:
Indonesia’s payment security standards, especially those outlined by Bank Indonesia, are aligned with international standards, such as ISO 27001 for information security management and PCI-DSS for card payment data security.

Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 18/40/PBI/2016 on the Implementation of Payment Systems sets out the requirements for the operation and security of payment systems in Indonesia:
- Article 7 requires payment system operators to implement security measures to ensure that payment services are secure and reliable, focusing on the integrity and confidentiality of payment data. The regulation also includes provisions for the authentication of users and data encryption, which align with global security standards like PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) but are customized for local implementation.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money 2018
indicators.impact:
Regulation No. 11/12/PBI/2009 last amended by the Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 requires that any e-money issuer must be licensed by Indonesia's Central Bank. In addition, the Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 added the maximum amount of stored e-money which is IDR 2 million for unregistered e-money and IDR 10 million for registered e-money.

Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money regulation governs electronic payments and e-wallet services in Indonesia. E-commerce providers offering digital payment services must comply with Bank Indonesia’s requirements for electronic money issuance and usage. 
- Article 4: Stipulates that electronic money issuers must obtain a license from Bank Indonesia.
- Article 9: Specifies minimum capital requirements for non-bank e-money issuers, which are linked to the value of managed floating funds. E-money issuers managing a floating fund of IDR 1 billion or more are required to obtain a license from Bank Indonesia. This applies to both closed-loop and open-loop e-money systems. Non-bank issuers managing significant floating amounts must have a minimum paid-up capital of IDR 3 billion. If the floating funds exceed IDR 9 billion, the issuer must increase their capital to IDR 10 billion plus 3% of the total floating fund. For unregistered users, the maximum floating fund per user is capped at IDR 2 million, For registered users, the cap is IDR 10 million.

Article 82: Entities conducting e-money operations prior to the regulation’s enactment (May 4, 2018) were required to apply for a license within six months of the regulation taking effect. Foreign e-commerce businesses operating in Indonesia are generally subject to the same requirements if they act as e-money issuers or integrate payment systems and must obtain a license if they issue e-money or provide similar services within Indonesia. Articles 8 and 10 specify the capital and Ownership Restrictions. At least 51% of the shares in a non-bank e-money issuer must be owned by Indonesian individuals or entities, with a maximum of 49% foreign ownership.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money 2018
indicators.impact:
Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money regulation Article 45 specifies limits on the value of electronic money that can be stored and transacted. For instance:
- Unregistered electronic money can hold a maximum value of IDR 2,000,000 (approximately 130 USD). 
- Registered electronic money can hold a maximum value of IDR 10,000,000 (approximately 650 USD). 

Note that Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 11/12/PBI/2009, last amended by Bank Indonesia Regulation No.20/6/PBI/2018 regarding E-money.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
There are no explicit mandate for the use of specific intermediaries for online payments in Indonesia. However, the requirement to work with authorized payment system providers is emphasized in several regulations, particularly for compliance with security, consumer protection, and licensing standards. 

Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 20/6/PBI/2018 on Electronic Money:
- Article 5 states that payment service providers, including electronic money issuers, must obtain authorization from Bank Indonesia. This implies that businesses using electronic money or payment systems must work with authorized providers (e.g., acquirers, switchers, and clearing operators).
- Article 7 requires licensed issuers to ensure their systems are secure and integrated with Indonesia’s domestic payment processing networks.

Government Regulation No. 80/2019 on E-Commerce:
- Article 60 requires all e-commerce payment systems to comply with Indonesian regulations, indirectly mandating collaboration with authorized local payment intermediaries.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 23/6/PBI/2021 on Payment Service Providers 2021
indicators.impact:
Bank Indonesia Regulation No. 23/6/PBI/2021
Article 19 and Article 20 of the regulation stipulate that for Non-Bank Institutions applying for a Payment Service Provider (PJP) license, at least 15% of the shares must be owned by Indonesian citizens or Indonesian legal entities (Article 19). Furthermore, at least 51% of the voting rights must be held by domestic parties (Indonesian citizens or legal entities) (Article 20). The regulation also allows Bank Indonesia to set further policies regarding ownership composition, considering factors like materiality and national interest.

indicators.question_description: Low De Minimis
indicators.impact: The Ministry of Finance Regulation No.199/2019 as replaced by Ministry of Finance Regulation No. 96/2023, last amended by Ministry of Finance Regulation No. 04/2025 regulate that Indonesia's de minimis rule is 3 USD or equivalent to approximately 2 SDRs per shipment/consignment.

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Regulation on Domain Name Management No.23 2013
indicators.impact:
Under the Regulation No. 23 of 2013, Indoesia Internet Domain Name Registry (PANDI) has overseen the registration of .id domain. 
Article 39 
1.State institutions and State-owned enterprises must use Indonesian Top-Level Domains.
2. Businesses and organizations domiciled in Indonesia with non-Indonesian Top-Level Domains must prioritize using Indonesian Top-Level Domains.
3. Foreign companies operating in Indonesia with electronic systems and non-Indonesian Top-Level Domains must also prioritize using Indonesian Top-Level Domains.
4. Users may manage subdomains as needed in compliance with laws and regulations.

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Domain Name Registration Policy Version 9 No.002/K/DNP/Policy of Domain Name Registration/IX/2024/PANDI-Publik 2024
indicators.impact:
Second Level Indonesian Domain name applied, and divided according to the allocation categories, that include: .co.id (Clause 8.1) is allocated for legal or business entities operating within Indonesia. To register this domain, entities must provide a Business Identity Number (NIB) and valid identification such as a KTP-el or Passport. For brand-related registrations, a Brand Certificate or Power of Attorney from the brand holder is required.

Additionally, Clause 9 providing that document requirements of domain name registration include identity document and legality document (a copy of incorporation document of an institution/legal entity/business entity issued by the official institution of the Republic of Indonesia, according to the allocation of Domain Name).

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.80 on Trading Through the Electronic System (E-commerce Law) 2019
indicators.impact:
There is no explicit mandate in Indonesian law or regulations requiring the use of a .id domain name for foreign or domestic e-commerce businesses. However, the Government Regulation No.80/2019 encourages its use as part of creating a local digital presence.

Under the Regulation No.80/2019, e-commerce law states that subject to certain thresholds, foreign business actors that actively conduct e-commerce activities with consumers in Indonesia are deemed as physically present in Indonesia and conducting fixed business activities in Indonesia. These thresholds are related to (i) number of transactions, (ii) transaction value, (iii) number of shipped packages, and/or (iv) volume of traffic or number of users. A foreign business actor that meets any of the thresholds must appoint an Indonesian representative that can act on its behalf.

The regulation includes provisions related to the use of local domain names. Specifically, Article 21 of Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019 mandates the prioritization of using Indonesia’s top-level domain name (".id") for Electronic Systems in the form of websites. It also establishes sanctions for violations of this obligation, which may include: written warnings; inclusion in the priority monitoring list; inclusion in the blacklist; temporary blocking of domestic and/or foreign PPMSE services by the relevant authorized agency; and/or revocation of business licenses. 

Article 7 specifies that foreign electronic system operators that meet certain criteria (such as transaction volume or user base) are considered to have a physical presence in Indonesia. These operators are required to appoint a local representative who can act on their behalf within the country.The specific criteria for foreign PPMSEs, as referred to in Article 18 of Minister of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023, include: (a) having conducted transactions with at least 1,000 consumers within a one-year period; (b) having delivered at least 1,000 packages to consumers within a one-year period; and/or (c) having at least 1% of domestic internet users accessing their platform within a one-year period.

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.impact: According Minister of Communication and InformaticsRegulation No. 5 of 2020, e-commerce platforms and digital service providers are encouraged to use Indonesian top-level domain names (TLDs), such as .id, as part of their registration and compliance with local regulations. Article 2 indicates that businesses operating electronic systems in Indonesia must ensure they are registered and comply with local guidelines, which include the registration of a local domain name when operating locally.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.source_legislation: Regulation of the Minister of Trade No.31 on Business Licensing, Advertising, Guidance and Supervision of Business Actors in Trading Through Electronic Systems 2023
indicators.impact:
Ministry of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023
Foreign e-commerce platforms must comply with certain operational requirements. For instance, under the Ministry of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023, foreign e-commerce operators that meet specific criteria, such as transacting with at least 1,000 consumers or delivering at least 1,000 packages annually, must establish a representative office in Indonesia. Additionally, if a foreign platform's traffic constitutes at least 1% of total local internet traffic, they are also required to set up a representative office.

Article 18
(1) Foreign e-commerce operators (PPMSE) that meet certain criteria must appoint a representative located within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia.
(2) The specific criteria for foreign PPMSE include:
- Having transacted with at least 1,000 consumers within a one-year period.
- Having delivered at least 1,000 packages to consumers within a one-year period.
- Having a traffic or user base that constitutes at least 1% of the total domestic internet users within a one-year period.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.impact:
The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5 of 2020, as amended by the The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 10 of 2021 on Private Electronic System Operators mandates foreign Private Electronic System Operators (ESOs) to register their businesses to the relevant ministry through the online single submission system. ESOs should also appoint liaison officers, who have to be domiciled in Indonesia. The duty of the liaison officer is to facilitate any access request by government authorities and takedown request. According to the regulation, ESOs are persons, business entities, or communities that operate an electronic system. ESOs include electronic system operators that are supervised by ministers or institutions in accordance with laws and regulations, and electronic system operators that have an online portal, site, or application through the internet. The requirement was first enacted with the Government Regulation No. 71/2019 regarding the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction.

For foreign electronic system operators, Article 4 (MOCI 5/2020) outlines that they must register if they provide services in Indonesia, conduct business in Indonesia, or have systems used or offered in Indonesia. This implies a need for some form of local presence, but it does not specify the requirement for a physical office or other commercial presence beyond registration.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.source_legislation:
Regulation of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia No.5 on Private Electronic System Operators 2020;

Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 10 on the Amendment to Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5 of 2020 on Private Electronic System Operators 2021
indicators.impact:
Digital service providers such as social media platforms, electronic commerce providers, and over-the-top (OTT) media services are required to register with the Ministry of Communication and Information under Article 2 of MOCI 5/2020. Additionally, these entities must establish a representative office in Indonesia.

For foreign electronic system operators, Article 4 (MOCI 5/2020) outlines that they must register if they provide services in Indonesia, conduct business in Indonesia, or have systems used or offered in Indonesia. This implies a need for some form of local presence, but it does not specify the requirement for a physical office or other commercial presence beyond registration.

While MOCI Regulation No. 5/2020 required foreign PSEs to register and implied the need for a local presence, Regulation No. 10/2021 did not explicitly mandate the establishment of a physical representative office in Indonesia. Instead, the focus is now on mandatory registration with the Ministry of Communication and Informatics (Kominfo) through the OSS RBA system and compliance with Indonesian laws, such as content moderation and taxation. There is no explicit requirement for a physical office or representative office in Indonesia under the updated regulations.

Note that Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5/2020, last amended by the Indonesia Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 10/2021.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Law No.8 on Consumer Protection 1999
indicators.impact:
Indonesia's Consumer Protection Law No. 8 is a comprehensive framework aimed at protecting consumer rights, ensuring transparency, and mandating the safety and quality of goods and services in electronic commerce. However, it does not raise specific e-commerce or distance sales issues. The Law forms the foundation of consumer protection in Indonesia.
- Article 4 enumerates consumer rights, including the right to safety, accurate information, and compensation for damages.
- Article 7 imposes obligations on businesses to provide clear, truthful information about goods/services and to guarantee their safety.
- Article 8 prohibits businesses from offering goods/services that fail to meet safety, quality, or labeling standards.

It is important to note that the Consumer Protection Law is the legal basis for the implementation of consumer protection in Indonesia, although it does not specifically regulate online consumer protection.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.impact:
Law (Law) No. 19 of 2016, Amendments to Law Number 11 of 2008 concerning Information and Electronic Transactions addresses digital and electronic transactions:
- Article 9 ensures consumer protection in electronic contracts, mandating transparency and clarity in terms and conditions.
- Article 18 governs the validity of electronic contracts, emphasizing fairness and requiring accessibility to contract information by consumers.

Moreover, the mechanism for regulating electronic contracts can also be found in Chapter X of Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.80 on Trading Through the Electronic System (E-commerce Law) 2019
indicators.impact:
Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019 explicitly stipulates that foreign Electronic System Operators in Trade (PPMSE) that meet certain criteria are deemed to have a physical presence in Indonesia and are therefore required to appoint a representative domiciled in Indonesia:
● The obligation to provide consumer complaint services is stipulated in Article 27. 
● The obligation to display clear and accurate product information is regulated in Article 13.
● Article 53 states that an electronic contract must include information on the procedure for returning goods and/or services in case of any discrepancies between what was received and what was agreed upon. However, the mechanism that is explicitly detailed pertains to the refund process, as outlined in Article 71.
● Article 32 relates to Electronic Advertising, the provisions concerning consumer rights in Electronic System-Based Trading (PPMSE) are found in Article 26. This article requires Business Actors to protect consumer rights in accordance with the prevailing laws and regulations on consumer protection;
● One of the key consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Law (UUPK) is the right to receive compensation, reimbursement, and/or replacement if the goods and/or services received do not match the agreement or are not delivered as promised.

In addition, PPMSE conducting business activities in the context of electronic commerce (PMSE) are obligated to comply with business licensing requirements in accordance with the prevailing laws and regulations.

Furthermore, Minister of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023 serves as a regulatory framework for the governance of PMSE, aiming to establish a healthy digital trade ecosystem and ensure consumer protection, while taking into account the ever-evolving nature of PMSE business models.

It is important to note that Regulation 31/2023 does not stand alone, but rather refers to and aligns with other relevant laws and regulations, including those governing goods distribution, electronic system operators, and others.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Regulation of the Minister of Trade No.31 on Business Licensing, Advertising, Guidance and Supervision of Business Actors in Trading Through Electronic Systems 2023
indicators.impact:
The Regulation of the Minister of Trade No.50/2020 is no longer valid, replaced by Regulation of the Minister of Trade Number 31 of 2023 concerning Business Licensing, Advertising, Guidance and Supervision of Business Actors in Trading Through Electronic Systems. 

Advertising is regulated in Chapter IV Electronic Advertising (articles 23-31). The obligation to have a complaint service is regulated in Article 9.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.71 on the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction 2019
indicators.impact:

- Article 28 mandates service providers to notify consumers in case of data breaches affecting their information.

indicators.question_description: Imposing trade defence measures (anti-dumping, countervailing duties and safeguards) on ICT-related products imported by other Asia-Pacific economies
indicators.source_legislation: Notification No. 21/2020-Customs (ADD)
indicators.impact:
On 29 July 2020, the Indian authorities imposed a definitive duty on imports of digital offset printing plates from China, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Chinese Taipei and Viet Nam. The rate of duty on imports from China is between USD 0.55 and 0.77 per square metre depending on the company. The rate of duty on imports from the Republic of Korea is USD 0.15 or 0.37 per square metre depending on the company. The rate of duty on imports from Japan is USD 0.13 or 0.27 per square metre depending on the company. The rate of duty on imports from Viet Nam is 0.60 per square metre. The rate of duty on imports from Chinese Taipei is 0.41 per square metre. The duty is in force for five years from 30 January 2020.

Imposition: 15.03.2020, definitive duty since July 2020.

indicators.question_description: Imposing trade defence measures (anti-dumping, countervailing duties and safeguards) on ICT-related products imported by other Asia-Pacific economies

indicators.impact:
On October 18th, 2013, the Indian Directorate General of anti-dumping & allied duties, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, initiated an anti-dumping investigation on imports of electronic calculators (at the exception of printing, graphing and programmable calculators) from China. On May 29th, 2015, the Indian Ministry of Finance issued the Customs Notification imposing this definitive anti-dumping duty. On 27 May 2020, the Indian authorities extended the definitive duty imposed on imports of the subject good from China. The rate of duty is USD 0.28 or 1.22 per unit depending on the company. The duty is in force for a period of five years.

In September 2019, the Indian authorities initiated an antidumping investigation on imports of electronic calculators from Malaysia. In June 2020, a definitive duty was imposed. The duty amounts to 0.92 USD per item. 

Imposition since May 2015; Imposition since June 2020.

indicators.question_description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
indicators.source_legislation:
Government of India,
Ministry of Commerce and Industry Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (Public Procurement Section) Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order 2017
indicators.impact:
As per the latest Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017, amended on 19 July 2024, Section 3 states that only Class-I local suppliers (with ≥50% local content) are eligible to bid for goods, services, or works in sectors where the nodal ministry has confirmed sufficient local capacity and competition.

In all other cases (except for Global Tender Enquiries), only Class-I and Class-II local suppliers (≥20% local content) may bid.

Non-local suppliers are only eligible when Global Tender Enquiry has been issued. Furthermore, the order also permits nodal ministries to prescribe higher minimum local content thresholds beyond the default 50%/20%.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Since June 2017, last amended in July 2024

Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) Order 2018; 

Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Manual for Procurement of Goods, Second Edition 2024
indicators.impact:
Every Central Ministry /Department / PSUs shall set an annual target for 25% procurement from MSE Sector, mandatory since 1st April 2015. A sub-target of 4% and 3% from within the 25% target shall be earmarked for procurement from Micro and Small Enterprises owned by SC/ST entrepreneurs and women, respectively.

From the referenced manual (2024) :) MSEs would be treated as owned by SC/ ST or Women entrepreneurs:
1) In the case of proprietary MSE, proprietor(s) are SC /ST or Woman;
2) In the case of partnership MSE, the SC/ ST or Women partners hold at least 51% (fifty-one per cent) shares in the unit;
3) In the case of Private Limited Companies, SC/ ST or Women promoters hold at least 51% (fifty-one per cent) share. 

Definition of MSEs: All MSEs having registration as per provisions of the Policy i.e. registration with District Industries Centre (DIC) or Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) or Khadi and Industries Board (KVIB) or Coir Board or National Small Industries Commission (NSIC) or directorate of Handicrafts and Handlooms or Udyog Aadhaar Memorandum or any other body specified by Ministry of MSME.

This automatically restricts foreign firms from participating in procurement activities.

Types of cyber security products included in the notifications are anti-virus, cloud security, mobile security, firewall, OTP gateway, encryption subscription etc. The list of products can be found in the Public Procurement (Make in India) Order 2019 for Cyber Security Products.

indicators.question_description: Specific requirements on source codes, encryption and trade secrets
indicators.source_legislation:
Government of India, Ministry of Communication and Information Technology, Policy on Adoption of Open Source Software for Government of India 2015; 

Government of India, Ministry of Communication & Information Technology, Framework for Adoption of OSS in eGovernance Applications 2015
indicators.impact: The Indian government adopted a formal preference for open-source software for e-government procurement opportunities related to its digital agenda. The policy is reported to be one of the most far-reaching and restrictive preference schemes that has been implemented to date. The Policy calls for a change from using Closed Cloud Software (CSS), which is licensed under the exclusive right of the copyright holder. The Indian Government wants all governmental organisations to move towards the use of Open Source Software, which the government argues would ensure strategic control of eGovernance applications and reduce the cost of ownership of projects. The Framework provides a set of procedures and recommendations for promoting, adopting and managing OSS in e-Governance systems. The framework provides guidance on the selection of software and the induction of the OSS software.

indicators.question_description: Specific requirements on source codes, encryption and trade secrets
indicators.impact:
Section 84A of the Information Technology Act (Modes Or Methods For Encryption) states: “The Government may, for secure use of the electronic medium and for promotion of e-governance and e-commerce, prescribe the modes or methods for encryption.” However, no rules have been introduced under this section. 

There exists a requirement to surrender patents (make it available on a royalty free basis) for those open standards identified as "Identified Standards". Per clause 4.1.2- The Patent claims necessary to implement the Identified Standard shall be made available on a Royalty-Free basis for the life time of the Standard. Open standards refer to the freedom to encode and decode data and network protocols.

indicators.impact:
Classes of Local Suppliers based on local content as per the revised PPP-MII Order dated 04.06.2020 issued by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) are as under:

A supplier or service provider, whose goods, services or works offered for procurement is classified as follows based on local content: Class-I Local supplier - has local content equal to or more than 50%., Class-II Local supplier has local content more than 20% but less than 50%. and Non-Local supplier has local content less than or equal to 20%.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation:

Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Guidelines for Government Departments On Contractual Terms Related to Cloud Services 2017;

Government of India,
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Invitation for Application/Proposal for Empanelment of Cloud Service Offering of Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) 2017
indicators.impact:
In 2015, India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY) issued guidelines under "1.2 Guidelines for Procurement of Cloud Services" for a cloud computing empanelment process under which cloud computing service providers may be provisionally accredited as eligible for government procurements of cloud services.

The Invitation for the Empanelment of Cloud Service Offerings provides certain mandatory requirements to be followed for cloud service providers. Under 5.12. Legal Compliance Requirements subsections 4 and 5, it is required that such cloud providers store all data in India to qualify for the accreditation and that no legal frameworks outside Indian law is applicable to the operation of the service and the information contained in it.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation:

Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises Order 2012;

indicators.impact:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology noted that cyber security is a strategic sector and preference will be provided by procuring governmental entities to domestically manufactured cyber security products. 'Domestically manufactured Cyber Security Product' is a product where the IP is owned by an Indian company such that the company can distribute, modify or commercialise the product without third party consent. Further, products with multiple sub-components can fall within this definition of a domestically manufactured cyber security product if the minimum local content is 60% of the total cost of the product and the total licensing fee to a third party does not extend 20% of the total cost of the product. 

As per the Public Procurement (Make in India) Order 2019 for Cyber Security Products, preference is granted to a company which is incorporated and registered in India or startup firms that meet the definition set out by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), provided the revenue from the product and IP licensing accrues to the firm in India.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation:
Government of India, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, Preference to Domestically Manufactured Electronic Products in Government Procurement, 2013;

Government of India, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, Guidelines for Providing Preference to Domestically Manufactured Electronic Products in Government Procurement, 2015
indicators.impact:
The Preferential Market Access (PMA) Policy provides that domestically manufactured equipment receives preferences in government procurement and in some types of private sector procurement. The underlying objectives are India’s goals to expand its domestic manufacturing capacity and to protect the security of its telecommunications networks. India revised the PMA in December 2013, but the revised policy continues to require that domestically manufactured goods constitute a certain percentage of the electronic products procured by government entities. Detailed guidelines on the implementation of the policy were issued in November 2015. 

The Notification stipulates that each Ministry or Department will satisfy a minimum percentage of their electronic product demand with local products which fulfil the minimum value addition prescribed for each item. The 2015 Guidelines provide that the minimum percentage of domestic procurement for any electronic product is 30%. The percentage of total procurement value for which preference is provided to domestic manufactured electronic products should be fixed so that competition is maximized while at the same time domestic manufacturing is encouraged. The 2013 Notification will be in operation for 10 years. 

The electronic products notified in the 2013 Notification include notebooks, tablets, desktop PCs, servers, printers, keyboards, monitors, USBs, ATMs, photocopiers, scanners, faxes, smartcards, mobile handsets, hand held terminals, PC projector, POS based services. The telecom products notified in the 2013 Notification include SIM Cards, encryption platforms, leased line network equipment, WiFi access systems etc.

indicators.impact:
As per Para 5.2.15.3 of the FDI Policy [as amended vide Press Note 4 of 2019 and Press Note 1 of 2018] , 100% FDI is allowed in Single Brand Retail Trading (SBRT) under the automatic route subject to compliance of stipulated conditions. Para 5.2.15.3 (2) of the FDI Policy stipulates the following conditions for FDI in SBRT:
a) Products to be sold should be of a ‘Single Brand’ only.
b) Products should be sold under the same brand internationally i.e. products should be sold under the same brand in one or more countries other than India.
c) ‘Single Brand’ product-retail trading would cover only products which are branded during manufacturing.
d) A non-resident entity or entities, whether owner of the brand or otherwise, shall be permitted to undertake ‘single brand’ product retail trading in the country for the specific brand, either directly by the brand owner or through a legally tenable agreement executed between the Indian entity undertaking single brand retail trading and the brand owner.
e) In respect of proposals involving foreign investment beyond 51%, sourcing of 30% of the value of goods purchased, will be done from India, preferably from MSMEs, village and cottage industries, artisans and craftsmen, in all sectors. The quantum of domestic sourcing will be self-certified by the company, to be subsequently checked, by statutory auditors, from the duly certified accounts which the company will be required to maintain. This procurement requirement would have to be met, in the first instance, as an average of five years’ total value of the goods procured, beginning 1st April of the year of the commencement of SBRT business (i.e. opening of the first store or start of online retail, whichever is earlier). Thereafter, SBRT entity shall be required to meet the 30% local sourcing norms on an annual basis. For the purpose of ascertaining the sourcing requirement, the relevant entity would be the company, incorporated in India, which is the recipient of foreign investment for the purpose of carrying out single-brand product retail trading.
f) For the purpose of meeting local sourcing requirement laid down at para (e) above, all procurements made from India by the SBRT entity for that single brand shall be counted towards local sourcing, irrespective of whether the goods procured are sold in India or exported. SBRT entity is also permitted to set off sourcing of goods from India for global operations against the mandatory sourcing requirement of 30%. For this purpose, ‘sourcing of goods from India for global operations’ shall mean value of goods sourced from India for global operations for that single brand (in INR terms) in a particular financial year directly by the entity undertaking SBRT or its group companies (resident or non-resident), or indirectly by them through a third party under a legally tenable agreement.
g) An SBRT entity operating through brick and mortar stores can also undertake retail trading through e-commerce. However, retail trading through e-commerce can also be undertaken prior to opening of brick and mortar stores, subject to the condition that the entity opens brick and mortar stores within 2 years from date of start of online retail.

Conditions mentioned at Para 5.2.15.3 (2) (b) & 5.2.15.3 (2) (d) will not be applicable for undertaking SBRT of Indian brands. Indian brands should be owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens and/or companies which are owned and controlled by resident Indian citizens.

indicators.impact:
According to Para 3.1.1 of the FDI Policy,
(a) A non-resident entity can invest in India, subject to the FDI Policy except in those sectors/activities which are prohibited. However, an entity of a country, which shares land border with India or where the beneficial owner of an investment into India is situated in or is a citizen of any such country, can invest only under the Government route. Further, a citizen of Pakistan or an entity incorporated in Pakistan can invest, only under the Government route, in sectors/activities other than defence, space, atomic energy and sectors/activities prohibited for foreign investment.
(b) In the event of the transfer of ownership of any existing or future FDI in an entity in India, directly or indirectly, resulting in the beneficial ownership falling within the restriction/purview of the para 3.1.1(a), such subsequent change in beneficial ownership will also require Government approval.

In April 2020, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry issued the Review of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy for curbing opportunistic takeovers/acquisitions of Indian companies due to the current COVID-19 pandemic (Press Note. 3). As per the Press Note an entity of a country which shares a land border with India or where the beneficial owner of an investment into India is situated in such a country, government approval would be required. Additionally, it is provided that in the event of any direct or indirect transfer of ownership of any existing or future FDI in India such that there is a change in beneficial ownership which falls within the purview of the circumstances envisaged in the Press Note, such subsequent change in beneficial ownership will also require governmental approval. 

The aforesaid change in the law was primarily targeted at China, in light of border tensions between India and China. Since the introduction of Press Note 3, as many as 150 private equity/venture capital investment approvals from China and Hong Kong, China are pending with the government.

indicators.question_description: Patent application issues
indicators.source_legislation:
Patents Act No.39 1970; 

Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Patent Rules (Amendment) 2003
indicators.impact:
In India, copyright, trademark, and patent applications can be filed online, while design applications require in-person or online filing (Copyright registration is not mandatory. Copyright is automatically granted to the creator). Regarding patents, applicants without a registered business in India must file through an Indian attorney or agent and provide an address for service in India as per Rule 5 of the Patents Rules, 2003 (as amended). This includes a postal and email address in India, which is essential for proceedings. Without this, the Controller is not obligated to act on applications or send notices.

The Patents Act, 1970 (as amended) and Patents Rules, 2003 (as amended) continue to mandate an address for service in India for filing patent applications, as reaffirmed in the Patent Rules Amendment, 2024, to protect applicant interests regardless of nationality.

Section 39 of the Patents Act, 1970 requires Indian residents to obtain prior written permission from the Controller to file patent applications abroad unless the same application is filed in India at least six weeks earlier. Violations result in deemed abandonment (Section 40), revocation of patents (Section 64), and penalties (Section 118). Permission requests are resolved within 21 days using a simple form (Form 25). These provisions apply only to Indian residents, not inventors, and remain unchanged in the Patent Rules Amendment, 2024, as they adequately safeguard applicant interests.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.impact:
In section 107 A, the Patents Act states the actions that are not considered as infringements of patent rights. Moreover, there are mentions of remedies, civil and administrative procedures and provisional measures to deal with infringements. For example section (108) in the Patents Act list injunction, damages/ an account of profits and seizure, forfeiture and destruction of infringing goods as a possible relief(s) for infringement. Moreover, the Indian Patent Office, under the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM); handles the civil and administrative procedure in patent related matters.It primarily handles grant applications, screening and grant/refusal. 

Order XXXIX of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (CPC) provides provisions for temporary injuctions where courts can exercise their powers to provide remedy to patent infrigements. Finally, the patent rules (2003) work in conjuction with the Patents Act largely lists the administrative procedures regarding patent opposition proceedings (Chaper 6 Opposition of Grant of Patents), amendments to patent specifications and claims (Provision 14) and compulsory licensing (chapter 13, prov. 96)

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures

indicators.impact:
Indian Patent Act, 1970 (as amended) is a fully TRIPS compliant meeting all international obligations and simultaneously utilizing the flexibilities provided in the international regime to address its developmental concerns.

The Indian Patents Act maintains a fine balance between private rights on one hand and the rights of the society at large on other hands. In order to streamline processing of Intellectual Property Rights case, Delhi and Madras High Courts have created the Intellectual Property Division (IPD) to exclusively deal with all matters related to Intellectual Property Rights in line with global practices. Additionally, some High Court including the Bombay, Calcutta, and Gujarat High Courts have designated specialized IP benches. This has fast-tracked the disposal of IP cases including patent cases. In the first year of the establishment of IPD in Delhi High court (DHC-IPD), more than two-thirds of all the original petitions concerning patents transferred from the Appellate Board to the DHC-IPD have been disposed.

indicators.question_description: Lack of copyright framework and exceptions
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Act No.14 1957
indicators.impact:
The legal copyright framework in India justifies the protection of innovations and creative works by granting exclusive rights solely to creators. This ensures that creators have the right to receive royalties as incentives, encouraging further innovation and contribution to the knowledge economy.

India currently follows the fair dealing model of copyright exceptions, in compliance with the three-step test and the copyright exceptions provided under Chapter XI – Infringement of Copyright Section 52(1) (Certain acts not to be infringement of copyright) of the Copyright Act, 1957, a fair dealing with any work (not being a computer programme) for the purposes of private or personal use, criticism or review and the reporting of current events and current affairs does not constitute an infringement of copyright. This approach is fully in line with all international conventions under the International Copyright regime, including the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) of the World Trade Organization (WTO), the Berne Convention, 1886, the WIPO Copyright Treaty, 1996, the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty, 1996, the Beijing Treaty, 2012, and the Marrakesh Treaty for Access to Published Works for Visually Impaired and Print Disabled Persons, 2013, of which India is a member.

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation:
Copyright Act No.14 1957; 

Ministry of Commerce and Industry Press Information Bureau: Existing IPR Regime Well-equipped to Protect AI Generated Works, No Need to Create Separate Category of Rights
indicators.impact:
The press release states that the current copyright framework is well equipped to handle issues of copyright infringement related to AI generated works.

The exclusive economic rights of a copyright owner such as the right of reproduction, translation, adaptation etc. granted by the Copyright Act, 1957 obligates the user of Generative AI to obtain permission to use their works for commercial purposes if such use is not covered under the fair dealing exceptions provided under Section 52 (Certain acts not to be infringement of copyright) of the Copyright Act. Since Intellectual property rights are private rights, these are enforced by the individual rights holders. Adequateand eﬀective civil measures and criminal remedies are prescribed under the Copyright Law against any act of infringement or unauthorized use of works, including digital circumvention.

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Act No.14 1957
indicators.impact:
In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 provides the legal framework for addressing copyright infringement, including online piracy. Section 51 of the Copyright Act defines infringement and provides that any person who, without a license granted by the owner of the copyright or the Registrar of Copyrights, or in contravention of the conditions of a license so granted or of any condition imposed by a competent authority under this Act, does anything, the exclusive right to do which is by this Act conferred upon the owner of the copyright, shall be deemed to infringe the copyright.

Section 55 of the Copyright Act empowers the courts to grant injunctions to prevent the infringement of copyright. It states that where the existence of the right to receive royalties in respect of any work has been established to the satisfaction of the court, the court may, in its discretion, grant an injunction to restrain the infringement of the right by the defendant or any agent of his or any person acting under his authority.

The District Level Commercial Courts and the Commercial Benches in all 25 High Courts of India have been set up under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015(as amended in 2018) and are functioning efficiently all over India. Moreover, the Delhi High Court has been at the forefront of addressing online copyright piracy through dynamic injunctions. In the landmark case of UTV Software Communications Ltd. v. 1337x.to, the court issued a dynamic injunction against various websites that were facilitating the unauthorized distribution of the plaintiff's copyrighted content. The court directed the blocking of these websites and also ordered that any new domain names or URLs used by these websites to infringe the plaintiff's copyright would also be covered by the injunction. Similarly, in the case of Sony Pictures Networks India Pvt. Ltd. v. the website known as 'dwatchseries.to,' the Delhi High Court granted a dynamic injunction restraining the website from hosting, streaming, reproducing, distributing, making available to the public, or communicating to the public any cinematograph work, sound recording, or musical work belonging to the plaintiff without authorization. In 2019, another recent case of Star India Pvt. Ltd. v. Moviestrunk. Com, the High Court passed an order of injunction restraining the defendant websites from ‘unauthorizedly streaming, downloading, communicating or distributing the cinematograph film ‘Mission Mangal’, including any extracts or clippings thereof.The Honourable Court further directed IPTV providers and ISP to block the unlawful websites and the various government departments to issue notices to IPTV and ISP to block the said website.

These judgments highlight the effectiveness of dynamic injunctions in combating online copyright piracy. By granting injunctions that can adapt to the changing online landscape, courts can effectively protect the rights of copyright owners and deter infringers from engaging in piracy. Dynamic injunctions have emerged as a crucial tool in combating online copyright piracy, particularly in the digital age where infringing content can spread rapidly across the internet. Dynamic injunctions arise when a continuing injunction is issued, the specific targets of which are not mentioned in the primary order but rather an emphasis is laid on the impugned subject matter and protected rights, thereby including in its ambit any potential infringements. This legal mechanism allows courts to issue injunctions that can adapt to the evolving nature of online infringement, ensuring that they remain effective in addressing the challenges posed by digital piracy.

In India, there is no law as such for the issuance of “dynamic injunctions,” but in order to meet pressing needs, the courts are granting such injunctions by exercising their inherent powers under Section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908. Parties can implead the mirrored websites under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC. In order to reduce the burden on courts, the joint registrar of the Delhi High Court has been delegated the power to adjudicate upon the issue of the additional website being added to the existing blocking order.

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation: Cinematograph (Amendment) Bill No. XlVI 2023
indicators.impact:
The lack of predictability around Section 31D and overly broad exceptions for certain uses have raised concerns about the strength of copyright protection in India. However, the Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023, was passed by the Indian Parliament on August 4, 2023. The amendment addresses various issues relating to film certification, including the issue of unauthorized recording and exhibition of firms and film privacy by transmission of unauthorized copies on the Internet and imposes strict penalties for privacy. These amendments are in harmony with the existing laws that addresses the issue of film privacy, viz The Copyright Act, 1957 and the Information Technology Act (IT) 2000. 

The new sections 6AA and 6AB of the Act prohibit carrying out or abetting (i) the unauthorized recording and (ii) the unauthorized exhibition of films. Attempting an unauthorized recording will also be an offense. An unauthorized recording means making or transmitting an infringing copy of a film at a licensed place for film exhibition without the owner’s authorization. An unauthorized exhibition means the public exhibition of an infringing copy of the film for profit: (i) at a location not licensed to exhibit films; or (ii) in a manner that infringes upon the copyright law. The above offenses will be punishable under the amended Section 7 of the Act with: (i) imprisonment between three months and three years; and (ii) a fine between three lakh rupees and 5% of the audited gross production cost.

The Copyright (Amendment) Act, 2012 has aligned Indian copyright law with the minimum standards set forth in the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT) and WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT), commonly referred to as the WIPO Internet Treaties. India acceded to these treaties in 2018. The enforcement of these provisions relies on rights owners seeking assistance from Indian courts to protect their rights against online piracy of their copyrighted content based on the relevant Copyright Act provisions.

Acceded to the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty in 2018 (Since September 2018, entry into froce since December 2018).

indicators.question_description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
indicators.source_legislation: Information Technology Act No.21 2000
indicators.impact:
Article 69 (Power to issue directions for interception or monitoring or decryption of any information through any computer resource) of the Information Technology Act states that if the Controller is satisfied that it is necessary or expedient so to do in the interest of the sovereignty or integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign Stales or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence, for reasons to be recorded in writing, by order, direct any agency of the Government to intercept any information transmitted through any computer resource. The subscriber or any person incharge of the computer resource shall, when called upon by any agency which has been directed under sub-section (1), extend all facilities and technical assistance to decrypt the information. The subscriber or any person who fails to assist the agency referred to in sub-section (2) shall be punished with an imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years. According to the regulation, information includes data, text, images, sound, voice, codes, computer programmes, software and databases or micro film or computer generated micro fiche.

Moreover, under Section 69 of the Information Technology Act, the government is empowered to control, supervise, or monitor any information in the interest of its sovereign functions or the security of the state. The government is allowed to keep an eye on any information flowing through its state or affecting its citizens. The Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Interception, Monitoring, and Decryption of Information) Rules, 2009 (IT Rules), have laid down the procedure for the above.

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.impact:
There is no stand-alone trade secret law in India at present. However, in India the trade secrets and confidential information are protected under the principles of equity, tort law, and common law principles of breach of confidence, etc. Indian courts have also applied Section 27 of the Contract Act, which deals with the restraint of trade, while addressing the issue of infringement of trade secrets by employees of companies as per the non-disclosure agreements.

As per the decision of Delhi High Court in 1995, a trade secret is defined as any information with commercial value, which is not available in the public domain and the disclosure of which would cause significant harm to the owner. Although there is no specific law or enactment on trade secrets in India, the Indian courts and tribunals have upheld protection of trade secrets under other laws such as contact law, copyright law, principles of equity and common law action of breach of confidence (which is basically breach of an obligation to keep a piece information secret). 

In addition to the above, the Information Technology law of 2000 also sets legal means of protection to confidential information in the form of the electronic records (Article 10 Power to make rules by Central Government in respect of digital signature). It is reported that India’s National Intellectual Property Rights Policy called for trade secrets to serve as an “important area of study for future policy development,” in 2016 but India appears to have not yet prioritized this work.

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.impact: According to a press release by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry posted on 21st july 2023, the IPR policy management framework launched in the IPR Policy 2016 covers 8 IPRs one of which is Trade Secret(s). According to the framework, trade secrets are covered in the common law approach covered through the Indian Penal Code, Contract Act, IP law and Copyright [Act].

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.source_legislation: Calcutta High Court in the Fairfest Media Ltd vs Lte Group Plc and Ors 2015
indicators.impact:
The ruling of the Calcutta High Court claims: whatever its source may be, a person who has obtained information in confidence is not allowed to use it as a springboard for activities harmful to the person who made the confidential communication. According to the High Court in the Fairfest Media Ltd vs Lte Group Plc and Ors, (2015), a party may not utilize information it obtained in confidence to harm the party it recieved said information from. The ruling in this case added to the already vast court upheld protections of trade secrets.

The "springboard doctrine" is a legal principle that prohibits improper use of trade secret information, such as theft or breach of confidence, to gain an unfair competitive advantage, even if the information is not protected by intellectual property rights. The springboard doctrine in India prohibits improper use of trade secret information to gain a competitive advantage over the rightful owner. Its application may vary depending on the specific facts and circumstances of each case. Courts will consider factors such as the nature of the information, how it was obtained, and the extent of the unfair advantage gained by the party using the information.

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.source_legislation: Amendment in Unified License relating to infrastructure sharing and Public Wi-Fi services
indicators.impact:
The amendment in License Conditions to allow active infrastructure sharing, inclding core Networks, between telecom operators, which will reduce costs and enhance roll out of services - Cellular Operators Association in India. Sharing of Active infrastructure amongst Service Providers based on the mutual agreements entered amongst them is permitted. Active infrastructure sharing will be limited to antenna, feeder cable, Node B, Radio Access Network (RAN) and transmission system only. This includes Internet Service. However, there are limitations on the sharing which are not stated within the amendment. The Licensee may share its own active and passive infrastructure for providing other services authorized to it under any other telecom license issued by Licensor

Moreover, as per Unified License, infrastructure sharing is enabled. The relevant clauses of Unified License are given below: 
33. Sharing of infrastructure:
33.1 Sharing of active/passive infrastructure shall be governed by the terms and conditions of respective service authorization and amendment/guidelines to be issued by the Licensor from time to time.
33.2 Sharing of Active infrastructure amongst Service Providers based on the mutual agreements entered amongst them is permitted. Active infrastructure sharing will be limited to antenna, feeder cable, Node B, Radio Access Network (RAN) and transmission system only. Sharing of infrastructure related to Wi-Fi equipment such as Wi-Fi router, Access Point etc. is allowed. Sharing of backhaul is also permitted.
33.3 The Licensee may share its own active and passive infrastructure for providing other services authorized to it under any other telecom license issued by Licensor. Other clauses related to infrastructure are mentioned in Chapters of other services in Unified license [Chapter VIII for Access Service: Clause no. 2.1(a)(ii), Chapter IX for Internet Service: Clause no. 2.1(i)].

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.impact:
In the newly implemented Telecommunications act in 2023, under provision 8 (2) (2) The Central Government may permit the sharing, trading, leasing and surrender of assigned spectrum, subject to the terms and conditions, including applicable fees or charges, as may be prescribed. This Act was also endorsed in the recommendations of The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) in the ‘Consultation Paper on Telecommunication Infrastructure Sharing, Spectrum Sharing and Spectrum Leasing’ released in 2024.

The consultation paper acknowledges that active and passive infrastructure sharing is permitted under Unified License but it doesnt provide specific provisions for passive sharing (Section 2.6)and there are ambiguities in the provisions related to sharing in different types of telecom service licenses/authorisations. During the consultations, stakeholders were of the consensus view that passive infrastructure should be shared across all types of telecom service licenses/authorisatons (Sec 2.21) and in section 2.23 the Authority concurs with this consensus, given a proper review of all types of service licenses. Final recommendation is in Section 2.34 (a) and (b).

indicators.impact:
In April 2018, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a one-page directive vide circular DPSS.CO.OD.No 2785/06.08.005/2017-18 stating that, within six months, all payment data held by payment companies should be held in local facilities. The Directive noted that this would help the RBI gain "unfettered supervisory access" to transaction data, which it needs to ensure proper monitoring.
 
Following a negative response from international payment companies such as MasterCard, Visa and American Express, the RBI has proposed (in "Frequently Asked Questions" of its website) to ease this restriction, so as to allow payment firms to store data offshore, as long as a copy was kept in India. The RBI has further clarified that for cross border transaction data consisting of a foreign component and domestic component, a copy of the domestic component may be stored abroad, if required. 

With respect to processing of payment transactions outside India, the RBI requires that the data must be stored only in India after processing and should be deleted from systems abroad and brought back to India no later than 24 hours after processing. Any subsequent activity such as settlement processing after payment processing done outside India, this must be undertaken on a real time basis pursuant to which the data must be stored only in India. 

The RBI has clarified that banks, especially foreign banks, can continue to store banking data abroad but in respect of domestic payment transactions, the data must be stored only in India.

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.source_legislation: Information Technology Act No.21 2000
indicators.impact: Section 79 (Network service providers not to be liable in certain cases) of the Information Technology Act provides intermediaries with qualified immunity for unlawful content, as long as they follow the prescribed due diligence requirements and do not conspire, abet or aid an unlawful act. However, the protection lapses if an intermediary with "actual knowledge" of any content used to commit an unlawful act, or on being notified of such content, fails to remove, or disable access to it.

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
indicators.impact:
Under Part II Due Diligence by Intermediaries and Grievance Redressal Mechanism, Rule 3 Due diligence by an intermediary, the Information Technology Rules provide that an intermediary, after receiving 'actual knowledge' through a court order or by being notified by a government agency must remove information that is prohibited by law in relation to the interest and sovereignty of India, the security of the state, friendly relations with foreign states, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence or information which violates any law which is in force. Such information has to be removed within a duration of thirty six hours from receipt of actual knowledge by the intermediary. 

Significant Social Media Intermediaries, defined as having more than 5 million registered Indian users, need to observe additional due diligence requirements to claim the immunity/safe harbour available. Rule 6 of the Information Technology Rules provides that even if a social media intermediary does not meet this user-threshold, the Central Government may still require an intermediary to meet these additional obligations if it believes that their operations create a material risk of harm to the sovereignty and integrity of India or to the security of the State. This discretion to the Central government may lead to the arbitrary imposition of additional obligations on certain intermediaries. The additional due diligence requirements include appointing certain personnel for compliance, enabling identification of the first originator of the information on its platform under certain conditions, and deploying technology-based measures on a best-effort basis to identify certain types of content.

indicators.impact:
India amended its IT law on to prohibit Facebook, Twitter and other social media firms from publishing, hosting or sharing false or misleading information about “any business” of the government and said the firms will be required to rely on New Delhi’s own fact-check unit to determine the authenticity of any claim.

Under part II "Due Diligence by Intermediaries and Grievance Redressal Mechanism" section 3(1) (b) point v states that deceives or misleads the addressee about the origin of the message or knowingly and intentionally communicates any misinformation or information which is patently false and untrue or misleading in nature [or is identified as fake or false by the fact check unit at the Press Information Bureau of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting or other agency authorised by the Central Government for fact checking or, in respect of any business of the Central Government, by its department in which such business is transacted under the rules of business made under clause (3) of article 77 of the Constitution]

Failure to comply with the rule, which also impacts internet service providers such as Jio and Airtel, risks the firms losing their safe harbor protections. The rule assigns a unit of the government arbitrary and over-broad powers to determine the authenticity of online content and bypasses the principles of natural justice. The notification of these amended rules cement the chilling effect on the fundamental right to speech and expression, particularly on news publishers, journalists, activists, etc. The fact check unit could effectively issue a takedown order to social media platforms and even other intermediaries across the internet stack, potentially bypassing the process statutorily prescribed under the Section 69A (Power to issue directions for blocking for public access of any information through any computer resource) of the IT Act, 2000.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.source_legislation: Government of India, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Foreign Direct Investment Policy Circular 2016, 2017, 2020
indicators.impact:
Under section 5.2.15.2 .3 (i) in all amendements India permits up to 100 percent Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in business-to-business (“marketplace-based”) electronic commerce, i.e. "providing of an information technology platform by an e-commerce entity on a digital & electronic network to act as a facilitator between buyer and seller." However, under (ii) India prohibits foreign investment in business-to-consumer (or “inventory-based”) electronic commerce, also defined as "e-commerce activity where inventory of goods and services is owned by e-commerce entity and is sold to the consumers directly". 

As per section 5.2.15.2.2 (iii) in all amendements , when a marketplace e-commerce entity exercises ownership or control over the inventory, the business is categorized into the inventory-based model. Additionally, India implemented regulations that expressly prohibit subsidiaries of foreign-owned marketplace-based electronic commerce sites from selling products on their parent companies’ sites. The rules also prohibit exclusivity arrangements by which electronic commerce retailers can offer a product on an exclusive basis. 

As per 2017 amendment, section 5.2.5.2, the only exceptions for FDI in inventory-based electronic commerce are for food-product retailing and single-brand retailers that meet certain conditions, including the operation of physical stores in India. Since 2020, under section 5.2.15.3 (g) of the 2020 amendment the FDI policy stipulates that retail trading through e-commerce can also be undertaken prior to opening physical stores, subject to the condition that the entity opens physical stores within two years from the date of start of online retail. Overall, it is reported that these narrow exceptions limit the ability of many electronic commerce service suppliers to serve the Indian market.

indicators.question_description: Low De Minimis
indicators.source_legislation: Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulation 2010
indicators.impact:
The Courier Imports and Exports Regulation distinguishes the values of "documents", "gifts", "low value dutiable consignment" and "samples" in Regulation 3. For "documents", they are not liable to any customs duty; for imported "gifts", they are bona fide articles for personal use not exceeding 10,000 rupees (INR 10,000) per consignment; for "low value dutiable consignment", invoice value does not exceed 1 lakh rupees (INR 100,000) (approximately USD 1,200 as of December 2023) and does not include documents, gifts and samples (which are below INR 10,000); for imported "samples", they are bona fide commercial samples and prototypes of goods supplied for free of charge with a value not exceeding INR 10,000 (approximately to USD 120 as of December 2023) per consignment. For the other goods the de minimis regime in place is 100 INR (Duty and GST exempt) and 1000 INR (GST exempt). 

The Central Government issued a notification exempting any acquisition, merger or amalgamation, if the enterprise being acquired, taken control of, merged or amalgamated has (i) assets less than INR 350 crore, or (ii) turnover less than INR 1000 crore. This exemption is valid for a period of 5 years from the date of publication of its notification in the official gazette. The de-minimis has been extended by Central Government for a further 5 year period vide notification dated 16th March 2022.

indicators.source_legislation: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020
indicators.impact: In July, 2020, the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 were introduced which apply to all goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic network including digital products, all models of e-commerce and all e-commerce retail. The Rules apply to any Indian entity engaging in e-commerce abroad or any foreign entity offering goods and services to Indian consumers over e-commerce platforms. The Rules introduce several requirements such as displaying requirements for name and details of sellers, details of return, refund, exchange, warranty and guarantee etc. The Rules require sellers on the platform to provide an undertaking affirming the accuracy of descriptions, images and other content of the goods or services on the platform, including that they correspond directly with the appearance, nature, quality and purpose. No seller can falsely represent itself as a consumer and post reviews about goods or services or misrepresent the quality of the features of goods.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: The Consumer Protection Act No. 35 2019
indicators.impact: This Act includes provisions specifically designed to protect consumers engaging in online transactions. It defines e-commerce entities, establishes liability for misleading advertisements, and sets out mechanisms for consumer grievance redressal. One important feature introduced by this act is the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), which has the power to take action against unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements online.

indicators.question_description:
Screening of investment and acquisitions
Exception: Anti-trust measures related to M&A are not considered a restriction, unless discriminatory.
indicators.source_legislation:
Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act (Act No. 228 of 1949);

Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act, Foreign Investment Screening System, Annual Report (FY2023)
indicators.impact:
Japan's inward direct investment screening system started with the Foreign Capital Act enacted in 1950 as a special law for the then (Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act) FEFTA. Please refer to page 7 of the FEFTA Foreign Investment Screening System Annual Report (FY2023). 

Under the FEFTA, the Paragraphs (3) through (5), Article 27 of FEFTA stipulate a series of process before the ministries finally determine to issue the orders for modification or discontinuance of inward direct investments. Please refer to the relevant paragraphs of FEFTA. Specifically, Article 27, Paragraph (3), (i) states that the Minister of Finance of Japan is responsible for evaluating the impact of an investment on the preservation of production foundations and technologies within specific business sectors. If the investment poses (a) a threat to national security, disrupts the maintenance of public order, or hinders public safety, the Minister has the authority to reject the foreign investment, and (b) has Significant adverse effect to the Japanese economy.

Certain business sectors requiring prior notification of inward direct investment are defined as ‘designated business sectors’, including business sectors that could significantly undermine national security, which are classified as ‘core business sectors’. Core business sectors, a type of business involving inward direct investments that are likely to undermine Japan’s national security, includes semi-conductors; certain cybersecurity-related business (such as network security monitoring, service providers of the programmes designed for critical infrastructures); and certain infrastructure-related business (such as electricity, gas, telecommunications, water supply, railway and oil).

Foreign investors who plan to acquire 1% or more of stocks and shares of Japanese companies engaging in designated business sectors are required to submit prior notifications for screening from the viewpoints of Japan’s national security and other objectives of FEFTA. (When digital trade in which investee Japanese companies engage fall into the designated business sectors, foreign investors are required to submit the prior notifications.) The Ministry of Finance and other ministries responsible for relevant business sectors screen the notifications to see if such investments impair Japan’s national security or other objectives under FEFTA. If the screening finds it does, the authorities may recommend or order the modification or discontinuance of the investments after hearing opinions from the Council on Customs, Tariff, Foreign Exchange and Other Transactions. If the screening finds it doesn’t, foreign investors are allowed to undertake investments after screening period.

For business in core business sectors, foreign investors cannot attend meetings of the target company’s board of directors or other committees that make important decisions on such business. Moreover, foreign investors cannot, by themselves or through their designated person, make proposals, in writing, to (a) the target company’s board of directors or other committees that make important decisions or (b) the members of such board or committees, requiring responses or actions by certain deadlines.

indicators.question_description: Patent application issues
indicators.source_legislation: Patent Act (Act No. 121 of 1959)
indicators.impact:
In principle, under Article 8 of the Patent Act, most all procedures cannot be conducted by non-residents directly with Japan Patent Office but have to be conducted by an appointed representative residing or domiciled in Japan. However, under Article 184-11(1) of the Patent Act, there is an exception for Form 53, and non-residents can submit it directly, without the need of appointing a representative in Japan.

Article 184-11 (Special provisions concerning patent administrators for overseas residents)
(1) Notwithstanding Article 8(1), an applicant of an international patent application who is an overseas resident may, until the National Processing Standard Time, undertake procedures without being represented by a patent administrator.
(2) The person prescribed in the preceding paragraph shall appoint a patent administrator and notify the Commissioner of the Patent Office thereof on or after the National Processing Standard Time, but not later than the time limit as provided in Ordinance of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.
(3) Where no appointment of a patent administrator has been notified within the time limit as provided in the preceding paragraph, the international patent application shall be deemed to have been withdrawn.
