Since July 2004, last amended in August 2024 ;

Since December 2020, last amended in September 2024

indicators.question_description: Deviation from international encryption standards (ISO, IEC, ITU, FIPS, AES, TDES, and ECC)
indicators.source_legislation:
Law No. 567-V on Communications, 2004 (Қазақстан Республикасының 2004 жылғы 5 шілдедегі N 567 Заңы) ; 

Order No. 595/NK of the Minister of Digital Development, Innovation and Aerospace Industry, 2023 (Қазақстан Республикасының Цифрлық даму, инновациялар және аэроғарыш өнеркәсібі министрінің 2023 жылғы 1 желтоқсандағы № 595/НҚ бұйрығы. Қазақстан Республикасының Әділет министрлігінде 2023 жылғы 6 желтоқсанда № 33727 болып тіркелді)
indicators.impact:
Article 26.3(1) of the law stipulates that international operators shall carry out traffic transmission using the protocols, supporting encryption with the use of a security certificate. Security certificate is a set of electronic digital characters used to route traffic containing protocols that support encryption determined by the National Security Committee of the Republic of Kazakhstan. 

In addition, Article 23(2) and 23(3) state that the procedure for organization of encrypted work in the authorized state bodies, military management bodies, national security and internal affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan and the procedure for ensuring governmental communication shall be developed by the Committee for national security of the Republic of Kazakhstan and determined by the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan.


The ST RK GOST R 34.10-2015 standard was officially adopted in Kazakhstan on December 1, 2023, as per Order No. 595/НҚ issued by the acting Minister of Investment and Development of the Republic of Kazakhstan. This order amended the existing regulations concerning the issuance, storage, and revocation of registration certificates, as well as the verification of the ownership and validity of electronic digital signature (EDS) public keys by the National Certification Authority (NCA) of Kazakhstan. The transition to this cryptographic standard was implemented on April 30, 2024, with the NCA RK commencing the issuance of EDS keys based on the ST RK GOST R 34.10-2015 algorithm from that date.

ST RK GOST R 34.10-2015 is a Kazakh adaptation of the Russian cryptographic standard GOST R 34.10-2012, which defines a digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curve cryptography and has been incorporated into the ISO/IEC 14888-3 standard.

indicators.impact:
According to Article 5(7), payment service providers adhere to certain security measures set by the National Bank of Kazakhstan. 

According to the Resolution of the Board of the National Bank of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 133 on Approval of the Program of National Payment System Development in the Republic of Kazakhstan until the Year 2025, payment services must comply with measures aimed at enhancing security and aligning with international standards. The adoption of the ISO 20022 standard is central to this initiative, as it promotes more efficient payment processing, improved security, and both domestic and international interoperability. Overseen by SWIFT, ISO 20022 is increasingly adopted by leading financial institutions worldwide, with European and American banks implementing it by 2022. This global shift is further supported by major international systems such as CLS and Euroclear, which encourage their participants to adopt ISO 20022 for streamlined, standardized communication. For Kazakhstan, implementing ISO 20022 in payment services will simplify interactions between national and international systems, contributing to a secure, efficient, and globally connected payment environment.

Additional requirements include operational rules approved by the organization's governing body, which must comply with regulations from the National Bank. The National Bank reviews these applications within ten working days and either assigns a registration number or issues a refusal with reasons. Registered payment organizations must display their registration number in public communications and notify the National Bank of any subsequent changes in their foundational documents within ten calendar days. Furthermore, foreign entities from non-compliant jurisdictions on the FATF list are prohibited from holding stakes in Kazakhstani payment organizations.

According to Article 44 of the Law on Payments and payment systems, the maximum amount of one operation performed by an unidentified owner of electronic money - an individual, should not exceed an amount equal to fifty times the size of the monthly calculation index established for the corresponding financial year by the law on the republican budget. Additionnally, the maximum amount of one operation performed by a simplified identified owner of electronic money - an individual, should not exceed an amount equal to one hundred times the monthly calculation index established for the corresponding financial year by the law on the republican budget. Finally, the maximum amount of one transaction performed by the owner of electronic money - an individual entrepreneur or a legal entity, should not exceed an amount equal to a thousand times the monthly calculation index established for the corresponding financial year by the law on the republican budget.

According to Article 9(4) of the Law on the Republican Budget of 204-2026, the Install from January 1, 2024, the monthly calculation index corresponds to 3.692 tenge (USD 7.55).

indicators.question_description: Low De Minimis
indicators.source_legislation:
Decision of the Eurasian Economic Commission No. 107 on the Categories of Goods for Personal Use and Methods of their Import, including Value, Weight, and Quantity Import Standards (О категориях товаров для личного пользования и способах их ввоза, включая стандарты по стоимости, весу и количеству импортируемых товаров);

Decision of the Eurasian Economic Commission No. 87 on the Value and Weight Limits for Goods Imported via International Mail for Personal Use (О пределах стоимости и веса товаров, ввозимых для личного пользования посредством международной почты)
indicators.impact:
The de minimis thresholds for duty-free importation of personal use goods into Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states have evolved over time and currently depend on the mode of transport and import date. The foundational framework was established by Decision No. 107 of 2017 Appendix 1, which first set the categories of goods for personal use and initial value, weight, and quantity standards. 

On October 22, 2024, the EEC Council Decision No. 87 dated October 18, 2024, introduced changes to the value, weight, and/or quantity norms within which goods for personal use are imported into the customs territory of the EAEU without payment of customs duties and taxes, as established by EEC Council Decision No. 107 dated December 20, 2017. The new version clarifies the value, weight, and/or quantity norms for the importation of goods for personal use sent by international postal shipments. These are as follows:
- For goods — the value does not exceed the equivalent of 200 euros, and the gross weight does not exceed 31 kg;
- For tobacco; tobacco products; vapes — 200 cigarettes, or 50 cigars (cigarillos), or 200 heated tobacco products (“sticks”), or 250 grams of tobacco, or assorted products with a total weight of no more than 250 grams.

Therefore, as of 2025, the EAEU maintains a de minimis threshold of €200 (approximately USD 230) and 31 kg for goods imported for personal use via international mail.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Law No.274-IV on Protection of Consumer Rights, 2010 (Қазақстан Республикасының 2010 жылғы 4 мамырдағы № 274-IV Заңы)
indicators.impact:
Articles 33-1 and 33-2 of the Law No.274-IV on protection of consumer rights establish an online consumer protection legal framework.

Precisely, Article 33-1 obligates electronic trading platforms to implement internal procedures that prevent false information and illegal trade, ensuring consumer rights are protected. Additionally, it mandates that software and hardware supporting e-commerce must operate through secure communication links, which further safeguards consumers during online transactions​. 

Futhermore, Article 33-2 requires that sellers (manufacturers or service providers) include contact details of authorized bodies responsible for pre-trial consumer dispute settlements, as well as information on the consumer’s right to approach these bodies or the courts for dispute resolution. This information must be made easily accessible through the e-commerce platform, ensuring consumers are well informed about their rights and available recourse​.

There are no anti-dumping, countervailing duty or safeguard measures against ICT products. Although Cambodia currently does not engage in any form of anti-dumping practices on ICT products, in October 2017, the National Assembly adopted the Law on Trade Remedies which would allow Cambodia to raise tariffs or restrict imports to counteract dumping. In July 2018, Cambodia notified the Law to the WTO.

Law on Trade Remedies 2017 is Cambodia's main regulatory framework for trade defense measures. It provides provisions for implementing anti-dumping, countervailing, and safeguard measures to protect domestic industries from unfair trade practices. The law outlines procedures for investigating and imposing duties to counteract the negative effects of dumping and subsidized imports.

indicators.impact:
Article 11 of the Amended Law on Public Procurement 2023 states that publicly competitive bidding is a procurement method for selecting suppliers, contractors, or service providers open to all local and international bidders. Publicly competitive bidding is a highly transparent procurement method that will be promoted in public procurement. Publicly competitive bidding methods include:
i). International Competitive Bidding: This method is used for procurement projects with large amounts of money and / or high technicality.
ii). Local Competitive Bidding: This method is used in cases where there is sufficient local production, service or construction capacity

Additionally, Article 24 on consulting services specifies that expressions of interest should be sought broadly, inviting both domestic and international consulting firms to participate.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Public Procurement 2012
indicators.impact:
According to Article 25 and 27 of the Law on Public Procurement, the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) requires all companies, contractors, and consultants that want to join any bidding for public procurement shall register with MEF. It means that all bidders have to go through the screening process by the MEF. It has been reported that the majority of foreign companies will not join the bidding because the process for awarding government contracts is not transparent and susceptible to corruption.

'Bidders shall register their types and levels of classification at the Ministry of Economy and Finance to be eligible to participate in public procurement. The Ministry of Economy and Finance shall classify the types and levels of bidders in accordance to their capacities to ensure the implementation of contracts.' (Article 27)

Prequalification of bidders shall be made by the Procuring Entity and is only for projects with complex technical specifications. The procedures for prequalification of bidders shall be determined by a Prakas of the Minister of MEF. (Article 28)

According to Article 11, International Competitive Bidding is the method used for ' projects with large amounts of money and / or high technicality' so it could be deemed that this additional requirement of registration that applies for technical projects is addressed to international bidders, rather than domestic. 

Moreover, Minister of Interior Sar Sokha recently highlighted concerns about rising complaints of fraud and corruption in Cambodia's bidding processes, especially in local projects funded by communes. He urged local authorities to tackle these issues, aligning with research that identifies significant corruption risks in public procurement across various levels in Cambodia. This call for action suggests increased scrutiny on integrity and transparency in local bidding processes, which may impact foreign and local bidders alike.

Article 24 of the Law of Investment (2021) states that "Digital Industries are entitled to investment incentives." In addition, these industries are not included in the Negative list and are open to 100% FDI. 

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, the legal framework in Cambodia establishes an open and liberal foreign investment regime with broad investment guarantees and places very few restrictions on the level of foreign participation in investments. Aside from the specific constitutional restrictions on land ownership, foreign investors can own up to 100% shares of their companies.

This is confirmed by the Law on Invesment, which states: Foreign investors shall not be subject to any discrimination on the basis of foreign nationality, except for land ownership as stipulated in the Constitution of the Kingdom of Cambodia and any other regulations in force (Artcle 15).

indicators.question_description: Joint venture requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Law on the General Statute of Public Enterprise 1996
indicators.impact:
Article 3 of the Law on Public Enterprise stipulates that public enterprise sector consists of (i) public establishments with economic characteristics, (ii) state companies; and (iii) joint ventures in which the State directly or indirectly hold more than 51% of the capital or the right to vote. Specifically, under Article 38, if the state holds more than 51% of the capital or voting rights, the venture is considered a public enterprise (Article 38). 

Accordingly, foreigners can participate in a public enterprise in the form of a joint venture in which the government of Cambodia directly or indirectly holds more than 51% of the capital or the right to vote.

indicators.question_description: Joint venture requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Commercial Enterprise (“LCE”) 2005
indicators.impact:
The Law on Commercial Enterprises (LCE) of Cambodia does not require foreign investors to enter the market through joint ventures in most sectors. Foreigners can fully own companies without needing a local partner. However, specific restrictions apply in the case of land ownership, where foreigners can only own up to 49% in joint ventures holding land.

This limitation on landholding is referenced under Article 101 of the LCE, which stipulates that a company must have more than 51% Cambodian ownership to be classified as having Cambodian nationality and thus be permitted to own land directly​.

Moreover, the Law on Commercial Enterprises (LCE) of Cambodia stipulates in Article 118 that any legally competent natural person over the age of 18 may serve as a director, without requiring specific nationality or residency status. This provision allows both Cambodian and foreign nationals to serve on the boards of Cambodian companies without additional nationality or residency prerequisites​.

indicators.question_description:
Screening of investment and acquisitions
Exception: Anti-trust measures related to M&A are not considered a restriction, unless discriminatory.
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Investment 2021
indicators.impact:
Chapter 4 of the Law on Commercial Enterprises covers the registration and implementation procedures for Qualified Investment Projects (QIPs), Expanded Qualified Investment Projects (EQIPs), and Guaranteed Investment Projects (GIPs). According to Article 10, individuals or entities interested in implementing these projects must submit a written application to the Council for the Development of Cambodia (CDC) or a Municipal-Provincial Investment Sub-Committee, with options for digital submission. Article 11 mandates that applications be accompanied by specific information detailed in a Sub-Decree. Upon receipt, as stated in Article 12, the CDC reviews the application using a One-Stop Service mechanism, coordinating with relevant ministries. If a project is not listed on the Negative List, a Registration Certificate is issued within 20 working days, featuring a barcode or QR code containing essential project data, streamlining subsequent registrations and compliance checks.

Once a Registration Certificate is obtained, Article 13 allows for automatic project implementation but requires additional permits as stipulated by law. All registered projects are subject to ongoing monitoring and inspections through the One-Stop Service mechanism, and project implementers must submit regular progress reports based on CDC guidelines. Although these reports are mandatory, they do not exempt projects from potential on-site inspections if deemed necessary by the CDC or in response to third-party complaints. Article 14 further states that specific procedures for project registration with Municipal-Provincial Investment Sub-Committees will be outlined in a separate Sub-Decree.

indicators.question_description: Commercial presence requirements to offer cross-border services in sectors relevant to digital trade
indicators.source_legislation:
E-commerce Law 2019;

Sub-Decree No.134 on Classification, Formalities and Procedures on Granting of Permit or License to Intermediary and E-commerce Service Provider and Exemptions 2020
indicators.impact:
As per the Sub-Decree, new licensing requirement also applies to offshore e-commerce operations without local presence or permanent establishment in Cambodia. A licence for Intermediaries and Online Services Providers via Electronic Platform will be provided to foreign companies after providing a document informing the name, registered address and contact number/email address of the business entity in Cambodia.
 
In particular, an e-commerce license is required for legal persons and branches of foreign companies carrying out the following activities: e-commerce web services, e-commerce platform services, online market services, online auction website services, and other similar services provided through software or smart devices for the promotion of e-commerce (Article 7). An e-commerce permit is required for natural persons and sole proprietors that operate a business via electronic system in Cambodia, including those who conduct business via social media and electronic system to supply or sell/purchase goods and services (Article 6). According to Articles. 6 and 7 of Sub-Decree No. 134, for issuance of an e-commerce license or permit, business and tax registration is required. 

Moreover, under Article 29 of the e-Commerce Law, minimum information is required such as the name, registered address and contact number/email address of the business entity in Cambodia. If it is a legal entity or foreign branch acting as an intermediary, it must enter into a contract with the business service providers regarding the requirement to provide minimum information.

indicators.question_description: Commercial presence requirements to offer cross-border services in sectors relevant to digital trade
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Commercial Enterprise (“LCE”) 2005
indicators.impact:
The Law on Commercial Enterprises (LCE) of Cambodia requires foreign businesses conducting ongoing commercial activities to establish a local presence through registration as a branch, subsidiary, or representative office. Specifically, Article 271 outlines that foreign businesses will be considered as "doing business" if they engage in activities such as renting space for manufacturing or services, employing staff for more than a month, or performing any act permitted by law to foreign entities. These activities necessitate establishing a branch or subsidiary, which must be registered with the Ministry of Commerce (MoC)​.

The structure required varies by the type of operations. Representative Offices are limited to promotional activities and cannot engage in direct commercial transactions. Branches, in contrast, can carry out business activities, including regular buying and selling, manufacturing, and other commercial operations, while subsidiaries—local entities with separate legal personalities—can operate similarly to local companies in most sectors.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation:
Law on the Patents, Utility Model Certificates and Industrial Designs 2003; 

Code of Civil Procedure of Cambodia 2006
indicators.impact:
The owner of the patent shall have the right (...) to institute court proceedings against any person who infringes the patent by performing, without his agreement, any of the acts referred in Article 42 of this Law or who performs acts which make it
likely that infringement will occur (Article 43). The owner of an industrial design shall have the right to institute Competent Court proceedings against any person who infringes his industrial design by performing, without the agreement, any of the acts referred to in Article 106 of this Law or who performs acts which make it likely that infringement will occur (Article 108).

IPR holders that suffer damage from an infringement are entitled to file civil claims for damages and specific relief from the infringer. The Cambodian Civil Code and the Civil Procedure Code provide procedures for civil remedies and provisional measures against IPR infringements in Cambodia. Civil proceedings begin with a statement of claims (lawsuit), which is to be filed with the competent court in Cambodia. Usually, the residence/location of the defendant will establish the jurisdiction.

The Cambodian Laws empowers its court to issue injunctions to halt infringement or impending infringement of patents, but leaves the criteria for obtaining injunctions undefined. However, under Cambodia’s Civil Procedure Code, the court can grant preliminary/temporary relief, pending a final judgment, when the plaintiff establishes a strong prima facie case on the merits, as well as a compelling argument that if the defendant is permitted to continue infringing the plaintiff’s design during the pendency of the action, it will be unable to recover damages. 

The Civil Code provides IP rights holders with civil and administrative procedures to address infringements, including remedies for enforcing specific obligations and seeking damages. According to Article 396 of the Cambodian Civil Code, an IP rights holder can request that the court enforce specific performance if the infringer fails to fulfill legal obligations, unless the nature of the obligation prevents this. Additionally, Articles 398 and 399 allow IP owners to claim damages if they suffer harm due to an infringement, provided the infringement was not caused by unavoidable circumstances. Here, compensation is calculated based on the damages sustained from the infringement.

The Civil Code also permits provisional measures to secure IP rights before a final judgment is issued. Article 545 allows for provisional attachment when there’s a risk that enforcing a claim may become difficult. This measure restricts the infringer’s access to certain assets, preventing their transfer or concealment. Further, Article 548 grants courts the authority to issue a provisional disposition over disputed assets, which may limit any alterations to the IP or infringing goods. As specified in Article 549, provisional disposition can involve restraining the infringer from taking specific actions or appointing a custodian to oversee the property at issue. If the infringer disputes these provisional measures, Article 550 allows them to file a motion of objection, which the court may use to reassess or modify the relief granted.

For enforcement, the Civil Code outlines procedures to execute provisional attachments against infringers’ assets to secure the IP holder’s claims effectively. Articles 567 and 568 detail the execution process against various types of assets, such as immovable property or vessels, thereby allowing IP holders to secure financial claims against substantial assets of the infringer.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Law on the Patents, Utility Model Certificates and Industrial Designs 2003
indicators.impact:
Article 5 of the Law states that an invention is patentable if it is new; involves an inventive step; and is industrially applicable. Article 8 of the Law states that an invention shall be considered industrially applicable if it can be made or used in any kind of industry. "Industry" shall be understood in its broadest sense. However, Article 9 of the Law states that inventions the commercial exploitation of which would be contrary to public order or morality shall not be patentable. 

In addition, Article 47 states that that the Cambodian Government has the right to exploit a patented invention itself, or allow third parties to do so, for the purpose of promoting ‘public interests’ including national defence, nutrition, health and development.This authorized exploitation must strictly adhere to the purpose defined by the Minister’s authorization and includes a requirement for adequate remuneration to the patent owner, based on the economic value of the government’s intervention. Importantly, the decision to allow such exploitation is made only after the patent owner and any interested parties have been given an opportunity to be heard.

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Copyright and Related Rights 2003
indicators.impact:
Article 62 addresses circumvention by prohibiting the production or sale of devices designed to bypass technological protection measures (TPMs). These TPMs include any technology, such as encryption, access control, or copy prevention, that rights holders use to safeguard their works from unauthorized digital access or duplication.
By making it illegal to create, distribute, or use circumvention tools, Article 62 supports DRM (Digital Rights Management) systems used widely on digital content platforms to prevent unauthorized copying, limit access to subscribed or purchased content, and control how content can be used or shared. 

Article 62 also prohibits the removal or alteration of rights management information (RMI), which includes details about the author, copyright holder, licensing terms, or usage conditions that are typically embedded in digital content files. RMI allows authors and copyright holders to maintain traceability and enforceability of their rights across digital platforms, as it informs users about the legal restrictions and ownership details of a digital work.
Unauthorized modification or removal of this information can lead to copyright infringement by concealing ownership or licensing terms. Protecting RMI ensures that copyright holders can better monitor and claim their rights, even when content is shared or distributed online.

Articles 57 and 58 empower rights holders to seek judicial remedies, including injunctions, damages, and orders for the confiscation or destruction of infringing materials. These articles allow copyright holders to pursue compensation for unauthorized use and have infringing copies removed from circulation, whether online or offline.

Customs enforcement (Article 63) also allows rights holders to request border control measures to prevent infringing goods, including pirated digital media on physical storage devices, from entering or leaving Cambodia. This can help limit the physical import or export of unauthorized reproductions and protect copyright on a broader scale.

Article 59 further allows for provisional measures to preserve evidence, which is particularly useful in the digital realm where infringement can be transient. Courts may order the seizure of digital storage devices or temporary restrictions on online access to prevent the destruction of evidence.

indicators.question_description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
indicators.source_legislation: TRIPS Agreement (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) 1994
indicators.impact:
Cambodia has not yet adopted a specific law on trade secrets. However, a draft Law on Trade Secrets and Undisclosed Information is currently being discussed. Up to now, there is no guarantee that the bidder's trade secret is protected. 

In Cambodia, there is no regulation that mandates the disclosure of trade secrets. Cambodian law protects trade secrets as confidential business information, provided reasonable efforts are made to maintain their secrecy. The Law on Marks, Trade Names, and Acts of Unfair Competition specifically aims to safeguard trade secrets by prohibiting unauthorized disclosure or use of confidential information.

The TRIPS Agreement, which Cambodia adheres to as a WTO member, also emphasizes protection for trade secrets and does not require their disclosure. This aligns with the principle that trade secrets should remain protected to ensure fair competition, as long as they are legally obtained and kept confidential.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since 1994, last amended in November 2011;

Last reviewed in November 2024

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.impact:
A specific law on trade secrets has yet to be adopted in Cambodia. However, a draft law is currently being negotiated. However, trade secrets may be protected under other laws. For example, to maintain information in employment or other contractual relationships, a non-disclosure agreement may be used and enforced pursuant to the Contract Law of 1998.

Cambodia does not yet have a specific law dedicated to trade secrets, however a draft law is under review. In the meantime, multiple existing laws impose confidentiality obligations and penalties for unauthorized disclosures. Non-disclosure agreements are frequently used to protect confidential information shared with employees or contractors, functioning as enforceable contracts under the Civil Code (2006). The Law on Commercial Enterprises (2005) also prohibits the unauthorized release of a company's financial statements and mandates that the Ministry of Commerce maintain confidentiality over most business documents. Additionally, the Law on Audit (2000) establishes a duty of confidentiality for government auditors.

Cambodia’s Law Concerning Marks, Trade Names, and Acts of Unfair Competition (2002) further supports the protection of trade secrets by defining unfair competition practices, including the misappropriation of trade secrets, which is viewed as contrary to honest practices. Article 23 of this law identifies acts of unfair competition as those intended to create confusion with a competitor’s establishment, discredit their goods or services, or mislead the public about a product’s characteristics or origins. Additional legal provisions, such as Article 221 of the Law on Negotiable Instruments and Payment Transactions, Article 47 of the Law on Banking and Financial Institutions, Articles 10 to 15 of the Civil Code, Article 308 of the Criminal Code, and Article 58 of the Law on the Bar, also emphasize confidentiality protections and prohibit the unauthorized divulgence of commercially sensitive information.

Moreover, as a member of the Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights, the regulations contained there also apply to Cambodia, who signed it in 2011. Article 39 of the TRIPS Agreement requires member countries to protect undisclosed information, preventing it from being disclosed, acquired, or used by others without consent if it has commercial value and reasonable efforts have been made to keep it secret.

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Telecommunications 2015
indicators.impact:
As per Article 31, and Article 32 of the Law of Telecommunications, "To ensure the efficiency of interconnection and administration of networks, physical infrastructures and the competition in the telecommunications sector, the telecommunications operators [must] Provide the utilization of shared infrastructures and networks or equipment with the telecommunications operators." As per the ITU (2022) database, Passive sharing is mandated and is effective in both the mobile and fixed sectors. 

Article 31 centers on the importance of network interconnection, mandating that telecommunications operators establish interoperable connections to enable seamless communication across different service providers. The article ensures that shared infrastructure use adheres to standards of technical quality and service, thus preventing operators from degrading quality to restrict competition. In emphasizing non-discriminatory access, Article 31 also addresses potential monopolistic behavior by barring practices such as creating artificial barriers to network access or employing technical measures to limit interconnectivity. Additionally, Article 31 requires operators to draft formal interconnection agreements and report them to the Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (TRC) within a set timeframe, empowering the TRC to monitor and regulate the fairness of these arrangements effectively.

Article 32 expands on the concept of network sharing by specifically focusing on the sharing of physical infrastructure, such as towers and ducts. While Article 31 speaks to network interconnectivity, Article 32 targets the actual physical facilities necessary for telecommunications. It mandates that operators grant access to these physical resources to other operators, thereby encouraging cost savings and resource efficiency across the industry.

Article 33 plays a complementary role, tasking the TRC with the maintenance of a centralized registry of all interconnection and infrastructure-sharing agreements. This registry promotes transparency, as it holds operators accountable and enables regulatory oversight of compliance with sharing obligations. 

Article 34 extends the scope of infrastructure sharing to a broader framework, where the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPTC) is authorized to coordinate telecommunications infrastructure planning with other national infrastructure sectors, including energy, water, and waste management. 

Finally, Article 36 allows the TRC to set further requirements for national and international infrastructure sharing.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in telecom sector
indicators.impact:
Article 63 of the Law on Telecommunications mandates that telecommunications operators must secure prior approval from the Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (TRC) before proceeding with any merger, acquisition, or alteration in shareholdings. This regulatory step ensures that changes in ownership, including potential increases in foreign equity, align with national interests and comply with the law’s broader objectives of safeguarding sovereignty and strategic control over the telecom sector. 

Sub Decree No.111 ANK/BK stipulates that Cambodia permits 100 percent foreign ownership in the telecommunication sector. However, Article 3 of Law on Public Enterprise states that the Cambodian government must directly or indirectly hold more than 51% of the capital or the right to vote in state-owned enterprises. While this provision is more applicable to public enterprises rather than private sector entities, it implies that should any telecommunications entity be designated as a public enterprise, state control would be required. Currently, Telecom Cambodia, a significant player in the sector, is wholly state-owned and serves as a public enterprise, reflecting state priority in retaining ownership of certain telecom infrastructure​.

Other telecom companies operating in Cambodia include: 
Metfone – Operated by Viettel, a Vietnamese military-owned company, Metfone is a private company in Cambodia but with foreign state ownership through its parent company. It is one of the largest providers of mobile and internet services, with a broad customer base and a significant infrastructure footprint.

Smart Axiata – Smart is a private company majority-owned by Axiata Group Berhad, a Malaysian multinational telecom corporation. It is one of the leading mobile service providers in Cambodia, known for its strong presence in mobile, data, and digital services.

Cellcard (CamGSM) – A fully private company, Cellcard is part of the Royal Group, a major Cambodian conglomerate. It is one of the oldest telecom operators in Cambodia.

Seatel – Initially established with Chinese investment, Seatel is a private company that provides mobile and internet services with a focus on high-speed data.

Since most of them are private and even come from foreign investments, it shall not be considered that Article 3 of the Law on Public Enterprise has a widespread effect. It can be deemed that foreign equity doesn't have limits.

indicators.question_description: Lack of functional/accounting separation
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Telecommunications 2015
indicators.impact:
Under the Telecommunications Act, competition in the telecom market is regulated under Chapter 10. TRC has authority to monitor, oversee and evaluate lawful and fair competition in the telecommunications market and report to MPTC for additional provisions (Article 60). 

According to Article 12, telecom operators must submit cost-based management information and financial reports audited by an independent auditor, which must be recognized by the Ministry of Economy and Finance. Article 55 also references the need for “cost base” financial reporting, which TRC and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPTC) rely on for setting service tariffs and assessing competition-related compliance. Additionally, Article 58 mandates that service tariffs must not fall below the calculated cost base, with TRC tasked to oversee this. 

However, there is no requirement for functional or accounting separation for operators with significant market power.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.source_legislation:
Law on Telecommunications, 2015; 

Sub-Decree on Mechanism for Implementation of Universal Service Obligation Program 2020
indicators.impact:
Telecom operators must obtain a permit, certificate, or license from the Telecommunications Regulator of Cambodia (TRC). Article 14 specifies that no person may conduct telecom operations without such authorization. Licensing is categorized based on the type of telecom activity, including:
- Permits for activities such as importing, distributing, and selling telecom equipment (Article 15).
- Certificates for certain authorized agents or certified types of equipment (Article 16).
- Licenses for building and operating telecom infrastructure, networks, and providing telecom services (Article 17)​. 

Applicants must follow a detailed application process, supplying required information and documentation to TRC. TRC may request further details to ensure compliance and may reject applications if requirements are unmet (Articles 19-20). Upon approval, operators are granted the license or permit with specific conditions that must be observed throughout the validity of the license (Article 20)​ 

Article 42 imposes a requirement for all licensed telecom operators to contribute 2% of their gross revenue annually to the Universal Service Obligation (USO) fund, which supports telecom access in rural and underserved areas. This requirement indirectly serves as a financial obligation, impacting the operational budget of telecom companies.Article 38 assigns the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPTC) the responsibility of setting criteria for service quality, which telecom companies are expected to meet. 

The Law on Telecommunications (2015) outlines requirements for licensing and compliance, but it does not impose strict conditions such as minimum capital requirements, explicit mandatory performance standards, or discriminatory provisions against foreign providers. Licensing focuses on regulatory compliance, service quality, and contributions to the Universal Service Obligation fund, but it generally allows for broad participation by both domestic and foreign entities without stringent entry barriers.

indicators.question_description: Not in the WTO Telecom Reference Paper
indicators.source_legislation: WTO Telecom Reference Paper
indicators.impact: Cambodia has attached the WTO Telecom Reference Paper to its schedule of commitments in October 2005.

indicators.question_description: Lack of independent telecom authority
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Telecommunications 2015
indicators.impact: Article 10 of the Law on Telecommunications states that "Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (TRC) has autonomy to perform its administrative, regulatory and financial duties and functions and is independently from telecommunications operators and persons involved with the telecommunication sector. TRC has self-budget by considering as annex of MPTC’s budget." This ensures that Cambodia has an independent telecommunications authority, the Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (TRC).

indicators.question_description:
Ban and local processing requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation:
Sub-Decree No.252 on the Management, Use, and Protection of Personal Identification Data 2021;

Draft Law on Personal Data Protection
indicators.impact: Cambodia does not currently have laws or regulations on domestic data storage or localization requirements. However, Articles 22 and 24 of the Draft Law on Personal Data Protection of the Kingdom of Cambodia contains a complete prohibition on all personal data transfers out of Cambodia. The original text of the law states that "a data controller may not transfer personal data to any country or territory outside the Kingdom of Cambodia unless authorized under this law and relevant legal instruments. Conditions, formalities, and procedures for transferring personal data outside the Kingdom of Cambodia shall be determined by prakas issued by the Minister of MPTC." This law has not come into force yet.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since December 2021;

Last reviewed in November 2024

indicators.question_description:
Local storage requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation:
Sub-Decree No.252 on the Management, Use, and Protection of Personal Identification Data 2021;

Draft Law on Personal Data Protection
indicators.impact: There are currently no data local storage requirements under the Cambodian law. However, Article 24 of the Draft Law on Personal Data Protection of the Kingdom of Cambodia contains a requirement to localize all personal data in Cambodia. This law has not come into force yet.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since December 2021;

Last reviewed in November 2024

indicators.question_description:
Infrastructure requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.252 on the Management, Use, and Protection of Personal Identification Data 2021
indicators.impact: There are currently no data localization requirements under the Cambodian law. Therefore, any foreign party that wishes to collect or process Cambodians' personal data is not required to establish local data storage facilities in Cambodia. Furthermore, the Draft Law on Personal Data Protection of the Kingdom of Cambodia states that "a data controller may store personal data in its own personal data storage system or a data center or a secure cloud system of a third party licensed by MPTC in accordance with other laws and regulations in force."

indicators.question_description:
Infrastructure requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.207 ANKr.BK on the Management of the CamDigiKey Platform Royal Government of Cambodia 2023
indicators.impact: For entities using the CamDigiKey eKYC system, there are some requirements for maintaining network security infrastructure. Members must have secure network infrastructure and security servers to protect the data within the CamDigiKey eKYC system (Article 20). However, these requirements focus on ensuring cybersecurity and do not mandate that the infrastructure be located within Cambodia.

indicators.question_description:
Conditional flow regimes
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: E-Commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact:
Cambodia has no conditional flow for cross-border data.

The E-Commerce Law (2019) addresses data security requirements for service providers handling consumer data but does not impose additional conditions for cross-border data flows. Article 32 mandates service providers to implement reasonable security measures to protect against unauthorized access, leakage, or loss of data. However, the law does not establish conditions to assess the adequacy of data protection in foreign jurisdictions, nor does it require government approval or individual consent for cross-border data transfers.

indicators.question_description: Not in an agreement with binding commitments on data transfer.
indicators.impact:
Cambodia has not joined any agreement with binding commitments to open transfers of data across borders. The country has incorporated data flow provisions, however, they are not binding. For example, Cambodia is a member country of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), a trade agreement that entered into force in 2022. And Article 12.15 "Cross-border Transfer of Information by Electronic Means" of the RCEP agreement states:
1. The Parties recognise that each Party may have its own regulatory requirements concerning the transfer of information by electronic means.
2. A Party shall not prevent cross-border transfer of information by electronic means where such activity is for the conduct of the business of a covered person.

Specifically, the Article establishes that Cambodia, Lao PDR, and Myanmar are not required to apply the obligations related to the cross-border transfer of information for five years after the entry into force of the Agreement. This period can be extended by an additional three years if necessary. This means that although Cambodia is part of the agreement, it is not immediately bound by the data flow obligations during this exception period. After the expiration of this transitional phase, Cambodia will be expected to fully comply with these commitments, making them binding once the exception period ends.

In addition to this framework, ASEAN members adopted the ASEAN Digital Data Governance Framework, which focuses on cross-border data flows, cybersecurity, and fostering digital innovation within the bloc. Under this framework, member countries are encouraged to develop interoperable legal frameworks that support data flows without compromising data security or individual privacy rights. This includes a recognition of the need for mechanisms, such as Mutual Recognition Arrangements (MRAs), which could allow certain data protection standards to be recognized across borders within ASEAN.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.source_legislation:
E-commerce Law 2019;

Draft Law on Personal Data Protection
indicators.impact:
While there is no general data protection law in Cambodia, there have been recent legislative developments addressing relevant areas. In particular, the E-Commerce Law, enacted on 2 November 2019, regulate the storage of electronic data and establish requirements for consent and the protection of consumer rights in certain circumstances.

The E-commerce Law contains provisions for the protection of consumer data that has been gathered for electronic communication. Article 32.2 of the Law prohibits any person from interfering in the electronic system, accessing, retrieving, copying, extracting, leaking, deleting, or modifying data, which is under the retention of any other person in bad faith or without permission. In addition, any person who violates those provisions shall be punished by criminal sanctions as stated in Article 60 of the Law. 

Currently there's a draft and not yet in force, that would establish a more comprehensive framework, defining terms such as “data controller” and outlining principles like purpose limitation, security safeguards, and data accuracy. Until this draft law is enacted, Cambodia lacks a fully developed data protection framework​.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since October 2019;

Last reviewed in November 2024

indicators.question_description:
Minimum period of data retention requirements
Exception: Not score requirement applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Customs, 2007
indicators.impact: The Law on Customs Article 51 states that traders and government agencies must keep accurate documents, records, and other information, including information in electronic format, pertaining to import and export of goods for a period of ten years.

indicators.question_description:
Minimum period of data retention requirements
Exception: Not score requirement applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact:
The E-commerce Law includes as well provisions that indirectly address data retention, primarily through record-keeping requirements for electronic transactions. Article 10 mandates that records, documents, and relevant data involved in transactions be stored in a manner that ensures accessibility and retrievability. This article does not set a specific duration for retaining data, instead focusing on the integrity and accessibility of retained information, as required for legal or business needs​.

While the E-Commerce Law also does not set a minimum time limit requirement for data retention, it does specify that when an intermediary or service provider becomes aware that information on record may lead to civil or criminal liability, they are required by law to preserve this information as evidence (Article 25 of the E-Commerce Law). This retention obligation would suggest that service providers and intermediaries are expected to retain data collected for a reasonable amount of time.

indicators.question_description: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) or Data Protection Officer (DPO) requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.252 on the Management, Use, and Protection of Personal Identification Data 2021
indicators.impact: Cambodia has no requirement to perform an impact assessment or have a data protection officer. The draft Personal Data Protection Law may potentially address these roles, as it is expected to outline more detailed data protection mechanisms, but it is still under review and not yet publicly available.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Telecommunications 2015
indicators.impact:
The Law on Telecommunications Article 6 requires that “All telecommunications operators and persons involved with the telecommunications sector shall provide to the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications the telecommunications information and communication technology service data”. In practice, this gives the Ministry unfettered rights to demand that all telecommunications service providers provide data on their service users. This could operate as an obligation for companies to surrender data without the requirement of a judicial warrant or other safeguards protecting the right to privacy.

Article 97 of the Law permits the secret surveillance of any and all telecommunications where it is conducted with the approval of a “legitimate authority.” There is no definition of what constitutes a “legitimate authority,” or the means by which such authority is competent to approve surveillance. This appears to create a power to secretly eavesdrop without any public accountability or safeguards to protect individuals’ right to privacy.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact: Article 32 of the E-commerce Law requires service providers to protect consumer data but also states that data may be disclosed with the consent of authorities. This provision suggests that, under specific circumstances, government bodies can access consumer data stored electronically, potentially broadening state access to personal data held by private entities​

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.23 on the Establishment of National Internet Gateway 2021
indicators.impact: The Sub-Decree No.23 on the establishment of National Internet Gateway enables significant government control over internet traffic, as it mandates that all internet communications within Cambodia pass through a state-controlled gateway. Article 6 of the NIG Sub-Decree grants the government broad surveillance powers, allowing interception and potential censorship of communications that could affect national security, revenue, or public order. The decree’s lack of clear limitations has raised concerns about enabling government overreach without sufficient oversight mechanisms​.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: Draft Cybersecurity Law
indicators.impact:
The Draft Cybersecurity Law includes articles that could grant extensive powers to the Digital Security Committee (DSC) and other inspectors. This draft law has provisions for cybersecurity inspections that may include access to data held by private entities. Moreover, the draft's lack of specificity on judicial or independent oversight has led to concerns about the potential for excessive state surveillance under the guise of cybersecurity​

Powers granted to the DSC include, among others, the authority to order a private organization to: “provide information and allow the use of related electronic devices” with the private organization’s consent, in order to prevent and mitigate risks caused by a cybersecurity threat or incident (article 19); “allow officers in charge of the DSC to access any relevant computer or computer system” where the private organization is unable to prevent and mitigate a cybersecurity incident that has reached a “critical level” (article 21); and “access computer data or other data” pursuant to a court order, in situations where a private organization is unable to terminate or mitigate the impacts caused by a cybersecurity threat (article 22).

The Draft Cybersecurity Law outlines as well various responsibilities and authorities for Cybersecurity Inspectors. According to Article 24, these inspectors are designated as “judicial police officers” by the Minister of the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPTC) to support the law's enforcement through monitoring, studying, inspecting, and strengthening cybersecurity measures. Articles 26 and 27 grant inspectors the authority to "investigate, observe, monitor, prevent, and respond to cybersecurity threats and incidents" and to "check, confiscate evidence, call on involved persons, and carry out other procedures in line with the Code of Criminal Procedure."

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact:
The E-commerce Law creates a safe harbor rule for e-commerce service providers and intermediaries whereby they are not liable for unlawful third-party content on their online platforms. 

Article 24 covers a broad spectrum of intermediary liabilities, stating that intermediaries are protected from liability for any civil or criminal issues linked to content stored or transmitted by users, provided they meet specific requirements:

Lack of Knowledge: The intermediary must not have actual knowledge of illegal activity in the content.
No Reasonable Awareness: They must not be aware of circumstances that would reasonably lead them to know of the illegal activity.
Response Upon Notification: If they are made aware, intermediaries are required to follow the procedures outlined in Article 25 to remove or disable access to the unlawful information.

Article 24 of the E-commerce Law states that the intermediaries and electronic-commerce service providers shall not bear civil or criminal responsibility related to the information contained in the electronic records related to service provision of such intermediaries and electronic-commerce service providers; in case s/he is not the one who sends such record and in case:

1. Such intermediaries and electronic-commerce service providers are not aware that the information sent leads to the civil or criminal responsibility;
2. Such intermediaries and electronic-commerce service providers are not aware of the fact or circumstances which they ought to know reasonably give rise to a likelihood of civil or criminal liability in respect of the information, or
3. The intermediary or electronic commerce service provider becomes aware of facts or circumstances from which the likelihood of civil or criminal liability in respect of the information ought reasonably to have been known and take action in accordance
with the procedure set out in Article 25 in relation to unlawful information and defamation in below.

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact:
The safe harbor provisions in Article 24 of Cambodia’s Law on Electronic Commerce (2019) extend to a broad array of illegal activities, not just copyright infringement. The language of Article 24 does not specifically limit the protection to intellectual property matters; instead, it refers broadly to "any civil or criminal liability" associated with content managed by intermediaries.

However, they must comply with certain mandatory content removal procedures upon becoming aware of such content. Additionally, they are obligated to comply with an e-commerce code of conduct.

indicators.question_description: User identify requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.41 on Equipment Identity Registration 2023
indicators.impact:
This Sub-Decree aims to prevent and curb the use of telecommunications equipment with fake SIM modules, stolen devices, and illegally imported goods, while also seeking to protect consumer health, safety, and rights, improve telecommunications service quality, foster fair competition in the market, and increase national revenue collection. The Sub-Decree encompasses a comprehensive framework for the identity registration of all telecommunications equipment with SIM modules (referred to as "Telecoms Equipment") in Cambodia.

Under Article 2, the Sub-Decree mandates that all Telecoms Equipment must be registered with the Equipment Identity Registration System (EIRS), a regulatory system managed by the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPTC). This registration requirement, however, includes an exception for tourists or travelers whose stay in Cambodia does not exceed 60 days. Mobile operators play a crucial role under Article 5, as they are required to verify the International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) of each device against an Equipment Identity Register (EIR) they maintain, which is connected to the EIRS. Only Telecoms Equipment with an approved IMEI are authorized to connect to the mobile network. This framework aims to prevent unauthorized devices from accessing Cambodian telecommunications networks and ensures that all registered equipment is traceable.

Additionally, the Sub-Decree places importance on data security, with both the MPTC and mobile operators required to establish cybersecurity systems to protect data stored in the EIRS and EIR. Article 7 further reinforces the requirement for mobile operators to maintain accurate and updated records for each SIM-registered device, thus ensuring compliance with the identity verification requirement essential for SIM registration.

The Sub-Decree also categorizes Telecoms Equipment into three distinct lists based on the IMEI’s status. Authorized equipment is listed as eligible to connect to the network, while conditional authorization is given to devices, like those belonging to tourists, that are used within Cambodia on a temporary basis. A suspension list is designated for equipment that is not permitted to connect to the network, including stolen or unregistered devices. To enforce compliance, the Sub-Decree outlines administrative penalties and fines for breaches, with fines escalating for repeated offenses, which underscores the Cambodian government’s commitment to securing its telecommunications infrastructure and ensuring lawful use.

indicators.question_description: User identify requirements
indicators.source_legislation:
Notification on
Strengthening the Sales, Distributions and Uses of SIM in Accordance with Applicable Regulations, Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (“TRC”) 2024
indicators.impact: The Telecommunication Regulator of Cambodia (TRC) issued a notification to strengthen measures for the sales, distribution, and use of SIM cards, emphasizing identity verification as a prerequisite for SIM registration. Mobile operators and vendors are required to collect valid identification documents from users before activating services, with unregistered SIMs or those registered in bulk under a single name subject to deactivation. The regulation also prohibits the renting or leasing of SIM cards for illegitimate purposes, such as creating fake bank or social media accounts, and imposes penalties on vendors or users who enable wrongful acts by sharing SIM cards.

indicators.question_description: Monitoring requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Inter-ministerial Prakas No.170 on Publication Controls of Website and Social Media Processing via Internet in the Kingdom of Cambodia 2018
indicators.impact: Clause 7 of the Inter-ministerial Prakas No.170 requires that all Internet Service Providers who operate in Cambodia have to install software programs and equip themselves with internet surveillance tools to easily filter and block any social media accounts or pages that run their business activities and/or publicize illegally.

indicators.question_description: Monitoring requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.23 on the Establishment of National Internet Gateway 2021
indicators.impact: The Sub-Decree No. 23 on the establishment of National Internet Gateway enables significant government control over internet traffic, as it mandates that all internet communications within Cambodia pass through a state-controlled gateway. Article 6 of the NIG Sub-Decree grants the government broad surveillance powers, allowing interception and potential censorship of communications that could affect national security, revenue, or public order. The decree’s lack of clear limitations has raised concerns about enabling government overreach without sufficient oversight mechanisms​.

indicators.question_description:
Blocking or filtering commercial web content
Exception: Not score political content, criminal content (e.g., child pornography), aged-restricted content, defamation and other non-commercial content.
indicators.source_legislation: Inter-ministerial Prakas No.170 on Publication Controls of Website and Social Media Processing via Internet in the Kingdom of Cambodia 2018
indicators.impact:
The Inter-ministerial Prakas No.170 impacts both Internet Service Providers and relevant ministries. All Internet Service Providers, who operate in the Kingdom of Cambodia, have to install software programs and equip themselves with internet surveillance tools to easily filter and block any social media accounts or pages that run their business activities and/or publicize illegally (Clause 7.c).

Clause 4 provides that to ensure effective implementation of this Prakas, Ministry of Information and Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Posts and Telecommunication, have to establish specialized unit as secretariat in order to cooperatively monitor, study, research, find out illegal business activities and publications on websites and social media in order to take legal action against them following the procedure. 

Moreover, under Clause 5, that institutions and specialized units have to cooperate to each other in order to take actions against and prevent all news publication contents or written messages, audios, photos, videos, and/or other means willing to create turmoil leading to undermine national defence, national security, relation with other countries, national economy, public order, discrimination and national culture and tradition.

In recent years, the Cambodian government has systematically blocked independent media outlets, particularly during election periods, to limit public access to critical news coverage. Major outlets such as Radio Free Asia (RFA), The Cambodia Daily, and Voice of Democracy (VOD) have faced censorship orders that intensified during the 2018 and 2023 general elections. A directive issued in July 2023 required internet service providers to block websites that allegedly spread misleading information and harm the government’s honor, a justification widely criticized as a means to suppress dissenting voices. The crackdown includes surveillance mandates under the 2018 Inter-Ministerial Prakas on Website and Social Media Control, which grants authorities the power to block content considered a threat to national security or public order.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since May 2018;

Last reviewed in November 2024

indicators.question_description:
Blocking or filtering commercial web content
Exception: Not score political content, criminal content (e.g., child pornography), aged-restricted content, defamation and other non-commercial content.
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.23 on the Establishment of National Internet Gateway 2021
indicators.impact: The NIG Sub-Decree introduces a national internet gateway through which all internet traffic must pass, allowing enhanced monitoring and filtering of online content under Article 6, that states "NIG operators shall have the following functions and duties: (...) collaborate with the MPTC, TRC and relevant authorities to take action in blocking and disconnecting al network connections that adversely affect national revenue, safety, social order, dignity, culture, traditions, and customs".

indicators.question_description: Internet shutdowns
indicators.source_legislation: V-Dem, variable v2smgovshut
indicators.impact: The indicator "6.2.4 - Government Internet shut down in practice" of the V-Dem Dataset, which measures whether the government has the technical capacity to actively make internet service cease, thus interrupting domestic access to the internet or whether the government has decided to do so, has a score of 3.63 in Cambodia. This corresponds to "Never, or almost never. The government does not typically interfere with the domestic access to the Internet".

indicators.question_description:
Online advertising requirements
Exception: Not score requirements that advertising should not be misleading
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Consumer Protection, 2019
indicators.impact:
There is no online advertising restriction in Cambodia.

Cambodia's Law on Consumer Protection (2019) includes several provisions relevant to online advertising, but always focusing on consumer protection against deceptive practices. Articles 23 and 24 establish the 'Standards of information for consumers' as well as the obligation for those doing advertising (among other activities) to adhere to these practices. Article 27.2 establishes the Sample of Content of the Information Standard for Consumers, where the written information shall include the Khmer Language following the Prakas of the competent regulators. Under Article 15 Bait advertising is defined. Article 9 prohibits misleading advertisement, as it deceives consumers regarding the quality, price or cost of the good or services.

indicators.question_description:
Licensing requirements for online content providers and applications (social media platforms, new providers, VPN, cloud servics, etc.)
Exception: Not cover license for telecommunication facilities and service providers (captured under Pillar 5), License for e-commerce platform (captured under Pillar 12)
indicators.source_legislation: Law on the Press 1996
indicators.impact:
Media outlets in Cambodia are required to obtain licenses. Article 8 of the Law on Media states that "Before distribution, the press, employer or editor shall file an application with the Ministry of Information in order to identify itself. A receipt shall be issued to the press by this Ministry after receiving the whole file. (...) Any employer or editor who publishes without respecting this formality in advance shall be fined from 500,000 to 1,500,000 riel. In case of repeated violations, the fine shall be double the original amount." 

Article 9 establishes the information required: "The formality, which shall be completed by the employer or editor, shall primarily consist of:
- Identify of the press organ.
- Name and address of the employer or editor.
- Name and address of the printing house.
- Certification of criminal record.
Any change in the above information shall be notified to the Ministry of Information 5 days in advance, except in cases of force majeure.

Moreover, the government regularly revokes the licenses of online news outlets following their reporting, sometimes also requiring the news sites to remove online content. In February 2023, the government revoked the media operating license of VOD’s parent organization, the Cambodian Center for Independent Media (CCIM), effectively shutting down VOD—one of the country’s last independent news outlets—and blocking its website over its reporting on Hun Manet’s role in the government.

indicators.question_description: Import ban applied to ICT goods and online services (e.g. network equipment, servers, handsets, applications, and data processing)
indicators.impact:
Article 8 of the Laws of Customs enables the Royal Government of Cambodia to issue an Anukret determining goods to be considered prohibited or restricted. As of 2024, this Anukret has been amended thrice:

The Anukret 209 dated 31st December 2007
The Anukret 17 dated 26th February 2020
The Anukret 370 dated 28th December 2023 consisting of 05 main annexes:
Annex 1 – List of Prohibited Goods: Goods that are prohibited from exportation, importation or international transit through Cambodia’s territory unless permitted by the Royal Government of Cambodia.
Annex 2 – List of Restricted Goods: Goods that are required to have export or import permit or similar document issued by competent government ministries/agencies prior to the exportation or importation.
Annex 3 – List of Goods to be accompanied with export certificate: Goods that are not required to obtain prior import permit in the case of importation in Cambodia, but they are required to obtain export certificate or similar document issued by competent authority in the exporting country.
Annex 4 – List of Goods Restricted for International Transit: Goods that are required to obtain prior transit permit from competent government ministries/agencies.
Annex 5 – Explanatory Note which provides explanation on how the list could be read, definition of certain keywords, and some other additional notes on goods that could not be technically classified based on the AHTN, yet are also subject to restriction or prohibition, and such.

According to Cambodia's "Anukret No. 370 ANK.BrK," several ICT-related goods are banned from importation. These include electronic cigarettes and similar vaporizing devices, as well as various types of electrical and electronic waste, particularly those containing hazardous substances like lead and cadmium. These bans aim to mitigate environmental and health risks associated with these products.
references: https://tools.customs.gov.kh/documents/reader/16357/17170663763358226/អនុក្រឹត្យលេខ_៣៧០_(អនក្រ_បក)_ចុះថ្ងៃទី២៨_ខែធ្នូ_ឆ្នាំ២០២៣

indicators.question_description: Other import restrictions on ICT goods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.370 ANK.BrK on the Promulgation of the List of Prohibited and Restricted Goods 2023
indicators.impact:
The import of certain ICT goods is restricted under "Anukret No. 370 ANK.BrK." Under Article 2, for commodities listed in the annexes of this sub-decree and intended for multi-sectoral purposes, an export-import permit is mandatory from one of the ministries or institutions specified in the annex. Alternatively, the permit may be issued by another competent ministry based on the intended use or business objective. Prohibition, requirement of a license, permits, or conditions concerning the exportation, importation and transit of goods are set out in the annexes of this sub-decree (Article 4).

Annex 2 provides the List of Goods which required Permit on Importation or Exportation (AHTN 2022), covering ICT products:
- 85.17: Telephone sets, including smartphones and other telephones for cellular networks or for other wireless networks; other apparatus for the transmission or reception of voice, images or other data, including apparatus for communication in a wired or wireless network (such as a local or wide area network), other than transmission or reception apparatus of heading 84.43, 85.25, 85.27 or 85.28.
- 85.25: Transmission apparatus for radio-broadcasting or television, whether or not incorporating reception apparatus or sound recording or reproducing apparatus; television cameras, digital cameras and video camera recorders.

Specifically, used computers require prior authorization from the Ministry of Environment, aiming to limit environmental risks from electronic waste since these items may contain hazardous materials (85.49: Electrical and electronic waste and scrap). Additionally, some ICT-related components and electronic devices may need permits from relevant ministries, especially if they involve potentially harmful substances or pose regulatory concerns.
references: https://tools.customs.gov.kh/documents/reader/16357/17170663763358226/អនុក្រឹត្យលេខ_៣៧០_(អនក្រ_បក)_ចុះថ្ងៃទី២៨_ខែធ្នូ_ឆ្នាំ២០២៣

indicators.question_description: Other import restrictions on ICT goods and online services
indicators.source_legislation:
Instruction on the Application for Certificate and Permitted Letter for Importing Radiocom and Telecom equipment 2014;

Announcement on The Use of Online System for Application for Import Permit for Radiocommunication Equipment and Telecommunication Equipment, and Application for Certificate of Qualified Agent 2024
indicators.impact:
A recent notification has been issued by the Telecommunications Regulator of Cambodia (TRC) on April 24, 2024, regarding the import of radiocommunication and telecommunication equipment. The TRC now requires that applications for import permits and certificates for qualified agents for importing, supplying, and distributing these types of equipment be submitted through a newly launched online portal: https://service.trc.gov.kh.

To legally import, supply, or distribute telecom equipment in Cambodia, applicants must obtain:
- A qualified agent certificate,
- An import permit, and/or
- A type approval certificate.

Failure to comply with these requirements may result in fines ranging from 1 to 5 million riels for individuals and 10 to 50 million riels for legal entities, along with potential seizure of equipment and other criminal penalties​.
references: https://trc.gov.kh/en/សេចក្ដីណែនាំ/
https://trc.gov.kh/en/ការដាក់ឱ្យប្រើប្រាស់ប្/

indicators.question_description: Local content requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Council for the Development of Cambodia 2024
indicators.impact: Currently, there is no local content requirement in Cambodia. In other words, there is no restriction on the use of imported materials, parts, and components for producing the export goods unless they are harmful to the health, environment, or society (Council for the Development of Cambodia).

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: Sub-Decree No.370 ANK.BrK on the Promulgation of the List of Prohibited and Restricted Goods 2023
indicators.impact:
Under Sub-Decree No. 370 ANK.BrK dated December 28, 2023, Cambodia restricts the export of certain ICT goods due to environmental and security considerations. Specifically, the regulation requires permits for exporting various types of electronic waste and scrap, including lead-acid accumulators and copper-containing electronic waste, with oversight from the Ministry of Environment (as outlined in the Annex under codes like 8549.11.20 and 8549.11.30). 

Additionally, the export of toy drones (classified under subheading 9503.00.99) regulated due to potential dual-use concerns, requiring permits from the Ministry of National Defense and the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications, as specified in Anex 5 (II. Notes). Restrictions may apply to used computers too, which need authorization from the Ministry of Environment, as specified in the same Anex.
