indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Standards of Cambodia 2007
indicators.impact:
Law on Standards of Cambodia 2007 establishes the National Standards Council in 2009 (Article 10). The Council has the responsibility to approve, amend and cancel any national standards lie with the National Standard Council (Article 12). Regarding the members of the NSC, Article 11 states that 'The member of the Council shall have the following qualifications:
- being a Cambodian citizen,
- never been convicted of a crime or misdemeanor,
- being graduated in sciences or engineering area, and
- having at least five years of professional experience.

However, regarding the formation of Cambodia standards, the Institute shall publish, at least in one daily newspaper in Khmer language for a period of not less than seven days, an announcement stating the intention of the declaration and a summary content of any standard. Any person wishing to protest shall submit his/her written protest to the Institute within thirty days from the date of publication. Interested persons are permitted to attend and comment in the hearing (Article 17). 

Cambodia mainly uses the ISO/IEC Guide 21-1 and 21-2:2005 as a national guide to adopt international standards as national standards or technical regulations. As in 2017, nearly 83% of Cambodian standards are aligned with international standards.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Standards of Cambodia 2007
indicators.impact:
It is required that several products sold in Cambodia obtain national certification, although this certification is often based on international standards. To obtain the local certification, foreign manufacturers need to sign an agreement with the Institute of Standards of Cambodia.

Under Articles 44 to 46 of the Law on Standards of Cambodia (2007), holding an accreditation or registration certificate enables organizations and individuals to operate as qualified conformity assessors or testing bodies, but it does not permit self-certification. Article 44 specifies that organizations such as conformity assessment bodies, testing laboratories, or training organizations can apply for accreditation or registration, which allows them to carry out conformity assessments. However, Article 45 clarifies that while certificate holders can use their accreditation to demonstrate adherence to specific standards, this is only permitted after auditing and certification by the Institute. Furthermore, Article 46 underscores that the Institute retains authority over certificate holders by reserving the right to suspend or revoke certifications if terms are violated. This regulatory framework maintains strict oversight by the Institute and does not allow for self-certification.

Under Article 38, any organization seeking a system certification for its management practices must apply to the Institute, undergo a conformity assessment, and pay a certification fee. The Institute assesses the organization’s management system against the relevant standard before issuing a system certificate, valid for three years and renewable under compliance with prescribed conditions. Certified organizations are required to submit all relevant documents and information related to their certification process if requested by the Institute’s Director. 

Any entity can apply for a license that would allow it to use the ISC Certification Mark. The license has a validity of three years can be extended for further periods of three years at a time, subject to satisfactory operation of the license. (Articles 24 to 37)

Article 48 of the Law on Standards of Cambodia states that no person or organizations can announce that they have received a standard-conformity certificate, although they have been certified by a local or foreign certification body, unless they have been registered and received approval from the Institute of Standards of Cambodia.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation:
ASEAN Sectoral MRA for Electrical and Electronic Equipment (ASEAN EE MRA) 2002;

ASEAN Harmonized Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulatory Regime (AHEEERR) 2005
indicators.impact: The ASEAN Framework Agreement on Mutual Recognition Arrangements signed in April 2002 provides the principles for developing sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangements (MRAs) among ASEAN member states. A member state shall accept or recognize the test reports and certifications issued by the testing laboratories and certification bodies of other parties (ASEAN EE MRA Article 3 General Provisions).

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation:
ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) 1998;

Asia-Pacific Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation (APLAC), 2019
indicators.impact:
The ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangements (MRA) plays a central role in third-party certification recognition. This allows Cambodia to recognize test reports and certifications from recognized Conformity Assessment Bodies (CABs) in other ASEAN member states. Article 2 of the ASEAN Sectoral MRA states that the parties will accept test reports and certifications issued by CABs in other ASEAN countries provided they are listed under the MRA​. Further, Article 3 of the ASEAN MRA stipulates that Cambodia must accept test reports and certifications issued by accredited Testing Laboratories and Certification Bodies in other ASEAN countries. Article 11 further outlines the accreditation standards, specifically referencing ISO/IEC 17025 for testing laboratories and ISO/IEC Guide 65 for certification bodies as necessary standards for third-party recognition​.

Foreign suppliers outside the ASEAN region may still have their certifications recognized by Cambodia if the certification bodies meet internationally recognized standards.

indicators.question_description: Product screening and testing requirements
indicators.impact:
The "Information Booklet for Electrical and Electronic Equipment" outlines the mandatory compliance procedures for local and foreign manufacturers intending to market regulated products in Cambodia. Chapter 7 states, "For local or foreign manufacturers producing regulated products, according to Ministerial Regulation, all regulated products shall conform to Cambodian standards, so that they shall apply for Product safety mark license or product certification mark license to label the mark on their products before placing into Cambodian market."
Chapter 11 elaborates that Cambodia accepts testing results from third parties recognized by the Ministry of Industry, Science, Technology, and Innovation (MISTI) for electrical and electronic equipment. The regulation promotes accountability and facilitates the conformity of products with domestic industrial standards.

indicators.question_description: Deviation from international encryption standards (ISO, IEC, ITU, FIPS, AES, TDES, and ECC)
indicators.source_legislation: Draft Law on Cybercrime 2022
indicators.impact:
There are no mandatory encryption standards that deviate from international standards reported in Cambodia. 
According to several analysis on the Cybercrime Law Draft, it settles "Unreasonable obligations of “service providers, as the Law requires service providers to manage “subscriber information” and turn that information over to RGC authorities. Depending on how the Law is interpreted, these requirements could make using the internet anonymously impossible and prevent the use of encryption and other safety features."

In this sense, Article 8 in Cambodian regulations requires service providers to retain traffic data for at least 180 days, accurately manage user registration, and be technically capable of providing subscriber information to authorities. This mandate poses two significant issues for privacy and data protection. First, the broad requirement to maintain and manage undefined personal data may infringe on users' privacy rights under the ICCPR by necessitating the collection of identifiable information, potentially compromising the anonymity essential to safeguarding free expression. Second, requiring 180-day data retention risks enabling bulk data collection, expanding state surveillance, and heightening the potential for unauthorized data access or breaches.

These requirements challenge encryption and data security practices by imposing obligations that could discourage or weaken privacy safeguards, such as encryption, essential for secure and anonymous communications. The Special Rapporteur warns that compelling service providers to implement interception capabilities for state surveillance or discouraging encryption use could infringe on users’ privacy and the confidentiality of communications, underscoring the need to balance state security measures with individual rights to privacy and data protection.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.source_legislation:
Law on Investment 2021;

E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact: Cambodia does not implement foreign equity cap on e-commerce business. Article 24 of the Law of Investment (2021) states that "Digital Industries are entitled to investment incentives." In addition, these industries are not included in the Negative list and are open to 100% FDI. Additionally, E-commerce Law does not introduce foreign equity cap in e-commerce sector.

indicators.question_description:
Online purchases and delivery limitations
Exception: Not score limitations on online purchases and delivery applied specifically to products related to consumer protection, notably restrictions on alcoholic beverages, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals.
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact: Cambodia does not implement any restrictions regarding limits on e-commerce purchases and online delivery. There are no specific legal provisions in Cambodia that limit the number of products that can be purchased online or impose strict restrictions on the delivery of products bought online, aside from general consumer protection, regulated product requirements, and compliance with customs laws for cross-border transactions. These rules do not restrict the overall quantity or general accessibility of products available for online purchase.

indicators.question_description:
Licensing scheme for e-commerce providers (B2B and B2C)
Exception: Licenses pertiaining to other aspects of e-commerce businesses, such as license to operate online payment services and delivery are not captured.
indicators.impact:
In Cambodia, the E-commerce Law and related regulations, including Sub-Decree No. 134 and Prakas No. 290, establish clear requirements for e-commerce providers and intermediaries. According to Article 26 of the E-commerce Law, e-commerce service providers and intermediaries must obtain a permission letter or license from the Ministry of Commerce (MoC) and the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPTC), along with an Online Service Certificate from the MPTC. Prakas No. 290, specifically in Article 3, mandates that natural persons or sole proprietorships engaged in e-commerce acquire an E-commerce Permit, while legal entities or foreign branches need an E-commerce License (Article 5). The Permit is valid for two years, and the License is valid for three years, with both issued by the MoC.

Requirements for a License, as detailed in Article 5 of Prakas No. 290, include documents like a Certificate of Incorporation, Patent Tax Certificate, Online Service Certificate from the MPTC, and proof of a licensed payment provider approved by the National Bank of Cambodia. For e-commerce intermediaries, Article 7 of Sub-Decree No. 134 outlines conditions for obtaining a license, including business registration, accurate electronic systems, and established consumer protection measures. Additionally, Sub-Decree No. 134 Article 2 governs all e-commerce services operating within or into Cambodia, covering various digital services such as e-commerce platforms, online auctions, and marketing services.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
The Cambodian Law on Foreign Exchange (1997), Prakas on Third-Party Processors, and other regulations create a layered framework for handling international and domestic payment transactions. The Law on Foreign Exchange (1997) sets a foundational rule requiring that all international settlements be handled by “authorized intermediaries,” specifically limiting this role to banks with a permanent establishment in Cambodia (Articles 5.1 and 5.2). This ensures that only NBC-authorized banks can facilitate cross-border payments, reinforcing regulatory control over international financial flows and compliance with Cambodian financial laws.

The Prakas on Third-Party Processors builds on this framework by allowing banks to outsource specific payment transaction services to third-party processors, provided these processors are licensed by the NBC and work exclusively on behalf of an authorized bank (Articles 1 and 3). The Prakas specifies roles that third-party processors can fulfill, such as managing inter-bank clearing, operating customer accounts, and providing mobile remittance and card payment services (Article 3). However, these processors do not replace authorized intermediaries; rather, they support banks in their service delivery under strict NBC oversight. Additionally, Article 5 subjects third-party processors to NBC's Prakas on payment clearing and systemic risk management, ensuring alignment with existing financial stability measures.

Finally, the Prakas on Management of Payment Transactions Services governs both Payment Transactions Services providers and Banks. However, services such as information technology support, data storage and processor, payment transactions using bank’s location and so on are excluded from the Prakas’s purview.

Unlike Third Party Processor, which is a service provider or processor to facilitate bank’s payment transactions services and operations, Payment Transactions Services provider is independent. The Prakas has stipulated the scope of business of Payment Transactions Services provider in Article 6 and 7 that it can engage in businesses such as deposit and withdrawal in payment account service, money transfer service, payment transaction service, providing short term credit, issuing electronic currency, money changer and so on. To operate as Payment Transactions Services provider, legal entities must obtain license from the NBC. Legal entities need to fulfill numbers of conditions to obtain license from NBC.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation:
Law on Foreign Exchange 1997;

Prakas on Third-Party Processors 2010
indicators.impact:
The NBC has been actively encouraging the use of the Khmer Riel in digital payments, particularly through the Bakong system, which allows users to conduct transactions in both currencies. The goal is to strengthen the riel’s role in cross-border transactions, reducing dollar dependence and enhancing Cambodia’s monetary policy autonomy. Cross-border transactions made through Bakong with countries like Thailand, Lao PDR, and Viet Nam are exclusively conducted in riel, a measure designed to promote the local currency internationally. However, according to Bakong itself, to register within the system one of the conditions is that 'Only individual accounts (savings/current accounts) in Khmer Riel and US Dollar can be used to register for Bakong System.' which indicates that dollars can still be used. 

The Prakas on Payment Service Providers (2017) and other related financial regulations require online and digital payment service providers to adhere to foreign exchange laws overseen by the National Bank of Cambodia (NBC). 

These regulations emphasize the use of the riel in domestic payments while permitting U.S. dollar usage in certain international transactions, reflecting an ongoing effort to gradually elevate the riel’s prominence in the economy.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact: National standards for payment security does not deviate from international standards. Article 47 of the E-Commerce Law specifies liability conditions for payment service providers, establishing that they must authenticate and validate electronic fund transfers. Service providers are held liable for unauthorized transactions, failure to meet customer instructions, and operational malfunctions, implying adherence to security standards to mitigate these liabilities​.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Article 46 of the E-Commerce Law states, “Any person operating a payment system, providing a payment service, issuing an electronic payment instrument or providing an electronic means of payment, or conducting any other operations to the public considered to be an electronic payment and shall obtain prior authorization or license from the National Bank of Cambodia.

As the Prakas on Third-Party Processors allows banks to outsource specific payment transaction services to third-party processors, the last must be licensed as well by the NBC and work exclusively on behalf of an authorized bank (Articles 1 and 3). 

Finally, under Prakas on Management of Payment Transactions Services, 2017, to operate as Payment Transactions Services provider, legal entities must obtain license from the NBC. Legal entities need to fulfill numbers of conditions to obtain license from NBC.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Prakas on Payment Service Providers 2021
indicators.impact:
The 2021 circular introduces the limit on daily transactions. The limits depend on the platform, customer information, and the payment institution's review stage:
In accordance with the different customer risk levels, customer identification procedures will be determined by the four following transaction types:
- Transactions between Bakong Accounts;
- Transactions between Bakong Accounts and Bank Accounts/E-Wallet Accounts;
- Transactions between E-Wallet Accounts and E-Wallet Accounts/Bank Accounts; and
- Transactions between Bank Accounts and Bank Accounts via Bakong (Backbone).

For transactions falling under items 1 – 3 above, customers are classified into three categories: basic customers, partial KYC and full KYC. In these categories, limits are:

(i) A basic customers: Customers who register through the online or mobile application but have yet to provide all the information as required by the member institution. The minimum information required is their phone number. Daily transaction amount is KHR 2 Million and USD 500.

(ii) Intermediate Customers: Customers who register through the online or mobile application and have provided all the information required by the member institution, but their information has not undergone the full Know Your Customer (“KYC”) review by the payment institution member. The requirements are: phone number; portrait photo; and photo of a valid National Identification Card or Passport. Daily transaction amount is KHR 12 million and USD 3000.

(iii) Full Customers: Customers who register through the online or mobile application or at the payment institution’s registration desk, and have undergone a full KYC review by the payment institution member. The requirements are: phone number; portrait photo; and photo of a valid National Identification Card or Passport. Daily transaction amount is 40 KHR million and USD 10,000.

For transactions falling under item 4 above, customers are considered as full KYC customers and the transaction limit is KHR 200 million (equivalent to USD 50,000) per day.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Prakas on Third-Party Processors 2010
indicators.impact: A non-bank entity cannot conduct payment transactions or offer money remittance services through mobile phones unless it is authorized by a bank to act as its third-party processor. In other words, a person cannot provide mobile money remittance services without a partnership with a bank (Article 3).

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact: No other restrictions on online payment implemented.

indicators.question_description: Low De Minimis
indicators.source_legislation: Circular on Customs Procedure for De Minimis No.004 MEF 2012
indicators.impact:
According to Cambodia's de minimis rule, goods with a value of up to 50 USD (35 SDR) are exempted from taxes and duties collected by the customs. Nevertheless, the owner or his/her representative shall follow a simple procedure by lodging a summary customs declaration and attaching supporting documents such as invoice, packing list, certificate of tax registration, airway bill/bill of lading, and other relevant documents if available.

Some risky commodities, however, are not considered as “De Minimis”. These commodities include:
- Goods on the list of prohibited and restricted goods of the current law and regulations.
- Highly sensitive goods that may potentially affect public security and safety such as weapons, explosives, military equipment, drug, drug pre-cursor, and other hazardous substances.

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.source_legislation:
Guidelines for the online application for Domain Name System Registration (.kh) 2018;

Sub-Decree No.287 on Management and Use of National Domain Names on the Internet 2021
indicators.impact:
Registering a top-level domain name ".kh", and a second level domain name ".com.kh" or ".net.kh" require a local presence and the registration of the company with the Ministry of Commerce of Cambodia. For a ".org.kh" domain name, a local presence and registration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation is required.

The Sub-Decree on the Management and Use of National Domain Name has been entered into force in April 2022 provides that legal persons registered in the Kingdom of Cambodia shall provide electronic addresses containing national domain names (Article 7). Moreover, under Article 5, domains are allocated for legal persons that are established or registered in accordance with the laws of the Kingdom of Cambodia, which means local presence is required.

According to Sub-Decree On Management and Use of National Domain Names on the Internet, Second Level Domains are allocated for legal persons that are established or registered in accordance with the laws of the Kingdom of Cambodia which have the following forms:
1. <applied name>.com.kh for commercial enterprises or public enterprises.
2. <applied name>.org.kh for organizations, associations or trade unions.
3. <applied name>.edu.kh for public and private education institutions.
4. <applied name>.net.kh for companies or institutions providing computer network services. (Article 5).

Under Article 9 "any person who intends to use national domain name can file an application with TRC through an automated system or with the registrar. A person who files application for national domain name registration through automated system shall complete the application form and provide relevant documents according to a Prakas of MPTC Minister. TRC shall review and decide on the application within 3 (three) working days after applicant fills in the correct information and provides sufficient documentation. In the event of incorrect information or insufficient documentation provided, TRC shall notify applicant to rectify information or provide additional documents within 3 (three) working days upon the date of notification. In the event that rectification has not been made, the application shall be annulled. TRC shall review and decide on the application within 3 (three) working days after applicant rectifies information or provides additional documents as required by TRC.
Upon the receipt of the decision of granting national domain name as stated in paragraph 2 of this Article, applicant shall pay the usage fee of national domain name in order to obtain the right to use."

Registered domain name shall have at least 1 (one) year validity period from the date of registration and can be renewed for subsequent years under the condition that the registrant pays the fee as required (Article 10).

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.source_legislation:
Notification No.0837 on the Requirement on Use of the
National Domain Name “.com.kh” and the National Domain Name Electronic Address when Filing an Annual Declaration of the Commercial Enterprises (the “ADCE”) 2022
indicators.impact:
The Notification, entry into force 1 January 2023, provides that registered companies in Cambodia are required to use a local domain name, such as .com.kh for their websites and email addresses (Article 7).

The Ministry of Commerce (the “MOC”) and the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (the “MPTC”) jointly issued a Notification on 1 April 2022 to inform all companies duly registered in the Kingdom of Cambodia, are required to use the national domain name level 2, type “.com.kh” and to provide an electronic address containing a domain name with the national domain name level 2, type “.com.kh”, when filing an ADCE with the MOC to update the status of companies. Accordingly, all registered companies, who have not used the national domain name level 2, type “.com.kh”, must urgently register to use the national domain name level 2, type “.com.kh” with the MPTC.

On 31 January 2023, the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (MPTC) issued a notification to inform the public about the automation National Domain Registration system. To facilitate the request for a national domain name quickly, easily, and efficiently, the MPTC has prepared and put into use the online “Domain Name.kh Registration”. 

As of 2023 the costs are reported to be around $100 for the initial registration and $30 for subsequent annual renewals. In comparison a .com domain typically costs around $13 for registration and renewal.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.source_legislation:
Sub-Decree No.134 on Classification, Formalities, and Procedures on Granting of Permit or License to Intermediary and E-commerce Service Provider and Exemptions 2020;

Sub-Decree No.287 on Management and Use of National Domain Names on the Internet 2021
indicators.impact: To acquire an E-commerce License, both legal entities and branches of foreign companies must meet specified criteria. This includes obtaining a certificate for Online Service and Domain Name from the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (Article 7.1). According to Article 5 of the Sub-Decree No. 287 on Management and Use of National Domain Names on the Internet, domains are allocated for legal persons that are established or registered in accordance with the laws of the Kingdom of Cambodia, which means local presence is required.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Consumer Protection Law 2019
indicators.impact: In 2019, Cambodia enacted the Law on Consumer Protection to protect the rights of consumers in general. In relation to consumer protection, Articles 23 and 24 establish the 'Standards of information for consumers' as well as the 'Obligation for those doing advertising' (among other activities) to adhere to these practices. Article 27.2 establishes the Sample of Content of the Information Standard for Consumers, where the written information shall include the Khmer Language following the Prakas of the competent regulators. Under Article 15 Bait advertising is defined. Article 9 prohibits misleading advertisement, as it deceives consumers regarding the quality, price or cost of the good or services.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: E-commerce Law 2019
indicators.impact: The Law on Electronic Commerce in Cambodia establishes consumer protection measures that promote transparency, security, and choice in online transactions. Article 29 mandates that online sellers provide clear information about their identity, terms, costs, and return policies, enabling informed consumer decisions. Article 30 protects consumers from unsolicited communications by requiring an opt-out option, and Article 32 enforces data protection by requiring businesses to secure personal information against unauthorized access or modification. Furthermore, Article 33 ensures that e-commerce businesses comply with broader consumer protection laws in Cambodia.

indicators.question_description: Not in the United Nations Convention of Electronic Communications
indicators.source_legislation: Lack of signature of the UN Convention on Electronic Communications
indicators.impact: Cambodia did not sign the United Nations Convention on Electronic Communications, however it is reported that the legislation includes substantive provisions of the Convention.

indicators.question_description: Not in the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce
indicators.source_legislation: UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce
indicators.impact: Cambodia adopted the UNCTIRAL Model Law on E-commerce in 2019 except for the provisions on certification and electronic signatures.

indicators.source_legislation: Lack of adoption of the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Signatures
indicators.impact: Cambodia has not notified its adoption of the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Signatures to the UNCITRAL Secretariat.

indicators.impact: The Lao People’s Democratic Republic (PDR) has become a new participant of both the WTO’s Information Technology Agreement (ITA) and ITA Expansion (ITA II) on January 1st, 2022
