indicators.source_legislation: Decree on Satellite Communications No. 471/GOL 2019
indicators.impact: Decree on Satellite Communications No. 471/GOL (2019) explicitly prohibits the export of satellite communication equipment without prior permission from the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications. Article 51: "Individuals, legal entities or organizations, both domestic and foreign, intending to export all types of satellite communications equipment must obtain permission from the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications"​.

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: Decision on Goods Subject to Licensing Prior to Import or Export No.0333/MOIC 2022
indicators.impact:
Under Decision on Goods Subject to Licensing Prior to Import or Export No. 0333/MOIC (2022), certain goods are required to obtain export licenses. While ICT goods are not explicitly listed, any goods requiring export licensing due to national security or public safety concerns may fall under this rule​.

Article 3 of the Decision on Goods Subject to Licensing Prior to Import or Export No. 0333/MOIC (2022) specifies that certain goods require export licenses. HS code 8517 for Satellite Phones and VSAT are explicitly mentioned in the list of goods. It also includes provisions for any products that may be deemed necessary for licensing due to concerns over national security, public safety, or other public interest considerations. This means that ICT goods are subjected to licensing requirements as determined to fall under these categories

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: Decree on Import and Export of Goods No.114/GoL 2011
indicators.impact:
Decree No. 114/GoL on Import and Export of Goods (2011): The general framework for export controls applies to any goods subject to national security, public safety, or environmental concerns. Export licensing is required for goods in this category, though specific ICT products are not directly highlighted​.

Article 6: The article establishes that goods which have implications for national security, public safety, or environmental concerns must obtain an export license. Although specific ICT products are not explicitly mentioned, any goods that fall under the categories of national security or public safety could require an export license as stipulated by this decree.

indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.source_legislation:
Standard Law (Amended) No.49/NA 2014;

Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No.234 2012
indicators.impact:
Lao Standards is the standards that is adopted by the National Standard Council and promulgated by the Ministry of Science and Technology. Lao Standards, the abbreviation in Lao is “mor lor” and in English is “Lao Standard or “LS” (Article 16 Lao Standards). 

The development of Lao Standards shall comply with the following principles to ensure the conformity with the foreign, regional and international standards (Article 17 Principles for Developing Lao Standards). The use of technical terms for the establishment of standards shall ensure consistent with the terminologies used by the International Standard Organization (ISO) (Article 15 Use of Technical Terms). 

Moreover, individual, legal entity, or organization and the National Standard Council wishing to develop Lao Standard shall submit a proposal to the Ministry of Science and Technology (Article 20 Procedures for Developing Lao Standards). Lao PDR became a signatory to the ASEAN Consultative Committee on Standards and Quality (ACCSQ), ISO, and the International Electrotechnical Commission Asia-Pacific Regional Centre (IEC-APRC). The ISO/IEC Guides 21-1 and 21-2:2005 are adopted.

The Standard Law (Amended) No. 49 encourages international cooperation and explicitly states that the Lao government promotes the involvement of both the domestic and foreign private sectors in standardization activities​. Article 4 (Policy on Standardization) specifically encourages foreign entities to participate in standardization activities, including development, implementation, and management of standards​. This includes participation in the development and implementation of standards, as well as management and inspection, suggesting that there is no formal restriction on foreigners or foreign entities from being involved in the process. 

Additionally, the Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No. 234 (2012): Article 3 (Participation between Public and Private Sectors): This article encourages the private sector, including foreign entities, to participate in the development of standards and conformity assessment procedures​.

Lao PDR has specific technical standards for ICT goods, impacting several product categories under relevant HS codes. These standards, which may differ from international benchmarks, favor products that can easily align with local regulatory requirements. According to Article 8 of the Decision on the Inspection and Certification of ICT Equipment No. 2118/MPT (2018), all imported ICT equipment, including products under HS Code 8517 (telecommunication equipment, e.g., mobile phones, routers) and HS Code 8525 (transmission apparatus), must comply with local standards related to RF, EMC, EMF, SAR, connection, and electrical safety. Article 12 further specifies these technical requirements.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.impact:
There is no explicit provision banning SDoC (Suppliers' Declaration of Conformity) entirely, but Lao PDR regulations emphasize third-party certification for certain products. Specifically, Article 50 (Voluntary Conformity Assessments) of the Standard Law (Amended) outlines that conformity assessment for technical regulations (e.g., products affecting safety) should be conducted by government conformity assessment bodies or accredited third-party entities. This suggests that SDoC might not be sufficient for some regulated product categories​.

According to Article 12 and Article 54, Lao PDR conforms to international standards for third-party certification and accepts conformity assessments from recognized bodies in countries with Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs). This implies that while SDoC is not universally permitted, third-party certifications from certain accredited bodies abroad are accepted.

Article 49 (Self-Conformity Assessment) of the Standard Law permits self-conformity assessment (SDoC) by suppliers or manufacturers, indicating that foreign businesses could use SDoC if the products are not subject to compulsory third-party conformity​. However, for high-risk products such as those involving safety concerns (e.g., EMC/EMI), third-party certification would likely be required. Thus, for some product safety related ICT (e.g., radio transmissions, EMC/EMI): SDoC is generally not allowed, and third-party certification is preferred, especially if covered under an MRA​.

Specifically, ASEAN Framework Agreement on Mutual Recognition Arrangements provides the principles for developing sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangements (MRAs) among ASEAN member states, for instance the ASEAN Sectoral MRA for Electrical and Electronic Equipment (ASEAN EE MRA) 2002. A member state shall accept or recognize the test reports and certifications issued by the testing laboratories and certification bodies of other parties (ASEAN EE MRA Article 3). 

In addition, Article 10 of the Decision on the Management of Telecommunications and ICT No. 3583/MoTC (2022) mandates that equipment under HS Code 8517 and HS Code 8526 (radar apparatus, radio communication equipment) be tested locally to ensure compliance with domestic standards. Article 22 requires the use of certification labels to indicate compliance. These regulations create a framework that can serve as an indirect local content requirement by imposing barriers on non-compliant products, including higher compliance costs and delayed market entry for products that don't meet local standards.

indicators.question_description: Product screening and testing requirements
indicators.source_legislation:
Standard Law (Amended) No.49/NA 2014;

Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No.234 2012
indicators.impact:
Article 8 (Types of Lao Standards) of the Standard Law (Amended) lists categories of products subject to Lao standards, including products, goods, services, and environmental standards​. ICT products that involve radio transmissions or electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) could fall under these categories if they relate to safety or environmental concerns. Article 45 (Standard and Technical Regulation Conformity) mentions that products linked to safety, public health, and environmental protection must comply with standards and technical regulations​. This could include ICT products, especially those with radio transmission and EMC/EMI considerations. Article 25 (Contents of Technical Regulations) of the Standard Law indicates that products falling under technical regulations would require testing and certification, and ICT products likely require compliance with performance and safety standards​). 

Article 46 (Principles of Conformity Assessment) stipulates that Lao PDR allows for self-assessments of conformity, including testing and inspection (for more information about the scope, see Article 5). Testing centers and laboratories shall be accredited or recognized by both domestic and foreign concerned accredited body (Article 68 Testing Centers, Laboratories). Specifically, Article 65 (Accreditation) of the Standard Law (Amended) mandates that testing centers and laboratories must be accredited and recognized by both domestic and foreign accredited bodies. The preparation, adoption and application of conformity assessment procedures shall be applied at least equally between the imported products and domestic products and between products originating in any other country (Article 53.1). 

Moreover, National Accreditation Bureau (LNAB) is a body that is officially recognized the capacity of individuals, legal entities or organizations in performing testing activities and certification of quality. The LNAB provides accreditation services for the accreditation of laboratories, certification and inspection bodies in accordance with the appropriate international ISO/IEC standards and guidance documents issued by the International Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation (ILAC) and the International Accreditation Forum (IAF) (for more information, see Article 67 Rights and Duties of the National Accreditation Bureau). Also, testing centers [and] laboratories shall be accredited or recognized by both domestic and foreign concerned accredited body (Article 68 Testing Centers, Laboratories). 

There is no blanket exemption from testing requirements. All products within the scope of technical regulations or standards in Lao PDR must undergo some form of conformity assessment. Lao PDR has clear measures in place for product testing, with acceptance of third-party results for certain products via MRAs. However, products under national technical regulations must comply with testing requirements through accredited bodies.

indicators.question_description: Deviation from international encryption standards (ISO, IEC, ITU, FIPS, AES, TDES, and ECC)
indicators.source_legislation:
Standard Law (Amended) No.49/NA 2014;

Decree on the Implementation of the Law on Standardization No.234 2012
indicators.impact:
Lao PDR has no policy on encryption standard.

Based on the general principles and obligations under the international agreements to which Lao PDR is a party, including its commitment to WTO and ASEAN guidelines, the country is bound to harmonize its standards, including technical regulations such as those related to encryption, with international norms.

Article 29 of the Standard Law (Amended) mentions that any technical regulations, including those potentially related to encryption, must align with international agreements and treaties to which Lao PDR is a party, such as WTO’s Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade and ASEAN guidelines​. Article 7 of the Decree on the Implementation of the Standard Law highlights the Lao government’s commitment to international cooperation, ensuring that standards and technical regulations (including encryption) are consistent with international agreements​.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.source_legislation:
Decree on E-Commerce No.296/GoL 2021;

Decision on Retail and Wholesale Business No.1005/MOIC.ITD 2015
indicators.impact:
In 2021, foreign investment in e-commerce in Lao PDR is subject to a limit of 90% of the entity’s shares, with a minimum registered capital requirement of LAK 10 billion (approximately USD 1 million). This decree does not replace existing laws and regulations governing specific goods or services, which may have additional requirements, such as licensing, notification, or minimum investment.

Foreign participation in retail and wholesale services is governed by the Decision on Wholesale and Retail Business, No. 1005/MOIC.DTD, dated 22 May 2015. Article 13 of this decision outlines the relevant foreign equity limits:
• A foreign shareholder holding up to 50% of the shares must invest at least LAK 4 billion (approximately USD 423,350).
• For businesses with registered capital between LAK 10 billion (approximately USD 1.05 million) and less than LAK 20 billion (approximately USD 2.1 million), foreign equity participation is capped at 70%.
• For businesses with more than LAK 20 billion in registered capital, foreign investors may hold 100% equity.
These foreign equity limitations apply broadly to the retail and wholesale sectors and can indirectly encompass e-commerce platforms under broader business classifications.

indicators.question_description:
Online purchases and delivery limitations
Exception: Not score limitations on online purchases and delivery applied specifically to products related to consumer protection, notably restrictions on alcoholic beverages, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals.
indicators.source_legislation: Decree on E-Commerce No.296/GoL 2021
indicators.impact: There is no limit on amount of products that can be purchases online and restriction to delivery of products bought online implemented.

indicators.question_description:
Licensing scheme for e-commerce providers (B2B and B2C)
Exception: Licenses pertiaining to other aspects of e-commerce businesses, such as license to operate online payment services and delivery are not captured.
indicators.source_legislation: Decree on E-Commerce No.296/GoL 2021
indicators.impact:
The Decree on E-Commerce No. 296/GoL requires the existing and new e-commerce businesses that trade through their platforms or electronic marketplaces to notify and submit documents to the Ministry of Industry and Commerce to receive an acknowledgment certificate. Traders using e-commerce platforms are required to provide information on goods and services, including their business operator’s information such as name, address, contact information, company registration certificate, and business operation license.

Moreover, electronic marketplace is required to be an incorporated entity and must secure an e-commerce business license from the Ministry. As for technical requirements, electronic marketplaces must obtain a Ministry of Technology and Communications certificate confirming their “technical conformity.” 

The licensing scheme for e-commerce providers, both B2B and B2C, is primarily regulated under the Decree on Electronic Commerce, No. 296/GoL, dated 12 April 2021, which outlines the rules and requirements for business entities that engage in e-commerce activities.

- Registration Requirement: Any entity conducting e-commerce activities (both B2B and B2C) must register with the Ministry of Industry and Commerce. This includes both domestic and foreign entities operating within Lao PDR.
- Types of Activities:
B2B (Business-to-Business): These platforms facilitate transactions between businesses, such as wholesale or service exchanges.
B2C (Business-to-Consumer): These platforms allow businesses to sell directly to consumers through online means.
- Licensing Documentation: To obtain a license, applicants must submit several documents, including:
A completed application form.
A business feasibility study.
Proof of business registration with the Ministry of Industry and Commerce.
Evidence of compliance with standards set by the Ministry of Science and Technology, where applicable​.
- Ongoing Compliance: Licensed e-commerce platforms must regularly report on their business activities and ensure that they comply with the terms of their license. This includes submitting annual reports, maintaining financial transparency, and ensuring the security of customer data​.
This framework ensures that e-commerce operations in Lao PDR, whether B2B or B2C, are regulated to protect consumers, ensure fair competition, and promote compliance with national trade and digital laws.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
There is a requirement for e-commerce platforms in Lao PDR to use a local bank account. Specifically, according to the Decision on Electronic Signatures, No. 1101/MPT, dated 29 May 2020, legal entities applying for an electronic signature certification must submit a certificate of a bank statement from a bank in Lao PDR as part of their application. 

Lao PDR Law on Payment System, Article 9 mandates for a Local Bank Account: Online payment services must utilize local bank accounts for processing payments, including both receipt and disbursement. This ensures compliance with local regulations regarding electronic payments. Article 6 imposes Compliance with Domestic Regulations: Service providers, including those enabling cross-border payments, are required to comply with the regulatory framework set by the Lao PDR authorities. This includes the use of electronic transaction systems approved by relevant ministries, such as the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications and the Bank of the Lao PDR.

Lao PDR Law on Electronic Transactions allows payments over the internet and other forms of electronic transactions, but it emphasizes that financial transactions must align with national security, financial stability, and anti-money laundering standards. Payments should be conducted through legally recognized systems, often implying the need for a local bank as the intermediary.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Notification on VAT obligations from electronic commerce and digital platform services in Lao PDR, No. 0541/MOF 2022
indicators.impact:
The Notification on VAT obligations from electronic commerce and digital platform services in Lao PDR, it is stated that foreign entities providing digital services in Lao PDR must register and fulfill VAT obligations through a local bank account. Specifically, the provider must report transactions and fulfill tax payments through the government’s online system, which requires the use of a local bank account for transactions​. Thus, this implies that setting up a local bank account is essential for both operational and regulatory purposes in Lao PDR. 

Article 2 of the notification on VAT obligations for electronic commerce and digital platform services in Lao PDR explicitly mentions the affected digital services. The services include platforms such as:
 • Streaming Services: Netflix, Apple TV+, Disney+
 • Digital Content and Applications: YouTube, TikTok, JOOX, Humble, Zoom, CODASHOP
 • Social Media Advertising: Facebook, Google
 • Booking Services: Agoda, Booking.com, Airbnb
 • E-commerce Platforms: Shopee, Lazada

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Article 6 (Domain of enforcement). This Law enforces to domestic and foreign individual, entity and organization that engaging in the Lao PDR’s payment system activities in domestic and abroad. 

Article 19 (Electronic Money) states that electronic money is a payment instrument with a money value which stored in the magnetic band, subscriber identity module or program for which the user spend cash or deposit to buy the value of electronic money from payment services provider in order to pay for goods, service and other debt. The unit of electronic money shall be in Kip only.

There is no specific mention of mandated currency requirements for international payments in the context of online payments. However, there are general references to the use of the national currency, Lao Kip, for transactions within the country, and foreign currency regulations apply broadly to cross-border transactions. 

To ensure compliance with these regulations, businesses conducting international payments typically need to adhere to the general foreign exchange laws and regulations. For example, under the Order on the Controlling Foreign Currency, No. 10/PM (2023), Article 2 states that businesses involved in cross-border transactions must use official foreign exchange channels, and payments must follow specific exchange guidelines to ensure the stability of the currency. This article mandates the use of official foreign exchange channels for transactions and provides detailed requirements to ensure compliance with the national foreign exchange policies.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation:
Decision on Electronic Signatures No. 1101/MPT 2020; 

Law on Electronic Transaction (Amended) No. 31/NA 2022
indicators.impact:
There are no specific national standards for payment security in Lao PDR that deviate significantly from recognized international standards. In fact, many of the security requirements in the Decision on Electronic Signatures, No. 1101/MPT (2020), align closely with international standards, such as the Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140-2, which is widely recognized internationally for cryptographic security.

Article 43 specifies that key pair generation for electronic signatures must follow FIPS 140-2 Level 3 standards.
Article 44 outlines cryptographic module controls and also mandates that key management practices follow FIPS 140-2 Level 3 standards, which is an international standard for secure cryptographic operations​.
Thus, while Lao PDR has its own set of regulations, these largely follow global standards for cryptographic security in digital transactions.

Lao PDR seem to align with international standards with respect to electronic transactions and digital signatures, as described in the Law on Electronic Transactions. The specific regulations for secure digital signatures (Article 26) are in compliance with the standards defined by the Ministry of Science and Technology. Additionally, the law allows for the recognition of foreign digital signature certificates if they meet equivalent levels of genuineness and reliability, consistent with international standards (Article 29).

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation:
Law on Payment System (Amendment) No. 45/NA 2023
;
Law on Anti-Money Laundering and
Counter-Financing of Terrorism No. 012/PO 2015
indicators.impact:
There are licensing requirements in place for electronic payment and signature providers in Lao PDR, which include some restrictive conditions:

Law on Payment System (Amendment) No. 45/NA 2023:
1- The requirements to be licensed to operate a payment business are outlined in:
* Article 7: This article specifies that applicants must demonstrate financial capability, have proper infrastructure in place, and comply with technical standards set by the Bank of the Lao PDR.
* Article 8: The applicant must meet specific financial and management requirements, including a minimum capital requirement and a clear organizational structure. Besides financial capacity, it also includes technical expertise, and compliance with legal and regulatory requirements specific to payment systems.
2- Factors for Granting a License and Timeframe: Article 9 specifies the factors considered when granting a license, such as the financial soundness of the applicant, the suitability of its shareholders, and the quality of its management. The decision on licensing must be made within 60 days of receiving a complete application, as outlined in Article 10.
3- The restrictions on the use of the license, including assignment, transfer, or letting someone else use it, are mentioned in Article 15. It prohibits license holders from assigning or transferring the license without prior approval from the licensing authority.

Law on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (AML-CFT):
- Article 19 requires financial institutions to implement AML/CFT programs, which include developing policies and ongoing training, auditing internal procedures, and evaluating AML efforts. These requirements must be adhered to by payment service providers for licensing and compliance.
- Article 20 outlines the need for risk assessment and risk-based management for financial service providers, including payment businesses, to mitigate risks associated with money laundering and terrorism financing.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Decision on Electronic Signatures No. 1101/MPT 2020
indicators.impact:
There are licensing requirements in place for signature providers in Lao PDR, which include some restrictive conditions. 

Article 11 (Minimum Registered Capital) of the Decision on Electronic Signatures, No. 1101/MPT (2020), specifies that entities applying for licenses to provide electronic signature services must have a minimum registered capital of 10 billion Kip. 
Moreover, Article 11(6) (Lao Technical Expertise) requires that service providers employ Lao technical personnel to manage the electronic signature certification system and database.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
There is no explicit ceiling on the maximum amount that can be paid through electronic payment methods. The regulations concerning online and electronic payments seem to focus more on taxation, compliance, and security requirements, rather than setting strict monetary caps for transactions.

Article 30 of the Law on AML-CFT, which states: The Bank of the Lao PDR is responsible for setting thresholds for cash transactions and wire transfers, which must be reported to AMLIO (Anti-Money Laundering Intelligence Office) if they exceed a certain threshold. However, the actual limit values are determined by the Bank of the Lao PDR and are not directly specified (Similarly mentioned in Article 14(13) of the Decree 127/Gov 2020).

However, Decision No:963/BOL - Article 2 specify reporting requirement of Wire transfers in exceeding the specified limit of wire transfers equaling 8,000,000 kip or more per instance, as specified by the AMLIO periodically. Furthermore, Article 11 (Exceptions) Reporting on Wire transfers in exceeding the specified limit is not needed for payment of goods or services through credit cards, debit cards, and others.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
The "Law on Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism" discusses financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions (DNFBPs), such as money transfer service companies and banks, that are subject to regulations aimed at preventing money laundering and the financing of terrorism​. However, it does not explicitly state that specific intermediaries must be used for online payments. Similarly, the Decision on Currency Exchange Service, No. 1026/BOL does not contain provisions that require the use of specific intermediaries for online transactions​.

Article 33 in the Law on Electronic Transactions defines an intermediary as any individual or legal entity that provides services to others for sending, receiving, or storing data messages, hosting temporarily, providing access to communication systems, or handling data messages and electronic documents. This article outlines that intermediaries play a significant role in facilitating electronic transactions. However, the law does not appear to mandate specific intermediaries for online payments. Instead, it establishes the roles and liabilities of intermediaries, such as compliance with regulations and procedures from relevant authorities like the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, and outlines their responsibilities, including liability in certain cases of civil or criminal wrongdoing​.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation:
Law on Electronic Transaction (Amended) No. 31/NA 2022;

Decision on Electronic Signatures No. 1101/MPT 2020
indicators.impact:
There is no requirements mandating the use of specific intermediaries for online payments. Restrictions on Secure Digital Signature Providers: Article 36 of the Law on Electronic Transactions prohibits digital signature providers from engaging in fraudulent activities or misusing personal information. They are also restricted from creating, using, or publishing digital signatures for any unlawful purposes, and from using information in ways that harm national stability, security, or social order.

Article 36 details the following prohibitions: Providing false information in registration applications. Using personal data for purposes other than stated. Engaging in unauthorized secure digital certification activities. Misusing signature certification services. Facilitating transactions that cause national security risks​.

Intermediary Liabilities: Article 38 of the Law on Electronic Transactions defines restrictions for intermediaries (e.g., payment processors, hosting services). Intermediaries are prohibited from: Providing online transaction services without proper authorization. Facilitating unlawful activities that could endanger national security or social order. Monitoring the contents of electronic messages for which they are not responsible, unless required by law.

Article 35 emphasizes the intermediary’s liability if they knowingly process transactions that violate legal or security protocols​. Prohibitions for Users of Digital Signature Services:

Article 37 of the Law on Electronic Transactions restricts users of digital signature services from: Using digital signatures for fraudulent purposes. Providing false information in digital signature applications. Continuing to use invalid digital signatures.
Engaging in unlawful activities through digital signatures that affect national stability. These restrictions aim to prevent users from exploiting digital signatures for malicious activities​

indicators.question_description: Low De Minimis
indicators.impact: Lao PDR did not have a de minimis rule until 2020. An Amendment of Law on Customs 2020 introduces a de minimis threshold for goods exempt from customs duties is set at 1,500,000 LAK (around 150 USD) (amended Article 94 Exemption of Customs Duties). This threshold applies to non-commercial imported goods, such as personal effects. For example, goods worth no more than this amount are subject to customs duty exemption.

indicators.question_description: Domain name requirements
indicators.source_legislation:
Decree on the Management and Use of Internet, and Domain Name of the Lao PDR No.164/Gov;

Law on Telecommunications No.09/NA 2011
indicators.impact:
The Decree No. 164/Gov Article 9 states that the National Internet Center (NIC) is the body that authorizes individual, legal entity and organization both within the country and abroad to be a sole service provider related to Domain Name in the Lao PDR. Individual, legal entities and organizations who wish to provide the service and use the internet under the Domain Name “.la” shall be registered with the National Internet Center. Individual and legal entity existed within the country and in abroad engaging in Internet related business can register and use the system of Domain name ".la" (Article 10). 

There are no specific references or articles requiring a physical presence or a local representative to register a local domain name for conducting electronic retail in Lao PDR. Additionally, there are no explicit restrictions related to domain name registration for electronic commerce. The laws primarily regulate electronic transactions, digital signatures, and service providers but do not impose strict requirements on the registration of domain names for retail businesses that involve the need for local physical presence or representative.

Lao PDR Law on Telecommunications No. 09/NA (2011), Article 12 does not mention specific conditions like physical presence, local representative, or other limitations. It only mentions that the Ministry oversees the assignment and management of domain names, without specifying additional criteria or restrictions for registrants. Article 13 does not mention specific conditions like physical presence, local representative, or other limitations. It only states that individuals, legal entities, or organizations must register their domain names with the telecommunication customer services or the office of Posts and Telecommunications.

indicators.source_legislation:

Decree on E-Commerce No.296/GoL 2021
indicators.impact:
Lao PDR does not impose any local presence requirements for digital services providers. 

The Decree on Electronic Commerce and the Law on Electronic Transactions do not explicitly require a local physical presence or a local representative for conducting electronic retail.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Law on Consumer Protection No.02/NA 2010
indicators.impact: The Law on Consumer Protection No. 02/NA, dated 30 June 2010, consumer protection laws in Lao PDR apply to all goods and services, including those sold online. Article 1 (Objectives) and Article 2 (Consumer Protection) outline the general objectives and scope of consumer protection, including the protection of consumers' rights, safety, and legitimate interests from impacts resulting from the consumption of goods and services​. Article 7 (Scope of Application) specifies that the law applies to individuals, legal entities, and organizations operating within the country, including those conducting online commerce, and thus consumer protection is applicable to e-commerce. This suggests that consumer protection laws are applicable to online commerce in the country​.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection

indicators.question_description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
indicators.source_legislation: Public Procurement Act 2064 (2007)
indicators.impact:
According to the Public Procurement Act 2064 (2007) Sections 15 in the Public Procurement Act, foreign enterprises can participate in public procurement in Nepal when goods cannot be procured at a competitive price from more than one supplier within Nepal, when there is no national bid has been submitted, or when the goods to be procured are certified by a public entity as complex and of special nature.

Section 15 (International level bidding): 
(1) While making invitation to bid pursuant to this Act, an international level bid shall be invited in any of the following
conditions:- 
(a) Where the goods or construction works as requisitioned by a Public Entity are not available under competitive price from
more than one construction entrepreneur or supplier within the State of Nepal,
(b) Where no bid was submitted in response to invitation to national level bidding for the procurement of goods, construction works or other services, and the same has to be procured from abroad,
(c) Where under an agreement entered into with a donor party, foreign goods or construction works have to be procured from
foreign assistance source,
(d) Where the Public Entity has certified that the goods or construction works, being of complex and special nature, have to be procured through an international level bidding.

(2) A notice on invitation to international bidding as referred to in this Section shall be published in English language; and all bidding or prequalification documents shall have to be made available in the English language.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation:
Public Procurement Regulation 2064 (2007) 

Standard Guide on Bid Evaluation: Procurement of Works and Goods 2002
indicators.impact:
Procurement regulated by Section 17 in the regulations (Goods Manufactured in Nepal to be Procured), in procuring goods by selecting any method as referred to in these Regulations, a Public Entity shall have to procure Nepali goods even if the price of the goods produced in Nepal is higher by up to ten percent than the foreign goods. 

Preference in international bidding regulated by Section 31 F in the regulations: This measure gives preference to domestic firms, organizations, or companies when public procurement is done through international bidding. If a domestic entity (either participating singly or through a joint venture with other domestic entities) bids a price that is up to 5% higher than the lowest bid made by a foreign entity, the domestic entity may still be accepted. This rule specifically applies to situations where international bidding is involved.

Moreover, the standard guide on bid evaluation also clarifies in section 3.2 on Preference for Domestically Manufactured Goods that bids can be classified into 3 categories:
Category I - bids offering goods manufactured in Nepal which meet the minimum domestic value added requirement; Category II - bids offering other goods manufactured in Nepal; and 
Category III - bids offering imported goods. 
c) The lowest evaluated bids shall be compared. If a bid from Category I or II is the lowest, it will be awarded the contract. d) If the lowest bid is from Category III, it will be compared with the lowest bid from Category I.

indicators.impact: Schedule (Relating to sub-section (2) of Section 3) lists the industries or business restricted for foreign investment: While, foreign investment in consultancy services is subject to a maximum foreign equity limit of 51%, Foreign investment is prohibited in "7. indicators.question_description: Joint venture requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act 2075 (2019)
indicators.impact: There are no strict requirements to engage in joint ventures in order to invest or operate in sectors relevant to the digital economy in sectors relevant for digital trade. Section 4 in the Act (2019) states that "Foreign investment may be made individually or jointly" but does not impose it as a requirement. Specifically, Section 4 states that a foreign investor may make foreign investment individually or jointly or by establishing an industry jointly with an industry established in Nepal or a Nepali citizen.

indicators.question_description: Nationality or residency requirements for board of directors or managers
indicators.source_legislation: Company Act 2063 (2006)
indicators.impact:
As per Section 185 of the Act is mandatory for companies with paid up capital more than 10 million rupees to employ a company secretary. Company secretary must be a Nepali national. Company secretary is responsible for keeping and updating records of the company, for calling general meetings, for keeping records of the decisions of these meetings, for receiving grievances of shareholders, etc.

Moreover, Chapter 6 of the Act regulates board of directors, including the required number and qualifications. However, there is no nationality or residency requirement for directors in Nepal.

indicators.question_description: Nationality or residency requirements for board of directors or managers
indicators.source_legislation: Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act 2075 (2019)
indicators.impact:
According to section 27 on the "Provision relating to experts, top-level technical and managerial employees": (1) An industry with foreign investment shall fulfill the positions of experts in its top-level management, high-level technical, managerial employees or technical employees from amongst the Nepali citizens." Although this section is not applied to board of directors, it is applicable to regulate managers.

Specifically, Section 27 stipulates that (1) An industry with foreign investment shall fulfill the positions of experts in its top-level management, high-level technical, managerial employees or technical employees from amongst the Nepali citizens.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), if an industry with foreign investment cannot fulfil the positions of experts in its top-level management, high-level technical, managerial employees or technical employees from amongst the Nepali citizens and it is necessary to transfer technical knowledge or skill through any technical or expert of another country in such an industry, the industry may employee any foreign citizen in accordance with the prevailing law.
(3) The concerned industry shall provide details relating to the foreign citizens employed in accordance with sub-section (2) to the Department. The Department shall provide the details also to the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of
Home Affairs and Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Security.
4) The employees and workers employed in any industry with foreign investment in accordance with sub-section (2) shall comply with the terms and conditions referred to in the prevailing Nepal law.

indicators.question_description: Nationality or residency requirements for board of directors or managers
indicators.impact:
Section 22 of the Amendment in 2017, Section 4(A) of amendment of the 1992 Act in 1998 and Section 13(1) of the labour rules do not allow hiring foreign workers if workers, including managers, with similar skills are found in the country. 

'Labour Rules', which came into effect in 2018, slightly relaxed this provision by allowing a company with foreign investment to have up to three foreign workers without performing the labor market test. The labor market test entails publishing the job vacancy in a daily newspaper. A foreign worker could be hired only if it can be shown that no Nepali national with the required skill could be found who could perform the job announced in the job vacancy. Therefore, foreign managers can still be hired if conditions are met.

Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act 2075 (2019); 

The Public Private Partnership and Investment Act 2075 (2019)
indicators.impact:
According to section 15 (Application to be made for approval to make foreign investment), except for a few sectors mentioned in the negative list, foreign investment is allowed. However, foreign investment in all the sector is subject to screening (approval) requirement. The current foreign investment law requires foreign investor wishing to make investment file an application to the foreign investment approving body. The application requires setting out the details of the investment, accompanied by a time schedule for bringing the investment into Nepal and action plan of the investment. Other procedures such as registration at different government agencies can be carried out only after the foreign investment approval body provides the approval. 

In the PPP and Investment Act, chapter 2 section 3 mentions the "Approval of Investment requirement. "The Board shall approve investment of the project having the costs estimate of six billion rupees or more"

indicators.question_description: Commercial presence requirements to offer cross-border services in sectors relevant to digital trade
indicators.impact: Circular issued by Nepal Rastra Bank (Nepal's Central Bank) has provisions whereby payments can be made in foreign currency to foreign service providers who supply their services without having commercial presence in the country. According to circular issued in 2012, individual/association/organization can make payments (up to US$10,000) to foreign service providers (cannot be an individual) through banks and financial institutions. According to circular issued in 2015, firm/company/organization can, through banks and financial institutions, remit payments of US$ 10,000 or less to foreign service providers. For payments more than US$10,000 approval of regulator is needed and application to Nepal Rastra Bank has to be filed.

indicators.question_description: Patent application issues
indicators.source_legislation: Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022 (1965)
indicators.impact:
Under Section 21B (Title Not to be valid Unless Registered in Nepal), foreign patents are not valid in Nepal unless they are registered in Nepal. However, as states in Section 21C (Registration of Foreign patents, Designs and Trade-Marks), foreign patents may be registered in Nepal without conducting any inquiries if the application for patent registration is accompanied with certificate of patent registration in a foreign country. 

Furthermore, Nepal is also a party to the 'Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property' since 2001.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022 (1965)
indicators.impact:
Nepal’s Patent, Design and Trademark Act, 2022 (1965) provides mechanisms for patent enforcement through civil and administrative procedures. However, the Act does not explicitly detail provisional measures.

Throughout the Act, there are sections that provide the penalty and punishment for violation of patent, trademarks and copying of designs. For instance, section 3 states how to acquire patent rights and Section 11. provides information on the Penalty for violation of Section 3: A person, who commits any of the acts, shall be fined as per gravity of offense by the order of the Department and the goods or commodities related to the offense shall be confiscated :
(a) A fine of upto Five Hundred Thousand Rupees for committing an offense mentioned in Sud-section 2 of Section 3 .
(b) A fine of upto Two Hundred and Fifty Thousand (Two lac fifty thousand ) Rupees for committing an attempt or abetment of an offense mentioned in Sud-section (2) of Section 3.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation:
Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022 (1965); 

Department of Industries
indicators.impact: Nepal's patent enforcement issues seem to be generally affecting all sectors and there are no current reports of any specific issues affecting the digital economy. The only law that governs Patent enforcement in the Patent, Design and Trademark Act of 1965.

indicators.question_description: Lack of copyright framework and exceptions
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Act 2059 (2002)
indicators.impact: Nepal's copyright law, specifically Chapter 4 Sections 16-23 regarding "Circumstances where the copyrighted materials can be used without authorization", make exceptions for both fair use and fair dealing. Section 17 allows for 'fair use' of portions of published work by making citations to the source and author's name. Furthurmore, fair dealing exceptions are made in the case of reproduction for personal use; reproduction for teaching and learning; reproduction by library and archives; reproduction, broadcast and communication for providing information to the general public; public exhibition, etc.

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Act 2059 (2002)
indicators.impact:
Nepal's copyright law Chapter 6 explores the infringement of Protected Right and Punishment. Section 27, 28 and 29 mention punishments on infringement of protected right, unauthorised copy and other punishments. Under these sections, infringer can be fines 10,000 to 100000 NPR or imprisonment for 6 months (escalating with every instance). Under chapter 7, sections 32 to 34 mention the powers to seize and destroy copyrighted work and stop the importation of unauthorised copies.

In 2021, eSewa posted an almost identical artwork to the 'Kauda' artwork posted by the Instagram Page "KreativeKira" belonging to an artist based in Australia. The copyright act (2059) is too outdated to deal with the copyright infringements online and the legal provisions are too complex to pursue a legal route.

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.source_legislation:
The Telecommunications Act 2053 (1997); 

The Infrastructure Sharing Bylaw 2078
indicators.impact:
The Telecommunicaions Act under Section 31 (Interconnection and Use of Telecommunications System Allowed) does not mandate but encourages sharing of information systems (equipment or series of equipment used or to be used for the Telecommunications). Specifically, Section 31 (1) The Licensee shall be allowed to mutually connect the Telecommunications System developed by him with the Telecommunications System developed by other Licensee
and use it. (2) If a Licensee requests, to connect and use the Telecommunications System developed
by another Licensee the Licensee shall be allowed to connect and use on the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon or on the terms and conditions determined by the Authority, if such agreement could not be reached.

However, the Bylaw created under Section 62 of the Act mandates National Telecommunications Authority licensees to jointly use passive infrastructure, including towers, optical fibre, land, building, battery, and diesel generators, and sets maximum monthly access charges. Sharing of passive telecommunications infrastructure is allowed on the basis of principles of non-discrimination and free competition. Sharing of active infrastructure (Base Transmitter Station (BTS), Node B, eNodeB, radio spectrum, antenna, feeder cable, radio access network (RAN). microwave radio equipment, billing platform, switching system, router, base station controller (BSC), radio network controller (RNC), and similar electronics infrastructure) is not allowed.

indicators.source_legislation:
The Telecommunications Act 2053 (1997);

Management Information System Vol.25
indicators.impact:
There is no requirement for functional and accounting separations for operators with significant market power. Section 33 of the Telecommunication Act requires that the licensee shall submit a description of the telecommunication service and details of incomes and expenses audited by a recognized auditor to the Authority in each fiscal year, but it does not specify for the accounting separation requirement.

However, in the Management Information System issued by the Nepal Telecommunications Authority 2009, there is a mention of a Expression of Interest published by the Nepal Telecommunications Authority for accounting separation guidelines under the Decision No.1619. It seems that while it is not a requirement in the Act itself, it may be be applied in practice.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.source_legislation: The Telecommunications Act 2053 (1997)
indicators.impact:
According to Chapter 5 (Provisions for License) in the Act, the operator of any telecommunications service must hold a license (Section 21). The Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA) is responsible for determining the number of licenses to be issued for each telecommunications service and publishing a public notice specifying the time limit to submit applications for a telecommunications license. 

Specifically, Section 22(1) provides that the Authority shall, before issuing any Licence relating to any Telecommunications Service other than those prescribed pursuant to sub-section (2) of Section 23, determine the number of Licence to be issued for such service and types of Telecommunications and publish a public notice specifying the time limit to submits application for the Licence. Under Section 22(2) of the Act prescribes the five-year exclusivity period. After issuing a license for a telecommunications service, no other licenses for the same service will be granted for five years except in cases where the licensee fails to provide the service or additional providers are deemed necessary.

Section 23(1) stipulates that the person, who desires to operate the Telecommunications Service pursuant to this Act and has capital, technical expertise and professional experience as prescribed, shall have to submit an application to the Authority, setting out the particulars as prescribed along with economic and technical study report as well as work plan in connection with the Telecommunications Service to be operated.

indicators.question_description: Lack of independent telecom authority
indicators.source_legislation: The Telecommunications Act 2053 (1997)
indicators.impact:
The Telecommunications Act 2053 (1997) under chapter 2 establishes that Nepal has an telecommunications authority, the Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA). Under section 3, a Nepal Telecommunications Authority is established with a view to managing and regularizing the Telecommunications Service and making it reliable and easily available to the public. Section 4, the Authority "shall be an autonomous and corporate body with perpetual succession":
(1) The Authority shall be an autonomous and corporate body with perpetual succession.
(2) The Authority shall have its own seal to carry out its functions.
(3) The Authority may, like an individual, acquire, use or otherwise manage movable and immovable property.
(4) The Authority may, like an individual, sue and be sued by its name.

However, government can override the NTA. In chapter 4, section 18. Power of His Majesty's Government to Operate or Cause to Operate theTelecommunications Service by itself: Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, His Majesty's Government may operate the Telecommunications Service by itself or cause it to be operated.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.source_legislation: The Privacy Act 2075 (2018)
indicators.impact: The Privacy Act acts as a legal framework for data protection as it is concerned with the protection and safe use of personal data. The Act requires consent to be obtained for collecting personal or family data of any person, and requires that data be used only for the purpose for which data has been collected. Consent is required to publish, or caused to be published, the details related to the following forms of data: health examination, property and income generation, employment, family matters, biometric details and thumb impression, electronic signature, political affiliation and election, and business or transactions. This information is summrised from sections throughout the document, in particular, chapter 2, section 3 Privacy of body and personal life of person, Chapter 6, section 12. To have privacy of data, chapter 9, section 19 to have privacy of electronic means, section 26, not to use personal information without consent.

indicators.question_description: User identify requirements
indicators.impact:
The Interim Directives for the Implementation of National Equipment Identity Registry (NEIR)-2072's objective is to outlines the procedures and policies regarding Equipment Identity Register (EIR) implementation in Nepal and is issued to accomplish the following objectives:
a. To meet the requirements for the national and consumer security
b. To identify the genuine mobile handsets and make the fake and non-genuine handsets inoperable in Nepal
c. To enable tracking/blocking of mobile handset that is lost/ stolen.
d. To encourage to import and sell genuine mobile handsets
e. To minimize the possible grey market and encourage mobile handsets import through the custom office(s).

In the Mobile Device Management System Bylaws, 2079 (2022), Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA) has framed these Bylaws for the implementation of Equipment Identity Register (EIR) system to ensure national and consumer security, to identify the genuine mobile handsets and make the fake and non-genuine handsets inoperable in Nepal, to enable tracking/blocking of mobile handset that is lost/stolen, to encourage import and sell of genuine mobile handsets and to eradicate grey market. 
Under section 8 Registration of Mobile Devices states that people importing or using a phone for personal/non-commercial use are required to register IMEI and SIM card.

Directives on the Operation of Social Networking (2023) is issued under the Electronic Transactions Act 2008. indicators.impact:
Standards are mostly based on international standards (such as those of the ISO,the IEC, and the Codex Alimentarius) or well-known national standards according to WTO's Trade Policy Review of Nepal conducted in 2018. 

The Nepal Standards (Certification Mark) Act, 2037 (1980) forms the Nepal Standards Coucil and Bureau of Standards " for determining the standard of any goods for the welfare of the public and for the use of the marks certifying the standard on such goods,".

While not specifically referring to foreign participation in standard-setting bodies, according to the draft National Standardization Strategy of 2021-2023, the sub-committee, technical committee, and the council currently responsible for drafting standards are multi-stakeholder committees representing "governments and regulators, manufacturers, consumers, academic institutions, experts, industry associations and users" under section 2.3 Constitution of Committees. Furthermore, current procedure for standard development in Nepal includes publication of committee draft for public comment and review of the comments and incorporation into the draft. Under section 2.5 Current Status of Standarization Practices, the strategy states that "Participation in international activities: Participation in international standardization activity will increase national capability as well as promote national interest in the field. These activities are limited and need to be enhanced. Nepal has to take more benefit from the ISO and upgrade its membership status in IEC."

indicators.question_description: Deviation from international encryption standards (ISO, IEC, ITU, FIPS, AES, TDES, and ECC)
indicators.source_legislation: Electronics Transactions Rules, 2064 (2007)
indicators.impact:
Nepal prescribes the use of international standards for specifying quality standards for services related to information technology. Under Chapter 2, Rule 6 addresses quality standard concerning information fechnology to be maintained by the Certifying Authority. 
(1) The parameter of standard of quality of service relating to information technology required to be maintained by the Certifying Authority shall be such as may be specified, from time to time, by the Controller. 
(2) Where the quality standard is not specified under Sub-rule (1), the parameter of a quality standard of service relating to information technology to be maintained by the Certifying Authority shall be as specified in Schedule 1. 
(3) The parameter of quality standard specified by the Controller under Sub-rule (1) shall have to make public by publication of notice in any national-level daily newspaper.

Regarding Schedule-1 relating to Sub-rule (2) of Rule 6, the Certifying Authority may bring into use the open standard and information technology system of reliable standards recognized in the world. To carry out different types of electronic transaction, at least the following standards shall have to maintain. 

For digital encryption and digital signature, PKCS #7 is prescribed as the minimum standard for digital encryption. PKCS #7 is a standard syntax for storing signed and/or encrypted data, and it is one of the family of standards called Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) created by RSA Laboratories. It is used for the generation and verification of digital signatures and certificates managed by a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). PKCS #7 proposes a broad-spectrum syntax and format for creating digital signatures, which is elaborated in detail in RFC 2315Use of international standards ("reliable standards recognized in the world") is prescribed while specifying quality standard for services relating to information technology. PKCS #7 is prescribed as the minimum standard for digital encryption.

Furthermore, they need license from Nepal Rastra Bank (Nepal's Central Bank) to operate as Payment Service Provider (PSP) or Payment System Operator (PSO). indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact: According to Section 1.2 of the Nepal's Central Bank's Directive, there is a maximum threshold on daily and monthly transaction amount on transactions carried out through card, internet banking, mobile banking, and e-wallets. For instance, the current limit, as amended in the 2020 directive, for debit card transactions is per transaction limit of 25,000 rupees, per day limit of 100,000 rupees, and per month limit of 400,000 rupees. Similarly, current transactions limit for mobile banking is Rs 200,000 per day and 1 million rupees per month. Current transactions limit for internet banking (merchant payment) is 1 million rupees per day and 3 million rupees per month. Similarly, current transactions limit for e-wallets is 25,000 rupees per transaction, Rs 25,000 per day, and 500,000 rupees per month.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Payment Systems Oversight Report, 2023/2024; Nepal Clearing House Limited
indicators.impact:
According to Table 5 of the Real Time Gross Settlement System in Nepal, there is a mandatory threshold for transaction in different currencies. These limits apply to cross-border and large-value transactions and could impact international retail payments on e-commerce websites: 
NPR: Minimum limit NPR 200,000; Mandatory threshold NPR 2 million or above
USD: Minimum limit USD 2,000; Mandatory threshold USD 20,000 or above
EUR: Minimum limit EUR 2,000; Mandatory threshold EUR 20,000 or above
GBP: Minimum limit GBP 2,000; Mandatory threshold GBP 20,000 or above
JPY: Minimum limit JPY 200,000; Mandatory threshold JPY 2 million or above​.

As mentioned on the NCHL website there is a limit of NRs. 3,00,000 amount paid by NepalPay QR. Nepal Clearing House Ltd. (NCHL) is a public limited company established on 23rd December, 2008 (8 Poush 2065) under the leadership and guidance of Nepal Rastra Bank (The Central Bank of Nepal).

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation: Cross-border Payments Operating Rules
indicators.impact:
The operating rules states that under 3.1 Participant Enrollment "The membership for cross-border transaction shall be open and eligible to all the existing direct members (BFIs) and technical members (PSPs) of Retail Payment Switch (RPS) and National Payments Interface (NPI). While direct members (BFIs) will have access to both cross border P2P and P2M as per the rules/ guidelines of Cross Border Payments Operating Rules, whereas the technical members (PSPs) will be allowed for incoming and outgoing P2P & P2M only to the extent allowed by Nepal Rastra Bank."

The Rules do not explicitly mandate the use of specific intermediaries, but participation by technical members (PSPs) is subject to the discretion of Nepal Rastra Bank. This creates ambiguity around whether access is broadly available or selectively granted, depending on how the Bank exercises its authority.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.source_legislation:
PaymentSystems Oversight Report, 2023/2024; 

Asset (Money) Laundering Prevention Act, 2064 (2008)
indicators.impact:
There is no other restrictions found for online payment in Nepal. The report highlights the problem of unverified KYC where some PSPs are permitting transactions up to NPR. 5,000 for KYCunverified customers which might lead to misuse of the platform for illegal activities, such as money laundering, fraud, or terrorism financing.

However, the Asset Laundering Act in Chapter 3 - "Provision Relating to Identity, Transactions and Details of the Customers" requires any bank, financial institution or non financial Institution shall maintain clear record of identity of a person while establishing any kind of business relationship with such person or while transacting the amount above the threshold, either in a single transaction or in series of transactions as prescribed by Rastra Bank from time to time by publishing a notice.

indicators.source_legislation:

indicators.impact:
In order to register a domain in Nepal, foreign companies are required to have an official presence in the country. This can be in the form of a joint venture, partnership, agent, or a licensee. In order to register a domain in Nepal, foreign companies are required to set branch or liaison office in Nepal. According to the policy for domain name registration under NP CCTLD, only foreign companies that register in Nepal or register their trade name (trademark) with the government can register a '.np' domain.

Specifically, under Clause 13, foreign corporation/multi-national company can only register domain that suggests its company or trade name and cannot register other generic domain. However, the applicant must have registered its company/trade name with Nepal Government. According to Nepal's official .np Domain Registration website, the required documents for foreign entities to register NP domain are: In case of foreign entities registered in Nepal : Certificate of registration of branch or liaison office or Certificate of affiliation with Social Welfare Council. This indicates minimum local administrative requirements for domain name requirements.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Consumer Protection Act 2075 (2018)
indicators.impact:
The Consumer Protection Act includes provisions for the right of easy access to goods or services, the right to choose quality goods or services at the fair competitive price, the right to be informed of the price, quantity, purity, quality of the goods and services, etc. For instance, Section 3 addresses the consumer rights to obtain quality goods and services. The Government of Nepal shall regulate the supplies, price, quality, measurement, label, advertisement of the goods and services regularly in order to protect the rights of the consumers (Section 4). 

Although the Act does not explicitly mention e-commerce, the Act is comprehensive in its scope, extending its protections to consumers engaging in e-commerce. The term "consumer" refers to a person or institution that consumes or uses any goods or services (Section 2(d)).

While there is no official document available yet, the Act puts in place ways to protect consumer rights, Eg., Consumers have the right to return products that do not match their descriptions without any penalty. In these cases, the seller must accept the return and give a replacement item of the same value, including taxes.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation: Directives on the Operation of Social Networking (2023) (सामाजिक सञ्जालको प्रयोगलाई व्यवस्थित गर्ने निर्देशिका, २०८०)
indicators.impact:
Directives on the Operation of Social Networking (2023) is issued under the Electronic Transactions Act 2008.

The provisions under Articles 5, 6, and 7 of the Directives establish a local presence requirement for social network platforms operating in Nepal. Article 6 (Provision of Point of Contact to be made) explicitly requires all social network platform operators to arrange a point of contact within Nepal for the purpose of addressing user grievances. In cases where a platform does not have an office in Nepal at the time the Directives come into force, the operator must either establish an office or designate a contact person within three months.

Additionally, Article 5 (Classification of Social Network Platform and Grievance Handling) requires platforms with more than 100,000 users—defined as “big social network platforms”—to appoint a residential grievance handling officer and a compliance officer responsible for monitoring adherence to self-regulation obligations. These officers must be available at the local point of contact. Article 7 (Responsibilities of Point of Contact) prescribes responsibilities of point of contact, such as identify contents disseminated in social networks that are contrary to these Directives.

indicators.impact:
Government Procurement Principle 2 states that government entities "[t]reat all suppliers equally – we don’t discriminate (this is part of our international obligations)." Government Procurement Rule 3 (non-discrimination and offsets) provides that suppliers must not be discriminated against because of the country the goods, services or works that they come from or their degree of foreign ownership or foreign business affiliations. The Government Electronic Tenders Service (GETS) is New Zealand's central online platform for advertising government procurement opportunities, including contracts for ICT goods and services. It enables both domestic and foreign suppliers to access tender documents and submit responses. GETS is freely accessible, promoting open competition and removing barriers for international suppliers.

indicators.source_legislation:
Companies Act 1993;

Companies Act Regulations 1994
indicators.impact:
Since May 2015, per Section 10 of the Companies Act 1993, a company incorporated in New Zealand has been required to have at least one director living in New Zealand, or living in an 'enforcement country' and is a director of a company that is registered in that enforcement country. Specifically, under Section 10, all New Zealand companies must have at least one director who lives in: New Zealand, or Australia, and who is a director of a company incorporated in Australia.

Per Section 12 of the Companies Act Regulations 1994, the only enforcement country currently named in the regulations is Australia. The residency requirement does not apply to a branch of an overseas company registered in New Zealand which merely "carries on business" in New Zealand, as defined in Section 332 of the Companies Act.

indicators.impact:

indicators.question_description:
Screening of investment and acquisitions
Exception: Anti-trust measures related to M&A are not considered a restriction, unless discriminatory.
indicators.impact:
Sectors relevant to digital trade are subject to New Zealand’s screening regime, the same as any other sector. 

As of June 2020, a foreign investment is potentially subject to a three-stage investment screening process.

Overseas investors need consent to invest in some sensitive New Zealand assets. Per Section 10 and 11 of the Overseas Investment Act of 2005, a foreign investor in a significant business asset must obtain consent. The Act also sets the criteria for when consent is required, primarily involving sensitive land (Section 12). Section 13 lays out what constitutes a significant business asset (generally, an investment activity that results in a 25% or greater ownership or whose value exceeds NZD 100 million (USD 71 million)). Section 18 provides criteria for approval of investment in significant business assets (the investor test), which include the necessary business experience and financial acumen to manage the investment. 

Some overseas investment consent applications may also be subject to a national interest assessment. If a consent application involves a strategically important business or a non-New Zealand Government Investor, it will require a mandatory national interest assessment. Strategically important businesses are businesses operating in a range of areas that are considered to be strategically important, including businesses involved in military or dual-use technology, ports or airports, electricity, water, telecommunications, and financial market infrastructure. 

Additionally, a foreign investment can be subject to the national interest test under the Urgent Measures Act of 2020. If a transaction is contrary to national interest, consent may be declined, per Section 20C. According to Section 20A, this kind of transactions includes investment in strategically important businesses, as laid out in the Foreign Investment Policy and National Interest Guidance, such as telecommunications infrastructure and media entities. 

Finally, these investment activities can also be subject to 'call in transactions," under which the government may block, impose conditions on, or order disposal of the activities if they pose a threat to national security or public order (Part 3 of the Urgent Measures Act). Specifically, a discretionary national interest assessment occurs if the relevant Minister calls-in the transaction. This power is intended to be used rarely. 

As part of the national interest assessment, a relevant New Zealand Minister will determine whether an investment would be contrary to New Zealand’s national interest prior to a decision being made to grant consent to an application.

indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Act 1994
indicators.impact: Fair dealing exceptions are provided in Sections 40 to 92 of the Copyright Act 1994. They include fair dealing for: the purposes of criticism, review and news reporting (Section 42), the purposes of research or private study (Section 43), educational purposes (Sections 44 to 48), copying by librarians or archivists (Sections 51 to 56), public administration (Sections 58-66), literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works (Sections 67 to 78), computer programs, sound recordings, and films (Sections 79 to 81A), communication works (Sections 82 to 91), and adaptations (Sections 92-93). indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Act 1994
indicators.impact:
The courts have a wide range of civil remedies available to compensate copyright owners for proven incidences of copyright infringement. These include: interim injunctions, search orders for the preservation of evidence, damages or orders to account for profits and ‘mandatory’ injunctions, including orders to deliver up infringing goods. If the successful civil enforcement actions do not lead to the infringement ceasing, the Copyright Act 1994 contains criminal offences for the infringement of copyright works for commercial gain. A person convicted for such activity may be imprisoned for up to five years or fined up to NZD 150,000. The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is empowered to initiate criminal prosecution against copyright piracy. 

The manufacture, importation, sale, distribution, lease, offer, or advertisement of technological protection measure circumvention devices (that is, devices capable of circumventing encryption or other measures designed to prevent the infringement of a copyright work) is prohibited under the Copyright Act.

Part 6 of "Copyright Act 1994" indicates the rights and remedies of copyright owner. Section 120: Copyright infringement is actionable by the copyright owner, who can seek relief through damages, injunctions, or other means. Section 121: Outlines the provisions for damages in infringement cases. If the infringer was unaware of the copyright, the plaintiff may be entitled to an account of profits instead of damages. Section 122: Allows for the court to order the delivery of infringing copies or objects to the copyright owner in civil proceedings 

"Copyright Act 1994" also provides terms regarding provisional measures. Section 197: Empowers the court to order the delivery of illicit recordings in civil proceedings if someone possesses these recordings in the course of business​. Section 202: The recordings must be retained until a decision is made, ensuring they are not destroyed or further distributed.
