indicators.question_description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
indicators.impact:
No mandatory disclosure of trade secrets is found.

Under New Zealand civil law there is no specific legislation that governs the protection of “trade secrets”. New Zealand does not have a specific law that mandates the disclosure of trade secrets. However, in certain situations, such as legal proceedings (Evidence Act 2006) or interactions with government agencies (for health, safety, or environmental regulations) (Official Information Act 1982), some disclosure may be required. These instances are generally governed by confidentiality protections.

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.source_legislation: Crimes Act 1961
indicators.impact:
Under New Zealand civil law there is no specific legislation that governs the protection of “trade secrets”. Before civil courts the protection of secret information is largely addressed by the judge-made action for breach of confidence.

However, the Crimes Act 1961 section 230 does make reference to trade secrets, which are defined as information that (a) is, or has the potential to be, used industrially or commercially; and (b) is not generally available in industrial or commercial use; and (c) has economic value or potential economic value to the possessor of the information; and (d) is the subject of all reasonable efforts to preserve its secrecy. 
According to the Crimes Act, section 230, dishonestly and without claim of right, taking, obtaining, or copying trade secrets is illegal. A person can be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years, if they had the intent to obtain any pecuniary advantage or to cause loss to any other person. 

However, it is reported that this definition has not been considered or applied in any case law and has seemingly not directly influenced the civil law.

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.source_legislation: Telecommunications Act 2001
indicators.impact:
Passive sharing is not mandated, but it is practiced in the market. 

Schedule 1, Part 3 of the Telecommunications Act 2001 provides a framework for voluntary co-location of cellular infrastructure. Under the "Co-location on Cellular Mobile Transmission Sites" section, this applies to structures like towers, masts, and associated sites. The "Limits on Access Principles" sub-section outlines conditions for sharing, requiring access providers to consider capacity, spectrum interference, compliance with the Resource Management Act 1991, health and safety, and third-party contracts.

According to Commerce Commission New Zealand, the expansion in the coverage of wireless and mobile networks in rural areas has been partly delivered through infrastructure sharing. Examples include co-location of equipment on cell sites under the Government’s initial Rural Broadband Initiative (RBI1), and the joint venture between the 3 MNOs participating in the Rural Broadband Initiative 2 (RBI2) programme.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Since December 2001, last amended in December 2023

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in telecom sector
indicators.source_legislation: Overseas Investment Act 2005
indicators.impact:
The Overseas Investment Act 2005, which regulates foreign investments in New Zealand, does not set explicit foreign equity limits in the telecommunications sector. It requires foreign investors to obtain consent for certain investments, particularly those involving sensitive assets or significant business assets.

However, in practice, Chorus owns most of the telephone infrastructure in New Zealand, and provides wholesale services to telecommunications retailers. Chorus’s constitution requires at least half of its Board be New Zealand citizens. It requires that no person shall have a relevant interest in 10% or more of the total voting shares for the time being without, and except in accordance with, the prior written approval of the Crown under the Deed and no person who is not a New Zealand national shall have a relevant interest in more than 49.9% of the total voting shares for the time being without, and except in accordance with the terms of, the prior written approval of the Crown given under the Deed (First Schedule).

indicators.question_description:
Ban and local processing requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Privacy Act 2020
indicators.impact:
New Zealand does not impose a ban on cross-border data flows. The Privacy Act 2020 establishes a conditional data transfer regime, but not a ban with exceptions regime.

The Privacy Act 2020 establishes a conditional cross-border data transfer regime. Under Information Privacy Principle 12 (IPP 12), personal information may be transferred overseas if the receiving country ensures comparable privacy protections, or with informed consent from the individual. The Privacy Commissioner may issue restrictions (e.g., prohibition notices) where standards are not met. These requirements aim to safeguard personal data without constituting a general ban on international data transfers.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Since June 2020, last amended in July 2024

indicators.question_description:
Local storage requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.impact:
Since its enactment in 1994, Section 22(2) of the Tax Administration Act 1994 has required certain classes of taxpayers to keep and retain specified records related to their tax liability in New Zealand at least for seven years unless an exception applies, so that the Commissioner of Inland Revenue may assess the taxpayer's tax liability. Under Section 22(5), the Commissioner of Inland Revenue may extend three additional years for an additional audit or investigation. Taxpayers are exempt from the local storage requirements under Section 22(8)-(9) if authorized by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue. This requirement has been in place since its enactment in 1994.

Pursuant to this section, Revenue Alert 10/02, which was issued in 2010 by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue but does not reflect its final position, provides that "[t]taxpayers are responsible for ensuring they comply with their record keeping obligations. Therefore, taxpayers using a cloud computing service will need to be satisfied that all their business records will be [also] stored in data centres located in New Zealand."

Section 75 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 mandates that GST-registered entities keep tax-related records for seven years, extendable by three years under Section 75(5) for further audits. While the Act does not explicitly demand local storage, exemptions may be granted by the Commissioner under Sections 75(6)-(7), as long as conditions are met, ensuring records are accessible for compliance purposes. 

However, Standard Practice Statement (SPS) 21/02 on Retention of Business Records in Electronic Formats, Application to Store Records Offshore and Keeping Records in Languages other than English or Te Reo Māori published by Indland Revenue confirms that offshore record‑keeping applications—including cloud and third‑party providers—are routinely approved, provided the records remain accessible and meet integrity and availability standards under relevant laws (Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017; Electronic Transactions Regulations). The Commissioner may also permit records in languages other than English or te reo Māori. These rules establish a conditional data localization regime with practical exemption pathways.

indicators.question_description:
Local storage requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Companies Act 1993
indicators.impact:
Since its enactment in 1993 as amended in 1994, Section 189 of the Companies Act 1993 has required registered companies to store specified internal records at the company's registered office (which must be an address in New Zealand) or another place in New Zealand at least for seven years after giving notice to the Registrar of Companies. These records include: minutes of all meetings and resolutions of shareholders, minutes of all meetings and resolutions of directors and directors' committees, certificates given by directors under the Act, copies of all written communications to all shareholders or all holders of the same class of shares. 
Furthermore, under the same provision, following records are subject to a minimum retention period of seven completed accounting periods of the company: copies of all financial statements and group financial statements required to be completed under the Act and accounting records. 
Despite this local storage requirement, the Act allows reporting entities to keep accounting records outside New Zealand if specific documents are kept in New Zealand such as the financial statements of any reporting entity and registered scheme it manages and any document annexed to those financial statements that gives legally required information (Section 456). The Act does not otherwise prohibit cross-border data transfers.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Since July 1994, last amended in March 2024

indicators.question_description:
Local storage requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Customs and Excise Act 2018
indicators.impact:
Since its enactment in 2018, Section 354 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018 has required businesses importing and exporting from New Zealand to keep specified records in New Zealand at least for seven years unless an exemption applies. However, the Act exempts companies from this requirement for certain records of companies importing or exporting if they apply to and are authorized by the Chief Executive of the New Zealand Customs Service to keep the prescribed records outside New Zealand (Section 355).

Section 354 states that (1) Every specified person must: (a) keep at a specified place, or cause to be kept at a specified place, any prescribed records for the prescribed period; and (...); (2) The period prescribed for the purposes of subsection (1)(a) must not exceed 7 years; (3) (...) specified place means (a) a place in New Zealand; or (b) a place outside New Zealand if, (i) after making an application under section 355(1), the specified person is authorised to keep the prescribed records, or to cause the prescribed records to be kept, at that place; or (ii) after making an application under section 355(2), another person is authorised to keep the prescribed records for the specified person at that place.

However, Section 355, Application to keep records outside New Zealand, provides a formal application process by which these entities can obtain authorization from the Chief Executive of the New Zealand Customs Service to store records offshore (e.g., cloud-based). The New Zealand Customs Service confirms that offshore record storage is permitted upon application and subject to accessibility and compliance conditions. This constitutes a conditional data localization regime with practical offshore exemptions.

indicators.source_legislation: Privacy Act 2020
indicators.impact:
The new Privacy Act 2020 which entered into force in December 2020 creates a conditional flow regime. Information Privacy Principle 12 in Section 22 of the Act governs cross-border data transfer. A business or organization may only disclose personal information to another organization outside New Zealand if the receiving organization:
- is subject to the Privacy Act because they do business in New Zealand; 
- is subject to privacy laws that provide comparable safeguards to the Privacy Act - or they agree to protect the information in such a way (e.g., by using model contract clauses), or 
- is covered by a binding scheme or is subject to the privacy laws of a country prescribed by the New Zealand Government. 
If none of these conditions is satisfied, a business may only make a cross-border disclosure with the permission of the data subject. 
This regime does not apply to an overseas organization to hold or process on the business's behalf (e.g., cloud service providers). 
Still, despite the IPP 12, a business may make a cross-border disclosure in urgent circumstances where it is necessary to maintain public health or safety or for the maintenance of the law. 
This regime does not affect or limit other New Zealand law that regulates the availability of personal information (Section 24).

Similar cross border requirements also apply to sectors subject to a Code of Practice under the Privacy Act 2020, specifically the health sector, telecommunications sector and credit reporting sector

indicators.source_legislation: Health Information Privacy Code 2020
indicators.impact: The Health Information Privacy Code 2020 is a Code of Practice issued by the Privacy Commissioner under section 32 of the Privacy Act which gives extra protection to health information because of its sensitivity. It covers health information collected, used, held and disclosed by health agencies and takes the place of the information privacy principles for the health sector. Rule 11 of the Code prohibits disclosure except where one or more of its exceptions apply. Rule 12 of the Code specifies the conditions for disclosure of health information outside New Zealand. Specifically, a health agency, referred to as 'A', has the discretion to share health information with a foreign body, denoted as 'B', under stipulated guidelines. This is permissible if: the relevant individual or their representative authorizes the sharing, being aware that B's data protection might not match the standards of the Act and its associated code; if B, conducting business in New Zealand, is believed by A to adhere to the Act and the code; or if A is confident that B’s privacy practices are on par with the Act and code, either through recognized global standards, specific binding agreements, or as mandated by section 30 of the Act.

indicators.question_description: Not in an agreement with binding commitments on data transfer.
indicators.impact:
New Zealand has joined agreements with binding commitments to open transfers of data across borders: the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP, Art. 14.11), and the Free Trade Agreement between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and New Zealand [Art.15.4(2)](Chapter 15).

The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) Agreement includes commitments on electronic commerce, which can involve rules governing data transfer. According to Chapter 12 - Electronic Commerce, members agree to facilitate cross-border data transfers for business purposes while ensuring data protection.

The New Zealand–European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) includes commitments related to digital trade and cross-border data flows. Chapter 12 of the agreement specifically addresses digital trade, detailing conditions that must be met for data transfers, including ensuring privacy and data security are upheld.

Digital Economy Partnership Agreement (DEPA) between New Zealand, Chile, and Singapore: Emphasizes the free flow of data while allowing each country to maintain measures to protect personal data, public policy, and national security, provided these are not arbitrary or discriminatory

NZ-Singapore Closer Economic Partnership's Chapter 9 focuses on cross-border data transfer commitments, particularly in: Article 9.10: Allows cross-border data transfers for business, with exceptions for public policy, privacy, and security;Article 9.11: Prohibits forced data localization unless needed for legitimate public policy reasons.;Article 9.7: Mandates a legal framework for protecting personal information in electronic commerce

Moreover, ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (AANZFTA), upgraded by the Second Protocol, signed in August 2023 and in force since April 2025, added commitments on electronic commerce including rules governing cross-border data transfers (Chapter 10, Article 18). However, the included cross-border data flows provision is non-binding.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.source_legislation: Privacy Act 2020
indicators.impact: The Privacy Act 2020 is a modernized framework that replaced the Privacy Act 1993, which was similiar in scope. It applies to nearly all agencies across New Zealand's economy (e.g., both the public and private sectors), regardless of sector or size. The Privacy Act has 13 Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) that govern how agencies can collect, store, use and share personal information. These principles are based off the basic principles of national application set out in Part Two of the OECD Guidelines Governing the Protection of Privacy and Transborder Flows of Personal Data. Moreover, the Act also introduces protections such as breach notification, access and correction rights, and accountability mechanisms.

indicators.source_legislation:
Tax Administration Act 1994;

Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
indicators.impact:
Since its enactment in 1994, Section 22(2) of the Tax Administration Act 1994 has required certain classes of taxpayers to keep and retain specified records related to their tax liability in New Zealand at least for seven years unless an exception applies, so that the Commissioner of Inland Revenue may assess the taxpayer's tax liability. Under Section 22(5), the Commissioner of Inland Revenue may extend three additional years for an additional audit or investigation. Taxpayers are exempt from the local storage requirements under Section 22(8)-(9) if authorized by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue. This requirement has been in place since its enactment in 1994.

Pursuant to this section, Revenue Alert 10/02, which was issued in 2010 by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue but does not reflect its final position, provides that "[t]taxpayers are responsible for ensuring they comply with their record keeping obligations. Therefore, taxpayers using a cloud computing service will need to be satisfied that all their business records will be [also] stored in data centres located in New Zealand."

Since its enactment 1985, Section 75 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 has required registered entities to keep and retain specified tax-related records at least for seven years in New Zealand unless an exemption applies so that the Commissioner of Inland Revenue may assess the entity's goods and services tax liability. Under Section 75(5), which was inserted in 1992, the Commissioner of Inland Revenue may require taxpayers to retain such data for an additional period of 3 year in cases of a further audit or investigation. Taxpayers are also exempt from the local storage requirement if authorized by the Commissioner as long as the Commissioner imposes reasonable conditions under Section 75(6)-(7). This requirement has been in place since its enactment in 1985.

Pursuant to this section, Revenue Alert 10/02, which was issued in 2010 by the Commissioner of Inland Revenue but does not reflect its final position, provides that "[t]taxpayers are responsible for ensuring they comply with their record keeping obligations. Therefore, taxpayers using a cloud computing service will need to be satisfied that all their business records will be [also] stored in data centres located in New Zealand."

Additionally, Sections 19E to 19J (Records of supplies) of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 require GST-registered entities to maintain records of transactions. Under Section 75(3BA), such records must be retained either at a place in New Zealand or, if the Commissioner of Inland Revenue has granted approval, at a place outside New Zealand. The Standard Practice Statement (SPS) 21/02, in response to question 6.2.1, provides further guidance on when the Commissioner will exercise this discretion to permit offshore record-keeping.

indicators.source_legislation: Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013
indicators.impact:
Since its enactment in 2013, Sections 215 and 216 of the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 has required issuers of financial products to keep a register of their regulated products in New Zealand. Furthermore, Sections 455 and 456 require financial reporting entities such as issuers of financial products, registered banks, building societies, and credit unions to keep certain accounting-related records in New Zealand. 

Under Section 458 of the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013, accounting records, or copies of them, must be retained by the financial reporting entity for a period of at least 7 years after the later of (a) the date the records are made; and (b) the date of completion of the transaction to which the records relate. Despite this local storage requirement, the Act allows reporting entities to keep accounting records outside New Zealand if specific documents are kept in New Zealand such as the financial statements of any reporting entity and registered scheme it manages and any document annexed to those financial statements that gives legally required information (Section 456). The Act does not otherwise prohibit cross-border data transfers.

Section 461V of Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 outlines the requirements for climate reporting entities to keep records that enable compliance with climate-related disclosure frameworks. Section 461W specifies that these records must be kept in the prescribed manner, and Section 461X states that they must be retained for at least 7 years. It is important to note that these provisions are not local storage requirements for climate reporting entities but instead records must be readily identifiable and available for inspections within certain timeframes under Regulations 252A–C.
 
Additionally, Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill, an amendment bill recently introduced to Parliament proposes modernise these FMC Act record keeping provisions, including by facilitating cloud storage in Australia, and other appropriate jurisdictions (that can be recognized in regulations).

indicators.impact:

These records include: minutes of all meetings and resolutions of shareholders, minutes of all meetings and resolutions of directors and directors' committees, certificates given by directors under the Act, copies of all written communications to all shareholders or all holders of the same class of shares. 
Furthermore, under the same provision, following records are subject to a minimum retention period of seven completed accounting periods of the company: copies of all financial statements and group financial statements required to be completed under the Act and accounting records. 
Despite this local storage requirement, the Act allows reporting entities to keep accounting records outside New Zealand if specific documents are kept in New Zealand such as the financial statements of any reporting entity and registered scheme it manages and any document annexed to those financial statements that gives legally required information (Section 456). The Act does not otherwise prohibit cross-border data transfers.

indicators.impact:
Since its enactment in 2018, Section 354 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018 has required businesses importing and exporting from New Zealand to keep specified records in New Zealand at least for seven years unless an exemption applies. However, the Act exempts companies from this requirement for certain records of companies importing or exporting if they apply to and are authorized by the Chief Executive of the New Zealand Customs Service to keep the prescribed records outside New Zealand (Section 355).

Section 354 states that (1) Every specified person must: (a) keep at a specified place, or cause to be kept at a specified place, any prescribed records for the prescribed period; and (...); (2) The period prescribed for the purposes of subsection (1)(a) must not exceed 7 years; (3) (...) specified place means (a) a place in New Zealand; or (b) a place outside New Zealand if, (i) after making an application under section 355(1), the specified person is authorised to keep the prescribed records, or to cause the prescribed records to be kept, at that place; or (ii) after making an application under section 355(2), another person is authorised to keep the prescribed records for the specified person at that place. 

Moreover, Section 355 (Application to keep records outside New Zealand) provides a person may apply to the chief executive for authorisation to keep records for specified persons at a location outside New Zealand. After considering the application, the chief executive must either grant or decline the authorisation. If granted, the authorisation may be subject to any terms, conditions, or restrictions the chief executive considers appropriate. The chief executive also has the authority to vary these terms, conditions, or restrictions, or to withdraw the authorisation entirely, by written notice.

indicators.impact:
The Privacy Act requires all organizations to employ a dedicated Data Protection Officer within their organization. The Privacy Act requires organizations to have at least one person who fulfills the role of privacy officer.

In the Privacy Act 2020 of New Zealand, Section 201 mandates the appointment of one or more Privacy Officers within an agency. The responsibilities of these officers include: Encouraging compliance with the Information Privacy Principles (IPPs); Handling requests made to the agency under the Act; Working with the Privacy Commissioner during investigations; Ensuring the agency complies with the Act While the Act mandates the designation of Privacy Officers, it does not require Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) to be conducted.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.impact:
In general, although the legislation grants the government the authority to access data on telecommunications networks, it requires court orders or other lawful interception authorizations for such access.

The Telecommunications (Interception Capability and Security) Act 2013 creates upon a network operator two duties: 
First, a duty to ensure that every public telecommunications network and services that the operator owns, controls, or operates have full interception capability (Section 9). This duty is satisfied "if every surveillance agency that is authorised under an interception warrant or any other lawful interception authority to intercept telecommunications or services on that network, or the network operator concerned, is able to," basically, identify and intercept telecommunications or data relating to the telecommunications as duly authorized (Section 10). 
Second, a duty to assist a surveillance agency upon an inception warrant or any other lawful interception authority (Section 24). Upon a showing of an interception warrant or any other lawful interception authority, the network operator must assist the agency in intercepting telecommunications (Section 24(3)). 
The interception warrants include: 
1) a surveillance device warrant that is issued by a judge on application under the Search and Surveillance Act 2012
2) an authorization such as an intelligence warrant, a removal warrant, and a practice warrant, for the carrying out of an activity by intelligence and security agencies under the Intelligence and Security Act 2017

"Lawful interception authority" includes emergency powers upon an international terrorist emergency to requisition property including a network's operator's network equipment under the International Terrorism (Emergency Powers) Act 1987 (Section 10). The powers authorize a constable under the Act to intercept private communications and connect any additional apparatus to any part of the telecommunications system. 
A network operator must, in order to comply with the assistance duty, decrypt a telecommunication on that operator’s public telecommunications network or telecommunications service "if (a) the content of that telecommunication has been encrypted; and (b) the network operator intercepting the telecommunication has provided that encryption." 
However, this does not require a network operator to "(a) decrypt any telecommunication on that operator’s public telecommunications network or telecommunications service if the encryption has been provided by means of a product that is (i) supplied by a person other than the operator and is available to the public or (ii) supplied by the operator as an agent for that product; and (b) ensure that a surveillance agency has the ability to decrypt any telecommunication.
The existence of these duties together mean that network operators cannot design and implement end-to-end encryption.

Moreover, the Privacy Act authorises government agencies to share personal information in several ways: (i) Approved Information Sharing Agreements (AISAs) (Part 7 Sub-part 1), (ii) Identity information (Part 7 Sub-part 2), (iii) Law enforcement information (Part 7 Sub-part 3), and (iv) Authorised Information Matching Programmes (Part 7 Sub-part 4). Additional information about these approaches is available at https://www.privacy.org.nz/about-us/information-sharing/

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.impact:
Under the Copyright (New Technologies) Amendment Act 2008, Internet service providers (ISPs) are not liable simply because a user infringes a copyright (Section 92B). However, ISPs may possibly face liability for copyright infringement as a result of storing an infringing material if an ISP has specific knowledge of the infringement, or caching if the ISP does not immediately delete or make unavailable the infringement material upon notice (Sections 92C and 92E).

Section 131 of the Copyright Act, which sets out criminal offenses in relation to copyright works, encompasses online dissemination of digital copies. As a result, it has been opined that Internet service providers are now potentially exposed to criminal sanctions in carrying out their day-to-day activities. New Zealand Law Society states that "ISPs in New Zealand, and overseas ISPs providing services to New Zealanders, will obviously be concerned as to the extent of their own potential criminal liability in this country for users infringing copyright online. It is not unrealistic to imagine this could have an impact on availability of online services for New Zealanders."
An "ISP" under the Act means an entity which (a) offers the transmission, routing, or providing of connections for digital online communications, between or among points specified by a user, of material of the user’s choosing, or (b) hosts material on websites or other electronic retrieval systems that can be accessed by a user (Section 4).

Copyright (Infringing File Sharing Amendment Act 2011 provides safe harbour protections for ISPs in New Zealand. Here's a brief overview of relevant sections: Section 5: Shields ISPs from liability for users' copyright infringements, as long as they comply with notice-and-takedown procedures. Sections 122A–122U: Establish a three-step process (detection, warning, enforcement notices) for handling copyright infringement claims related to file sharing. ISPs must issue these notices to maintain their immunity. Section 122P: Allows courts to suspend internet accounts of repeat infringers. Section 122Q: Rights owners can request account holder details from ISPs for legal action

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015
indicators.impact:
Under the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015, an online content host is not per se liable for illegal content posted by its user and consequently hosted in the platform. Section 24 provides a process that an Internet service provider should take to obtain protection against liability for specific content. However, the fact a host does not follow the process specified in Section 24 does not of itself create any civil or criminal liability for hosting the illegal content (Section 23). 

In the Murray v Wishart (2014) case, the court discussed the liability of online platform hosts for third-party content. This case is particularly relevant when considering the responsibilities of individuals or platforms in moderating user-generated content. The decision clarifies that an online host can be considered a publisher of defamatory third-party comments if they are aware of the content and fail to remove it in a reasonable time. 

There is currently no proposed legislation to remove these safe harbour protections.

Blocking or filtering commercial web content
Exception: Not score political content, criminal content (e.g., child pornography), aged-restricted content, defamation and other non-commercial content.
indicators.impact:
The 11 Voluntary principles to Counter Online Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse provide a common and consistent framework to guide the digital industry in its efforts to help combat the proliferation of online child exploitation. They have been co-designed with industry leaders to be applicable to the wide variety of digital industry and where taken onboard, will assist in preventing online platforms and services from being used to facilitate child sexual exploitation and abuse.

In addition, Department of Internal Affairs manages the Digital Child Exploitation Filtering System (DCEFS), which is an internet and website filtering system which blocks websites that host clearly objectionable child sexual abuse material. The DCEFS is available voluntarily to all New Zealand Internet Service Providers (ISPs).

The Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 restricts content that is harmful to public good, specifically targeting illegal content like child pornography, extreme violence, sexual exploitation, and material that promotes crime or terrorism. Section 3 defines such objectionable content, and Part 7A enables authorities to issue take-down notices to remove this type of harmful or illegal online material​.

The New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, under Section 14, guarantees freedom of expression but allows for justified limitations under Section 5. This requires that any content blocking or filtering be considered necessary and proportionate in a democratic society, but the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act does not override other statutes.

indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.source_legislation: Standards and Accreditation Act 2015
indicators.impact:
Standards are agreed specifications for products, processes, services, systems, and performance developed by committees of relevant subject matter experts employing an internationally recognised, consensus-based, decision-making process. In New Zealand this process is managed by Standards New Zealand (Standards NZ) and prescribed by the Standards and Accreditation Act 2015 (the Act). Decisions to approve or decline membership of standards development committees are made under this Act by the New Zealand Standards Approval Board, which is a statutorily independent, decision-making body appointed by the Minister for Commerce and Consumer Affairs. In making the decision about whether to appoint nominated individuals the Board must act independently, have regard to the importance of ensuring that members of a standards development committee constitute a balanced representation of the stakeholder interests relevant to the proposed draft standard; and ensure that each member of the standards development committee has skills, knowledge, and experience relevant to the standard to be developed or considered; or knowledge and experience of the sector or sectors most likely to use the standard.

While there is nothing explicitly prohibiting individuals nominated by foreign businesses from participating in on a standards development committee, the legal requirement to ensure that the individuals are appropriately qualified, and that membership is balanced, and representative ensure that any conflicts of interest are acknowledged and managed. When standards are approved and published, the list of organisations represented on the committee is included in the standard. This is a transparent, and auditable process. 

Regarding the authority of standards, while Standards NZ is a business unit within the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, it is not a regulator; rather, it manages the development, adoption, and publication of industry standards, and other standards-related products and services, including New Zealand, joint Australian/New Zealand, and international standards. Standards produced or adopted by Standards NZ are voluntary guidance and remain voluntary until deliberately cited within regulatory instruments by the relevant New Zealand regulator.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.source_legislation: Overseas Investment Act 2005
indicators.impact:
No foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector are found.

New Zealand does not have specific foreign equity limits in the e-commerce sector. Foreign investments are regulated under the Overseas Investment Act, which targets high-risk sectors like land or strategic businesses, but generally allows lower-risk e-commerce investments without restrictions​. 

However, an investor may have to apply for consent in some circumstances. An National Interest Assessment may also need to be carried out in some circumstances. This is the same test as for any other sector. Overseas investors need consent to invest in some sensitive New Zealand assets. The Overseas Investment Act 2005 sets the criteria for when consent is required, primarily involving sensitive land (Section 12), significant business assets (Section 13), and fishing quotas. Some overseas investment consent applications may also be subject to a national interest assessment. This would include land or assets used for strategically important businesses, including telecommunications businesses. It is up to a relevant New Zealand Minister to determine whether an investment would be contrary to New Zealand’s national interest prior to a decision being made to grant consent to an application.

indicators.impact:
There is no specific regulation for securing internet payments, but many merchant banks will require merchants to ensure that their internet payment systems comply with the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, which is a global payment card industry standard established by a non-government, international organization. Notably, some banks have their respective regulations for online payment limits. In New Zealand, there is no requirement for online payments to use a local bank card. The Retail Payment System Act 2022 allows multiple payment methods, including international cards and local systems like POLi, while the Electronic Transactions Act 2002 supports the use of electronic contracts. This framework ensures flexibility in payment options without mandating local cards

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.impact:
There is no specific legislation that governs electronic transactions. The general law relating to contracts in New Zealand applies, including the Contract and Commercial Law 2017 which also sets out default rules for the formation of contracts electronically. There are no legal limitations that would apply to electronic contracts, although certain instruments (such as bills of lading and negotiable instruments) cannot be delivered electronically. Part 4 of the Law provides that a requirement for writing and/or signature can be met by way of an electronic document and electronic signature.
Like brick-and-mortar businesses, online sellers are subject to the Fair Trading Act 1986, Consumer Guarantee Act 1993, and Privacy Act 2020. The Fair Trading Act prohibits misleading and deceptive conduct in trade, and requires certain disclosures to be made to consumers in some cases. The Consumer Guarantee Act establishes remedies and protections for consumers against suppliers and manufacturers of goods and services. The Privacy Act regulates the collection, use and storage of personal information. 

However, it should be noted that the official authority states on their website: 'If you bought an item online from an overseas seller, the Act might still apply, but it becomes much more difficult to resolve issues and enforce your rights.'

indicators.question_description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
indicators.source_legislation:
Public Procurement Rules 2004;

Mechanism for Blacklisting and Debarment of Bidders or Contractors 2024
indicators.impact:
Regulation 5 states that if Pakistan's public procurement rules conflict with international agreements or treaties that the Federal Government is part of, those agreements will take precedence. 

Under Rule 14(a), procurements related to national security can be excluded from public advertisement. This gives the government discretion to exclude foreign firms from ICT and digital service procurements that are deemed critical to national security.

Accroding to section 4 of the Mechanism for Blacklisting and Debarment of Bidders or Contractors 2024, the procuring agency shall constitute and notify a Committee comprising of an odd number of persons, not less than three members, as soon as the procurement process is initiated, to conduct blacklisting or barring action against the bidder or contractor.
Section 5, the reasons for Blacklisting and Debarment:
(a) Blacklisting & debarment on account of involvement in corrupt & fraudulent practices. If a procuring agency has sufficient reasons to believe that a bidder or contractor is involved in the corrupt and fraudulent practices as mentioned in Rule-2(f)(g) to (v) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2004, the Procuring agency shall blacklist and henceforth cross debar the bidder or contractor for participation in any public procurement or disposal proceedings for the period of not more than ten (10) years.
(b) Blacklisting & debarment on account of failure to perform contractual obligations:
(i) The blacklisting committee shall initiate blacklisting proceedings for a period of not more than three (3) years if the contractor failed to perform his contractual obligations during the execution of contract or breaches the contract due to his incapacity and incapability to perform or otherwise.
(ii) Procuring agency shall initiate such blacklisting or debarment proceedings after exhausting the forum of arbitration, provided that such provision exists in the conditions of contract, and if such failure or breach is covered in the respective dispute settlement clauses of the contract.
(c) Blacklisting & debarment on account of failure to abide by bid securing declaration. The Blacklisting Committee shall initiate blacklisting and henceforth cross debarment for participation in respective category of public procurement or disposal proceedings for a period of not more than six months if the bidder fails to abide with a bid securing declaration without being indulged in any corrupt and fraudulent practices.
In practice, various procuring agencies reported the domestic and foreign firms which they have blacklisted/debarred permanently or temporarily to PPRA.

Section 11(1) establishes investor obligations. indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Patent Rules 2003
indicators.impact:
Rule 18(Opposition to Grant of Patent) states that a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent must be in the prescribed form (Form P-7). The opposition must state the grounds on which the opponent intends to oppose the grant. It must be accompanied by a statement setting out the opponent’s interest, the facts relied upon, and the relief sought. The applicant has the opportunity to file a counterstatement within two months of receiving the opposition notice.
Rule 26(Revocation of Patents) states that an application for revocation must be made in the prescribed form (Form P-14), stating the grounds for the application. A copy of the application and a statement setting out the applicant’s interests and the facts relied upon must be sent to the patentee.
Rule 27(Surrender of Patent) states that a patentee shall offer to surrender a patent by giving notice in the prescribed form (Form P-15). Any person may give notice of opposition to the surrender within two months from the advertisement of the offer.
Rule 28(Amendment of Specification) states that an application to amend a complete specification must be made in the prescribed form (Form P-16) and must be advertised in the Official Gazette.
Any person wishing to oppose the amendment has two months from the date of the advertisement to give notice to the Controller.
Rule 32(Non-Voluntary License) states that an application for a non-voluntary license must be made in the prescribed form (Form P-22) and must be accompanied by a statement of facts and evidence. The Controller may, after hearing the applicant, decide whether to grant the non-voluntary license.This could be considered a provisional measure to promote public interest.
Rule 31 (Correction of Clerical Errors) states that requests for the correction of clerical errors must be made in the prescribed form (Form P-21). The Controller may advertise the request and the nature of the proposed correction in the Official Gazette. Any person may give notice of opposition to the proposed correction within two months from the date of the advertisement.
Rule 25(Restoration of Lapsed Patents) states that an application for the restoration of a lapsed patent must be made in the prescribed form (Form P-13) and must be accompanied by evidence in support of the statements made in the application. If opposition is given, the provisions of sub-rules (3) to (12) of rule 18 shall apply.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Patent Ordinance 2000
indicators.impact:
Regarding Civil and Administrative Procedures and Remedies:
Section 23 allows any person to oppose the grant of a patent within four months from the date of advertisement of the acceptance of a complete specification. The opposition can be based on various grounds, including non-disclosure, lack of clarity in the specification, or extending beyond the scope of the disclosure.
Section 46 states that a patent may be revoked by the High Court on the petition of any person interested or of the Federal Government, on various grounds such as the patent being obtained through concealment or misrepresentation, or if the patentee has failed to comply with the request of the Federal Government to make, use, or exercise the patented invention.
Section 47 allows that within twelve months after the sealing of a patent, any person interested can apply to the Controller for an order revoking the patent on grounds such as the invention not being new, lacking an inventive step, or not being capable of industrial application.
According to Section 48, the Federal Government may declare a patent revoked if it is mischievous to the State, prejudicial to the public, obtained through concealment or misrepresentation, or if the compulsory license granted to prevent abuse has not been sufficient.
Section 49, a patentee may offer to surrender a patent by giving notice to the Controller, which can be opposed by any interested person within a prescribed period.
Section 58, the Federal Government may authorize the exploitation of a patented invention by a government agency or a third person, even without the consent of the patent owner, under certain circumstances such as public interest, non-exploitation by the patentee, or anti-competitive practices.
Section 59, the Controller may issue a non-voluntary license to prevent abuses that might result from the exercise of patent rights, such as failure to work the patent or insufficient exploitation.
Section 60, a patentee may institute a suit in a District Court against any person who makes, sells, or uses the invention without a license, or counterfeits it.
Section 61 outlines the remedies available in patent infringement lawsuits, including the power of the court to grant relief by way of damages, injunctions, or accounts.
Section 62 provides circumstances under which damages shall not be awarded against a defendant in patent infringement proceedings, if the defendant can prove lack of knowledge or reasonable grounds to believe that the patent existed.
Section 63 deals with relief for infringement of partially valid specifications, allowing the court to grant relief in respect of any valid claim that is infringed.
Section 64 gives exclusive licensees the right to take proceedings in respect of any infringement of the patent committed after the date of the license.

Regarding Provisional Measures:
Section 61 also mentions that the court may order effective provisional measures to prevent an infringement and to preserve relevant evidence regarding the alleged infringement.
Section 62(2) involves the court's authority to order provisional measures, where appropriate, to prevent the entry of infringing goods into the channels of commerce and to preserve evidence, particularly where there is a risk of irreparable harm or evidence being destroyed.

indicators.question_description: Lack of copyright framework and exceptions
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright Ordinance 1962
indicators.impact:
Under the Copyright Ordinance, certain acts are not considered an infringement of copyright (Section 57 Certain Acts not to be Infringement of Copyright). A list of exceptions not constitute as an infringement of copyright:
(a) Fair dealing for research or private study, criticism, or review.
(b) Fair dealing for reporting current events.
(c) Reproduction for judicial proceedings or reports.
(d) Publication of reports of political addresses in newspapers.
(e) Reproduction of works in certified copies made or supplied under law.
(f) Reading or recitation in public of extracts from published works.
(g) Publication in collections for educational use.
(h) Reproduction or adaptation for instruction.
(i) Performance by educational institutions.
(j) Making records of literary, dramatic, or musical works.
(k) Causing recordings to be heard in public.
(l) Performance by amateur clubs or societies.
(m) Reproduction in newspapers of articles on current topics.
(n) Publication of reports of lectures.
(o) Making copies by libraries.
(p) Reproduction for research or private study of unpublished works.
(q) Reproduction or publication of government matters.
(r) Making or publishing of works of art.
(s) Making or publishing of works of artistic craftsmanship.
(t) Inclusion in cinematographic works.
(u) Use by the author of an artistic work.
(v) Making three-dimensional objects of two-dimensional works.
(w) Reconstruction of buildings or structures.
(x) Exhibition of cinematographic works after copyright expiration.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.source_legislation:
Pakistan Telecommunication (Re-organization) Act 1996;

De-Regulation Policy for the Telecommunication Sector 2003
indicators.impact:
Pakistan Telecommunication (Re-organization) Act 1996 details the procedures for licensing telecommunication services, including:
No person can establish or operate a telecommunication system without a license (Section 20).
The Authority has the exclusive power to grant licenses (Section 21).
The Authority can modify a license or its conditions with the consent of the licensee (Section 22).
The Authority can issue enforcement orders and levy penalties for contraventions of the Act, rules, or license terms (Section 23).
An Administrator can be appointed to manage the affairs of a licensee in case of contraventions (Section 24).
The Authority regulates tariffs for telecommunication services, including basic telephone service (Section 26).
Licensees have the right to share any Public Right of Way or Private Right of Way, subject to conditions (Section 27A).
The Authority may notify regulations for establishing national standards for telecommunication equipment (Section 28).
Terminal equipment must be approved by the Authority before connection to a public switched network (Section 29).
The Act outlines offences and penalties for various contraventions, including operating without a license or misusing a telecommunication system (Section 31).
The Authority or Board can obtain warrants to search for unlicensed telecommunication systems or equipment (Section 32).

De-Regulation Policy for the Telecommunication Sector outlines the de-regulation policy prepared by the Ministry of Information Technology for the telecommunication sector in Pakistan, including the license types and rights, the Local Loop (LL) and Long-Distance International (LDI) licenses are mentioned, allowing for both types to be held by the same company; Rights include contracting for the "Right of Way" (RoW) and access to numbering ranges and short codes for LDI licensees. According to the policy, LDI licensees must start the roll-out within specified timeframes and own a proportion of the transmission system and cables. PTA will not regulate tariffs of LL/LDI licensees until they attain SMP status, but has the right to intervene in cases of unfair pricing. Licensees have the right to interconnection, leased lines, and colocation facilities from incumbents like PTCL. Licensees are required to contribute to the USF and Research and Development Fund.

Section 8(3): The Federal Government may, from time to time, call for reports on the activities of the Authority and Board and provide for representation in meetings of international
telecommunication organizations. Therefore, the PTA is not an independent authority.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.impact:
In Pakistan, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 contains some provisions on data protection. It prevents unauthorized acts with respect to information systems and provides for related offences as well as mechanisms for their investigation, prosecution and trial. Under the Act, unauthorized access, copying, interference to information system or data is a punishable offence and shall be punished with imprisonment or fine.

Sections 69 and 70 of Payment Systems and Electronic Fund Transfers Act 2007 outline the confidentiality and privacy requirements for financial institutions or authorized parties when handling electronic fund transfers. They must not disclose any information related to electronic fund transfers, affairs, or accounts of consumers unless required by law, the consumer has given consent, or it is customary among bankers to disclose such information.

Regulation 8A of Telecom Consumers Protection Regulations 2016 states that all commercial practices, including Telecommunication Service Promotional Scheme(s), must be informed to the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) at least ten working days prior to starting them and must follow the prescribed manner by the Authority. Regulation 8B requires operators to ensure that textual information is easily legible, prominent, and presented in a way that does not require microscopic examination when launching any commercial practice or promotional scheme.

Specifically, the Public WiFi-Hotspots refers to a facilitation or access between licensees and consumers mobile devices providing a small boundary network of coverage and conveniences within the building or limited public places (Section 2.k). The information to retain includes full name of user, CNIC number/passport number, mobile number, data and time of login, data and time of logoff, data consumption with URLs, MAC address, Internet access log, source IP address, etc.

The investigation agency under this provision of PECA 2016 is the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), authorized through rule 3 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Investigation Rules, 2018.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016
indicators.impact:
Section 31 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act discusses “expedited preservation and acquisition of data”. An authorized officer can require a person to provide or preserve specific data if there is a risk that the data may be modified, lost, destroyed, or rendered inaccessible. This can be done by written notice to the person in control of the information system.

According to section 33, in certain urgent circumstances, an authorized officer may enter a specified place and search or seize information systems, data, devices, or other articles relevant to an offence without a warrant, if there is a risk of data being destroyed or lost. However, the officer must inform the Court within 24 hours of such action.

Section 39 allows for "Real-time collection and recording" of data: "[i]f a Court is satisfied on the basis of information furnished by an authorised officer that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the content of any information is reasonably required for the purposes of a specific criminal investigation, the Court may order, with respect to information held by or passing through a service provider, to a designated agency as notified under the Investigation for Fair Trial Act 2013 or any other law for the time being in force having capability to collect real time information, to collect or record such information in real-time coordination with the investigation agency for provision in the prescribed manner."

There have been concerns regarding lack of clarity, particularly with regards to what constitutes "willful intent."

No service provider shall be subject to any civil or criminal liability, unless it is established that the service provider had specific actual knowledge and willful intent to proactively and positively participate, and not merely through omission or failure to act, and thereby facilitated, aided or abetted the use by any person of any information system.

indicators.source_legislation: Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016
indicators.impact:
Section 37 of Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016 (PECA) state that the Authority have the power to remove or block or issue directions for removal or blocking of access to an information if it considers necessary in the interest of the glory of Islam or the integrity, security or defence of Pakistan or any part thereof, public order, decency or morality or in relation to contempt of court or commission or incitement to an offence under this Act. 
In June 2021, the Pakistan Telecom Authority (PTA) revealed that it blocked more than 25,000 URLs— including 25,000 Facebook accounts, 307 Twitter posts, and 224 YouTube videos—for allegedly carrying “anti-state material.” The PTA reported in September 2021 that it had blocked over 1 million links and websites. 
And in July 2024, from the news stating that Pakistan’s minister for information technology and telecommunication confirmed the government is implementing an internet firewall but rejected talk that the tool will curb free speech online, defending it as a cybersecurity upgrade.

indicators.question_description:
Blocking or filtering commercial web content

Removal and Blocking of Unlawful Online Content (Procedure, Oversight and Safeguards), Rules 2020 Statutory Notifications S. R. O. 1077(I)/2020;

Removal and Blocking of Unlawful Online Content (Procedure, Oversight and Safeguards) Rules 2021 S.R.O. 1343(I)/2021
indicators.impact:
The Removal and Blocking of Unlawful Online Content (Procedure, Oversight and Safeguards) Rules 2021—introduced in October 2020 and notified with minor amendments in October 2021—expands the PTA’s powers under section 37 of the PECA to block and remove content on the internet. The rules give the PTA vast powers to censor content considered offensive under the Pakistan Penal Code, including content containing indecency, blasphemy, or false information, without providing any definitions. Under the rules, social media companies must comply with content moderation decisions of the PTA within 48 hours normally and within 12 hours in emergency situations. If social media companies fail to comply within the time limits, the government may block their entire platform;

Moreover, the service provider, social media company and significant social media company shall not knowingly host, display, upload, publish, transmit, update or share any online content in violation of local law (Section 7.3). Section 7.5 states that the service provider, social media company, and significant social media company shall deploy mechanisms to ensure immediate blocking of live streaming through online information system in Pakistan. The blocking shall apply to terroism, hate speech, pornographic, incitement to violence and detrimental to national security on receiving the information from the Authority.

indicators.question_description: Imposing trade defence measures (anti-dumping, countervailing duties and safeguards) on ICT-related products imported by other Asia-Pacific economies
indicators.impact:
The Customs Modernization and Tariff Act (Republic Act No. 10863) incorporated trade remedy provisions but primarily focused on modernizing customs and tariff administration, streamlining trade procedures, and improving compliance.

Trade remedies for anti-dumping, countervailing duties, and safeguards are available under Philippine laws—Republic Acts 8752, 8751, and 8800, respectively:
- The Anti-Dumping Act (RA 8752) allows for the imposition of duties on products sold below their normal value, addressing situations where dumping causes material injury to local producers (Section 3).
- The Countervailing Duty Act (RA 8751) enables the government to impose duties on subsidized imports that harm local industries, ensuring fair competition by neutralizing the benefits of foreign subsidies (Section 4).
- The Safeguard Measures Act (RA 8800) offers immediate relief to industries threatened by a sudden surge in imports, regardless of whether the imports are fairly traded (Section 5), allowing the government to act swiftly to protect jobs and industries.

Since the implementation of the Philippine trade remedy laws in 1999 and 2000, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) has not ordered any anti-dumping, countervailing, or safeguard measures on digital goods. The Philippines maintains a non-restrictive policy environment for tariffs and trade defense measures applied on intraregional imports of ICT-related goods.

As of May 2025, based on information from the WTO and the DTI Philippines portal, the Philippines has implemented both anti-dumping and safeguard measures on other kinds of products:
- Anti-dumping duties have been applied to products such as cement from Vietnam, gypsum board from Thailand, and wheat flour from Türkiye.
- For safeguard measures, the Philippines has:
- Imposed a definitive safeguard duty on high-density polyethylene (HDPE),
- Imposed a provisional safeguard duty on cement, and
- Initiated an investigation on corrugating medium imports from various countries.
- The safeguard investigation on LPG cylinders was terminated in 2024, and no definitive safeguard duty was imposed.

indicators.question_description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act 12009 - New Government Procurement Act (NGPA);

The Implementing Rules and Regulations of Republic Act 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act (IRR)
indicators.impact:
Republic Act (RA) No. 12009 is an Act Revising Republic Act No.9184, otherwise known as the New Government Procurement Act (NGPA), together with its Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR), is the latest enabling legal framework for government procurement in the Philippines. While foreign bids/bidders are allowed, this is subject to undergoing registration with the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) and submission of eligibility requirements/documents/statements that are applicable for all bids/bidders regardless of nationality (as specified under Rule III, Section 20.2.9.2 of the IRR).

However, specific to foreign bids/bidders, the latter have to also satisfy certain circumstances/criteria (as specified under Rule VIII, Sections 52.4.1.2 and 52.4.2.2 of the IRR concerning Eligibility Requirements for the Procurement of Goods, Infrastructure Projects, and Consulting Services). The procurement of goods and infrastructure projects are open to foreign bids/bidders though with conditions. Specifically, the procurement of goods are open: 
a) When provided for under any treaty or international or executive agreement as provided in Section 4 of the Act and this IRR;
b) When the foreign supplier is a citizen, corporation, or association of a country, the laws, or regulations of which grant reciprocal rights or privileges to citizens, corporations, or associations of the Philippines;
c) When the goods sought to be procured are not available from local suppliers; or
d) When there is a need to prevent situations that defeat competition or restrain trade.
For iinvestment projects, they are open when provided for under any treaty or international or executive agreement as provided in Section 4 of the Act and this IRR.

Moreover, for consulting services, foreign consultants may only be hired in the event Filipino consultants do not have the sufficient expertise and capability to render the services required (as specified under Rule VII, Section 52.4.3.3).

indicators.question_description: Specific requirements on source codes, encryption and trade secrets
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act 12009 - New Government Procurement Act (NGPA);

The Implementing Rules and Regulations of Republic Act 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act (IRR)
indicators.impact: Under the NGPA and its IRR, there are no explicit requirements or provisions specifying technology or knowledge transfers, or to surrende source code, encryption, and other trade secrets, such as patents. However, while the law provides no requirements, procuring entities are not precluded from specifying or including in the tender/bid documents (e.g., contract, Terms of Reference, etc.) such technology or knowledge transfers as part of the domestic/foreign bidder’s deliverables.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act 12009 - New Government Procurement Act (NGPA);

The Implementing Rules and Regulations of Republic Act 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act (IRR)
indicators.impact:
Under Rule XIII of the IRR of RA No. 12009, procurement of goods may be sourced from either domestic or foreign suppliers, with participation open to all eligible suppliers, manufacturers, and distributors (Section 78). However, Section 79 establishes a framework for domestic preference. Specifically, the Procuring Entity is required to give priority and preference to Philippine products and services throughout the procurement process, including raw materials, ingredients, supplies, and fixtures (Section 79.1). For a period of ten (10) years from the effectivity of RA No. 11981 or the Tatak Pinoy (Proudly Filipino) Act, and for sectors covered by the prevailing Tatak Pinoy Strategy, the Procuring Entity must award the contract to a domestic bidder (Section 79.2). A domestic bidder is defined as any person or entity offering goods that are either unmanufactured products of Philippine origin or manufactured products substantially made from Philippine-grown, produced, or manufactured components.

After this ten-year period, domestic preference will continue through a margin of preference to be determined by the Tatak Pinoy Council, which shall not be lower than fifteen percent (15%) (Section 79.3). For goods and services under the Tatak Pinoy Strategy (TPS), the applicable domestic preference rules will be based on the IRR or guidelines issued under the Tatak Pinoy Act (Section 79.4). Additionally, the Procuring Entity may still award the contract to a domestic bidder if their bid is not more than twenty-five percent (25%) higher than the lowest foreign bid, subject to periodic review by the Government Procurement Policy Board (GPPB) (Section 79.5). To claim such preference, domestic bidders must obtain a certification from the appropriate agency confirming that the goods in their bid are substantially composed of Philippine-made components (Section 79.6).

The domestic preference requirements may be waived under specific conditions, such as if domestic production is insufficient or unavailable in commercial quantities, if the required quality cannot be met, if applying domestic preference would conflict with international obligations, or under other analogous circumstances (Section 79.7).

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation:
Commonwealth Act No. 138 - An Act to Give Native Products and Domestic Entities the Preference in the Purchase of Articles for the Government; 

The Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines 1987
indicators.impact: Domestic preference in the Philippines is rooted in the 1987 Constitution, particularly in Article XII, Section 12, which emphasizes the promotion of local goods and the protection of domestic industries. Commonwealth Act No. 138 operationalizes this preference by mandating a 15% price advantage for local bidders over foreign competitors in government procurement of materials and supplies. This legal framework encourages the government to prioritize sourcing from local suppliers.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.source_legislation: Publication of Resolution, Circular and Government Procurement Policy Board (GPPB) Issuances, 2024
indicators.impact: The latest updates in the Philippine Bidding Documents for the Procurement of Goods (BAC-GDS-2024-005R) reaffirm these principles while outlining procurement guidelines under the 2024 General Appropriations Act (GAA). It emphasizes the publication of Government Procurement Policy Board (GPPB) issuances, including resolutions and circulars, under a single-year Framework Agreement. The bidding process retains the domestic preference provision, allowing a margin of preference of up to 15% for Filipino entities. Additionally, eligibility requirements restrict foreign bidders to those from countries with reciprocal rights for Filipinos, as specified in RA No. 5183. The project’s timeline and specifications, such as pre-bid conferences and technical details, are detailed to ensure transparency and compliance with the 2016 IRR.
