indicators.question_description:
Foreign equity limits in sectors relevant to digital trade 
Exception: Not cover foreign equity cap in telecom sector (covered under Pillar 5) and e-commerce sector (covered under Pillar 12)
indicators.impact:
The 1987 Philippine Constitution establishes foundational restrictions on foreign ownership across several critical sectors, reflecting the nation's policy of protecting industries considered vital to its sovereignty. Under Article XII, Section 2, foreign equity in the exploitation of natural resources is limited to 40%, ensuring Filipino citizens or corporations with at least 60% Filipino ownership maintain control. Article XII, Section 10 further restricts foreign ownership in enterprises related to national defense, security, and public utilities, where only 40% foreign equity is allowed. This is reinforced by Article XIV, Section 4(2), which caps foreign ownership of educational institutions at 40%, and Article XVI, Section 11, which prohibits foreign ownership of mass media, ensuring only Filipinos can own or manage these entities. 

The Foreign Investments Act of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7042, last amended by the Republc Act No.11647) provides a legal framework for foreign investments in the Philippines while also codifying the restrictions mandated by the Constitution. This act allows 100% foreign ownership in enterprises not restricted by law or the Constitution. However, Section 8 of the law requires the creation and periodic update of the Foreign Investment Negative List (FINL), which specifies the sectors where foreign ownership is either limited or prohibited. 

List A of the FINL enumerates industries where foreign ownership is limited due to constitutional or legislative mandates. For instance,
- No foreign equity: mass media, except recording and Internet business (Section 11, Article XVI of the 1987 Constitution).
- No foreign equity: practice of professions (Section 14, Article XII of the Constitution) except in cases specifically allowed by law following the prescribed conditions. Electrical engineering, electronics engineering, and electronics technician are not allowed foreigners to practice except if subject to reciprocity as provided in the pertinent laws.
- Up to 30% foreign equity: Advertising (Section 11, Article XVI of the 1987 Constitution).
- Up to 40% foreign equity: Private radio communication network (Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution, Natoinal Telecommunications Commission Memorandum Circular No.10-8-91).
Moreover, private security agencies and small-scale mining are under List A. No foreign equity is allowed in Private Security Agencies (Section 4 of RA 5487; Rule IV, Section 1 of the implementing rules and regulations of RA 5487), and no foreign equity is allowed in Small-scale mining (Section 3, RA No. 7076).

List B restricts foreign ownership in industries related to national security and public safety, including private security agencies and small-scale mining operations up to 40 %, in line with the Philippine Constitution. In this sense: 
- Micro and small domestic market enterprises with paid in equity capital of less than the equivalent of US$200,000 (RA No.7042 as amended by RA No.9487)
- Micro and small domestic market enterprises: (i) that involve advance technology as determined by the Department of Science and Technology (DOST); or (ii) are endorsed as startup or startup enablers by the lead host agecies, namely the Department of Trade and Industry, Department of Information and Communications Technology or DOST pursuant to RA No.11337 otherwise known as the Innovative Startup Act; or (iii) with a majority of direct employees as Filipinos but in no case shall the number of Filipino employees be less than 15 with paid-in equity capital of less than the equivalent of US$100,000 (RA No.7042 as amended by RA No.11647).

indicators.question_description: Joint venture requirements
indicators.impact: The Foreign Investments Act of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7042) last amended in June 2022 by the Republic Act No.11647 serves as the primary legal framework for foreign investment in the Philippines. Section 8 mandates the creation of the Foreign Investment Negative List (FINL), which delineates the sectors where foreign ownership is restricted or prohibited. In these restricted areas, foreign investors typically engage in joint ventures with local firms to comply with the established 40% foreign equity limit.

indicators.question_description: Nationality or residency requirements for board of directors or managers
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 1123 - Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines of 2019
indicators.impact:
Section 4 of the Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines (RA 11232) mandates a residency requirement for select corporate officers, namely: the treasurer and the secretary. The treasurer is required to be a resident of the Philippines, while the secretary must be a Filipino citizen and a resident of the Philippines (section 24). This section provides for rules on the nationality and residency of corporate officers.

Filipino companies must have at least five directors, but no more than fifteen. If business activity is partly nationalized, the number of seats for foreigners on the board of directors is measured by a proportion of their present foreign equity to the number of directors as stated in the articles of incorporation. Additionally, the number of their seats should not exceed the proportion of the allowable foreign equity to the number of directors. The officers of entities engaged in nationalized activities are also required to be Filipinos. 

Additionally, under the Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines, Foreign Corporations are also required to designate a resident agent.

indicators.question_description: Nationality or residency requirements for board of directors or managers
indicators.source_legislation: Presidential Decree No. 715 - Amending Commonwealth Act No.108 of 1975
indicators.impact: According to the Commonwealth Act No. 108 or the “Anti-Dummy Law”, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 715, Section 2-A provides that the election of aliens/foreigners as members of the board of directors or governing body of corporations or associations engaging in partially nationalized activities shall be allowed in proportion to their allowable participation or share in the capital of such entities.

indicators.question_description:
Screening of investment and acquisitions
Exception: Anti-trust measures related to M&A are not considered a restriction, unless discriminatory.
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 7925 - Public Telecommunications Policy Act of the Philippines of 1995
indicators.impact:
A screening of FDI exists in the telecommunications sector, primarily through the necessity of acquiring licenses and even a legislative franchise from Congress. For instance, telecommunications service providers need to secure a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity from the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) as well as a legislative franchise from Congress. 

According to the Republic Act No. 11659, telecommunications are classified under Section 2 as critical infrastructure. Investment screening in the interest of national security for telecommunications is based on Rule IX of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of RA 11659, authorizing the review of investments in public service, public utility, and critical infrastructures.

According to the Republic Act No. 7925 or the Public Telecommunications Policy Act of the Philippines, the NTC has the authority to monitor telecommunications providers under Section 24. Moreover, under Section 16, no person shall commence or conduct business of being a public telecommunication entity without first obtaining a license. It further provides that the National Telecommunications Commission may grant Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity and impose such conditions as to duration and termination of the privilege, concession, or standard or technical aspects of the equipment, rates, or service, not contrary to the terms of the franchise.

indicators.question_description:
Screening of investment and acquisitions
Exception: Anti-trust measures related to M&A are not considered a restriction, unless discriminatory.
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 8762 - Retail Trade Liberalization Act of 2000;

The Republic Act No. 11595 - Amendment to the Retail Trade Liberalization Act of 2000
indicators.impact:
The Retail Trade Liberalization Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8762) and its amendment (Republic Act No. 11595) include investment screening mechanisms for foreign retailers, which extend to online retailers:

Section 5 of Republic Act No. 11595 mandates that foreign retailers must meet minimum paid-up capital requirements (originally PHP 25 million, lowered to PHP 10 million for enterprises after the 2021 amendment) before they can operate in the Philippines. This requirement applies to both brick-and-mortar and online retailers. The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) is empowered to pre-qualify foreign retailers (Section 5), essentially acting as an investment screening body to ensure that foreign retailers meet financial and other regulatory standards before operating. This serves as a mechanism to safeguard local markets and ensure that foreign entrants have adequate financial backing.

Since January 2022

indicators.question_description:
Screening of investment and acquisitions
Exception: Anti-trust measures related to M&A are not considered a restriction, unless discriminatory.
indicators.impact:
According to the Republic Act No. 7042 or the Foreign Investments Act of 1991, as amended by Republic Act No. 11647, Section 16 provides that upon the order of the President, the Inter-Agency Promotion Coordination Committee, in coordination with the National Security Council and the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (previously National Economic and Development Authority), shall review foreign investments involving military-related industries, cyber infrastructure, pipeline transportation, or such other activities which may threaten territorial integrity and the safety, security, and well-being of Filipino citizens, when:
(a) made by foreign government-controlled entities or state-owned enterprises, except independent pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and multi-national banks; or
(b) located in geographical areas critical to national security.

indicators.question_description: Commercial presence requirements to offer cross-border services in sectors relevant to digital trade
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 11232 - Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines of 2019
indicators.impact: Section 141 of the Corporation Act requires any foreign corporation doing business in the Philippines to obtain a license to do business from the Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Section 142 of the Corporation Act establishes that a foreign corporation applying for a license to transact business in the Philippines shall submit to the Commission the address, including the street number, of the principal office of the corporation in the country or State of incorporation; the name and address of its resident agent authorized to accept summons and process in all legal proceedings and all notices affecting the corporation, pending the establishment of a local office; and the place in the Philippines where the corporation intends to operate.

indicators.question_description: Patent application issues
indicators.impact:
Section 33 of Republic Act No. 8293 does require foreign applicants who do not reside or have a principal place of business in the Philippines to appoint a local agent or representative: "An applicant who is not a resident of the Philippines must appoint and maintain a resident agent or representative in the Philippines upon whom notice or process for judicial or administrative procedure relating to the application for patent or the patent may be served."

This is confirmed by the Rule 422 of the Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations for Patents, Utility Models, and Industrial Designs of 2022 sets the requirement for non-resident applicants to appoint and maintain a Philippine resident agent or representative in the Philippines. Failure to appoint a Philippine resident agent within one month from the issuance of an action directing the appointment will result in the application being deemed withdrawn. 

The law does not provide any provision that allows for the rejection of patent applications based on the nationality of the applicant. Section 7 of the IP Code provides that any person, whether natural or juridical, including foreign entities, may apply for a patent, and their application will be processed according to the same standards applied to local applicants. The criteria for patentability (novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability) are applied universally without regard to the applicant's nationality.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 8293 - Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines of 1997;

The Republic Act No. 10372 - An Act Amending Certain Provisions Of Republic Act No. 8293, Otherwise Known As The "Intellectual Property Code Of The Philippines," And For Other Purposes of 2013;
indicators.impact:
The legal process for addressing patent infringement begins with the filing of a complaint. According to Section 76 of the Intellectual Property Code, any person who uses, makes, sells, or imports a patented invention without the authorization of the patent holder during the term of the patent commits patent infringement. 

Remedies for patent infringement include civil and criminal options. Under Section 76.2, the patent holder can file a civil action to recover damages, attorney’s fees, and secure an injunction against further infringement. If actual damages are difficult to ascertain, the court may award reasonable royalties as per Section 76.3. In certain cases, damages may be tripled under Section 76.4, depending on the severity of the infringement. The court also has the authority to order the destruction or removal of infringing goods from the market (Section 76.5). Moreover, individuals who contribute to the infringement, such as by supplying components specifically intended for infringement, are also liable as contributory infringers under Section 76.6. For repeat offenders, Section 84 provides for criminal sanctions, including imprisonment of six months to three years, and fines between PHP 100,000 and PHP 300,000. 

Section 216 outlines the remedies for infringement and includes measures that can be deemed provisional such as injunctions [ 216.(a) ] that allow the court to issue injunctions in order to restrain the infringer from continuing their infringing activities. This means that even before the final resolution of the case, the court can order the infringer to cease their actions that violate copyright.

Foreign nationals or entities are also allowed to file infringement suits in the Philippines, even if they are not licensed to do business in the country, provided they hold valid patents, as per Section 77. In the case of process patents, Section 78 establishes that an identical product is presumed to have been produced using the patented process unless proven otherwise, shifting the burden of proof to the alleged infringer.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since June 1997, last amended in February 2013; 

Since February 2013;

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 8293 - Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines of 1997;

The Republic Act No. 10372 - An Act Amending Certain Provisions Of Republic Act No. 8293, Otherwise Known As The "Intellectual Property Code Of The Philippines," And For Other Purposes of 2013;
indicators.impact:
The enforcement of patent rights in the Philippines is governed by specific limitations outlined in the Intellectual Property Code, particularly Sections 72 through 75. These provisions aim to balance the rights of patent holders with public interests, especially in healthcare and innovation. Key exceptions include the exhaustion of rights, which allows third parties to use patented products already sold in the market, particularly for drugs and medicines, thereby enhancing accessibility. Other exceptions permit private and non-commercial use, experimental use for scientific purposes, and regulatory testing, facilitating research and development while protecting the interests of patent owners.

Additionally, prior user rights allow individuals who used an invention in good faith before the patent application to continue its use, safeguarding established businesses. The government can exploit patented inventions without the owner's consent under certain conditions, such as national emergencies, ensuring public health needs are met. Additionally, the law does not state that the owner of the patent must be remunerated.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since June 1997, last amended in February 2013; 

Since February 2013;

indicators.question_description: Lack of copyright framework and exceptions
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 8293 - Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines of 1997;

The Republic Act No. 10372 - An Act Amending Certain Provisions Of Republic Act No. 8293, Otherwise Known As The "Intellectual Property Code Of The Philippines," And For Other Purposes of 2013;
indicators.impact:
The Philippines' Intellectual Property Code provides several copyright exceptions aimed at balancing the rights of creators with public access to information and culture. One key exception is fair use (Section 185), which allows copyrighted works to be used without permission for purposes like criticism, commentary, news reporting, teaching, or research. The determination of fair use depends on factors such as the purpose, nature, and effect of the use on the market value of the copyrighted work. For instance, excerpts for academic purposes or quotations for reviews may qualify as fair use.

Other exceptions include private performances or displays not intended for profit (Section 184.1) and the reproduction of works for personal use (Section 184.2). Educational institutions can use copyrighted materials for instructional purposes, and libraries may reproduce works for preservation or research (Section 184.3). Broadcasting organizations can make ephemeral recordings for scheduling purposes (Section 184.1(c)), and certain public performances in government or public spaces are permitted if there is no charge (Section 184.1(e)). Additionally, copyrighted works can be used in judicial proceedings or for public security (Section 184.1(f)).
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since June 1997, last amended in February 2013; 

Since February 2013;

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation:
Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) Memorandum Circular 2020-049 - Revised Rules of Procedure on Administrative Enforcement Intellectual (IP) Rights of 2021

The Republic Act No. 11904 - Philippine Creative Industries Development Act of 2022
indicators.impact:
The Philippines’ legal framework for copyright explicitly includes administrative and civil remedies for online infringement under Republic Act No. 8293 (Intellectual Property Code) and its amendments via Republic Act No. 10372. Digital works such as software, multimedia, and databases are protected as published works under Section 171, ensuring coverage of online content. Section 6 of Republic Act No. 10372, which amends the Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 8293), introduces two critical subsections to Section 171: Section 171.12 defines "technological measures" as technologies, devices, or components that restrict unauthorized actions concerning a work, performance, or sound recording, while Section 171.13 introduces the concept of "rights management information", which refers to identifying details about the work, sound recording, or performance, as well as information on the author, producer, performer, or rights owner. It also includes terms and conditions of use and any associated codes or identifiers. 

Administrative procedures, such as the takedown mechanism (Section 216), would allow copyright holders to issue notices to Internet Service Providers (ISPs) hosting infringing material. Civil remedies include injunctions, damages, and destruction of infringing goods (Section 216), while administrative penalties may involve fines or cease-and-desist orders issued by the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL). The notice-and-takedown system exemplifies a provisional measure, allowing expedited removal of infringing content to mitigate damages during ongoing investigations.

indicators.question_description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 10175 - Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012
indicators.impact: Section 14 of the Republic Act No.10175 sets the Disclosure of Computer Data : "Law enforcement authorities, upon securing a court warrant, shall issue an order requiring any person or service provider to disclose or submit subscriber’s information, traffic data or relevant data in his/its possession or control within seventy-two (72) hours from receipt of the order in relation to a valid complaint officially docketed and assigned for investigation and the disclosure is necessary and relevant for the purpose of investigation". This is the only situation of mandatory disclosure of business trade secrets.

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.impact:
The Revised Penal Code prohibits the unauthorised revelation of secrets or confidential information by either private individuals or public officers. The revelation of secrets with abuse of office is penalized under Article 291 and revelation of industrial secrets under Article 292 of the Revised Penal Code.

The Intellectual Property Code recognizes the protection of undisclosed information as an independent IP right (Section 4. g). Section 168 addresses unfair competition, which includes misappropriation of confidential business information and trade secrets by third parties. Unauthorized use or disclosure of trade secrets by competitors or former employees can be pursued through civil actions under this law. 

The Supreme Court (ruling Air Philippines Corporation v. Pennswell, Inc.) also ruled that trade secrets may not be the subject of compulsory disclosure. In this ruling the Supreme Court has given parameters and standards to determine what may constitute a trade secret. A trade secret is defined as "any formula, pattern, device, or compilation of information that is used in one’s business and gives the employer an opportunity to obtain an advantage over competitors who do not possess the information".

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 7925 - Public Telecommunications Policy Act of the Philippines of 1995;

Department Circular No. 008 Policy Guidelines on the Co-Location and Sharing of Passive Telecommunications Tower Infrastructure for Macro Cell Sites 2020
indicators.impact:
Section 4(g) of RA 7925 mandates a fair and reasonable interconnection of facilities among authorized public network operators, which supports the rationale for sharing infrastructure to ensure universal access to services. 

Section 11 of the Circular outlines the guidelines for passive telecommunications tower infrastructure (PTTI) sharing, mandating that all PTTIs built, improved, or updated after the effectivity of this Circular must provide ample access slots for mobile network operators (MNOs) and the DICT. The infrastructure should allow co-location and shared use of antennas, transmitters, receivers, and other similar equipment. Agreements for co-locating in shared PTTIs must provide fair, cost-based, reasonable, non-exclusive, and non-discriminatory terms (Section 11(b)). The DICT also monitors the charges and fees imposed by PTTI owners (Section 11(c)), and mandates that all installations after the effectivity of this Circular must be co-located unless there are meritorious grounds (Section 11(d)).

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in telecom sector
indicators.source_legislation:
The Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines 1987;

Republic Act No.11659 - An Act Amending Commonwealth Act No.146 Otherwise Known as the Public Service Act, as Amended 2022
indicators.impact:
Under the Philippine Constitution public utilities are restricted to 60% Filipino ownership. This means that foreign ownership in telecommunications companies has traditionally been capped at 40% (Article XII, Section 11).

However, RA 11659, passed in 2022, liberalizes foreign ownership in certain industries, including telecommunications. The law distinguishes between public services and public utilities, with only public utilities subject to the 60-40 ownership restriction.Telecommunications is now classified as a public service, not a public utility, under this amendment. This change effectively allows up to 100% foreign ownership of telecommunications companies, provided national security concerns are addressed.

RA 11659 includes provisions to safeguard national security. It empowers the President of the Philippines to suspend or prohibit any investment in a public service (such as telecommunications) that poses a risk to national security. The law also mandates that foreign investors in critical public services are subject to national security reviews.

With the enactment of RA 11659, the previous 40% cap on foreign ownership in the telecommunications sector has been lifted, allowing for up to 100% foreign equity, subject to national security reviews and other regulatory requirements.

indicators.question_description: Shares owned by the Government in telecom companies
indicators.source_legislation: The Common Wealth Act No.146 - Public Service Act of 1936
indicators.impact:
The Common Wealth Act No.146 - Public Service Act of 1936 amended by the Republic Act No.11659 of 2022 The leading public service telecom operators in the Philippines, such as PLDT, Globe, and Dito Telecommunity, are currently open to foreign ownership. Sction 14 states that the terms "public service" or "public utility" used in this Act include every individual, copartnership, association, corporation, or joint-stock company, whether domestic or foreign, their lessees, trustees, or receivers appointed by any court whatsoever, or any municipality, province, or other department of the Government of the Philippines, that now or hereafter may own, operate, manage, or control in the Philippines,...telephone, wire or wireless, telegraph system, plant or equipment, and broadcasting stations, when owned, operated, managed, or controlled for public use or service within the Philippines.

The leading public service telecom operators in the Philippines, such as PLDT, Globe, and Dito Telecommunity, are currently open to foreign ownership. According to the last report of Globe Telecom, there's no significant government share in this company. 
Dito Telecommunity is a telecommunications company in the Philippines that was established as a consortium primarily owned by Udenna Corporation, led by Davao businessman Dennis Uy, and China Telecommunications Corporation, a state-owned enterprise. The ownership structure is divided as follows:
- Udenna Group (DITO Holdings Corporation): 60%
- China Telecom: 40%

As a result, the government does not have a direct ownership stake in Dito Telecommunity, but it could have a stake through China Telecom, which is state-owned.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since November 1936 as amended on April 2022;

Last reviewed in October 2024

indicators.question_description: Lack of functional/accounting separation
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 7925 - Public Telecommunications Policy Act of the Philippines of 1995
indicators.impact: In accordance with Section 19 (Uniform System of Accounts), telecommunications entities are required to establish a uniform system of accounts to serve as a basis for rate-setting. If a single entity operates across multiple telecommunications categories, separate accounting records must be maintained for each service classification, ensuring transparency and accountability in financial reporting​. However, there is no specific mention of functional separation being mandated in the Philippines regulations.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 7925 - Public Telecommunications Policy Act of the Philippines of 1995
indicators.impact:
Section 7 of the Republic Act No.7925 states that "a telecommunications entity shall be authorized to operate in one or more of the telecommunications categories mentioned in this Act."

Futhermore, Telecommunications service providers need to secure a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity from the National Telecommunications Commission Public Telecommunications Entities are also required to secure a legislative franchise from Congress.

Therefore, the procedures and authorizations necessary for telecommunications services in the Philippines could pose obstacles and lead to increased operational expenses for businesses. The process of obtaining a franchise through legislative action in the Philippine Congress might extend from nine months to over a year. Similarly, the assessment period for applications seeking basic service authorization, like the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity, could span from six months to a year. Moreover, the duration for processing business permits and licenses from other government bodies varies, taking anywhere from three days to a few weeks, particularly if site inspections are involved. The National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) mandates payment of permit fees and supervision fees for all types of issued authorizations, with the specific amount contingent on the type of permit. The supervision fees generally correlate with the company's capital stock or equipment value. Additionally, radio frequency (RF) license holders are obligated to cover spectrum user fees calculated based on factors such as bandwidth, service area coverage, or the number of radio stations.

There are also mandatory performance requirements that telecommunications providers must adhere to, regardless of whether they are local or foreign. These include commitments to provide universal service, maintain quality standards, and ensure network coverage in underserved areas. For example, Section 8 mandates local exchange operators to offer universal basic telephone services and prohibits them from denying service based on competitive pressures​. Furthermore, under Section 10, international carriers must demonstrate their capacity to provide local exchange services in underserved areas within three years of being granted authority​.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.source_legislation: Department Circular No. 002 Implementing Rules and Regulations on National Policy for Expanding the Provision of Internet Services through Inclusive Access to Satellite Services
indicators.impact:
DICT Circular No. 02 s 2021 provides for the licensing and regulation of satellite systems providers and operators (SSPOs) for internet services. Specifically, Section 9 (“DICT Accreditation Certificate; Renewal”) requires that all Satellite Systems Providers or Operators (SSPOs) obtain and maintain a valid accreditation certificate from the DICT. This certificate is valid for five (5) years and must be renewed by submitting an application within the third month before expiry. 

Under Sections 7 (Requirements for satellite systems providers or operators (SSPOs) and 8 (Reciprocity requirement for foreign or international SSPOs), SSPOs desiring to provide satellite services by directly engaging with ISPs, value-added service providers, enfranchised telecommunications entities or public telecommunications entities, and broadcast service providers (authorised entities) shall have an adequate digital presence in the Philippines, such as having a readily accessing website with sufficient content and information; have an adequate local presence by setting up a branch or representative office, having an institutional agent or official distributor, or a combination of such modes; have the capacity, coverage and satellite footprint in the Philippines for the purposes of providing adequate satellite services to covered areas; be accredited by the Department of Information and Communications Technology; and be a national of a country that does not prohibit Philippine satellites to operate within its territories and does not prohibit its citizens or subjects to access Philippine satellite systems.

indicators.source_legislation: Executive Order No. 546 Creating a Ministry of Public Works and a Ministry of Transportation and Communications of 1979
indicators.impact: The National Telecommunications Commission of the Philippines (NTC) was created under Executive Order No. 546 promulgated on July 23, 1979 (Section 14). The National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) is the regulatory body responsible for regulating the telecommunications industry in the Philippine. The NTC is tasked with promoting fair competition, ensuring efficient allocation and use of radio frequencies, and protecting the interests of consumers. The NTC is also responsible for issuing licenses to telecommunications companies and enforcing compliance with regulations

Ban and local processing requirements
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 10173 - Data Privacy Act of 2012;

Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of the Data Privacy Act of 2012 of 2016
indicators.impact:
There is no ban on the cross-border transfer of data in the Philippines. The Data Privacy Act (DPA) allows for cross-border data transfers, but certain conditions must be met to ensure that personal data is adequately protected:

Section 21 of the DPA specifies that cross-border transfers of personal data are permitted provided that the recipient country or organization ensures an adequate level of data protection. Adequacy is determined by the National Privacy Commission (NPC), taking into account factors such as the rule of law, human rights, and enforcement mechanisms in the receiving country.

Specifically, personal information refers to any information whether recorded in a material form or not, from which the identity of an individual is apparent or can be reasonably and directly ascertained by the entity holding the information, or when put together with other information would directly and certainly identify an individual (Section 3 definitions of terms).

indicators.question_description:
Conditional flow regimes
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation: Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Department Circular No. 2017-10 - Prescribing the Philippine Government's Cloud First Policy of 2017
indicators.impact:
The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Department Circular No. 2017-002, later amended by Department Circular No.10, establishes critical requirements regarding data protection levels for cross-border data transfers, particularly in the context of the Philippine government's cloud-first policy. This circular mandates that government agencies ensure the data protection measures of their cloud service providers (CSPs) align with those of the partner country. It also regulates security for government-contracted cloud services, focusing on international security assurance controls and industry-standard encryption methods to protect government data during migration.

A key provision of the circular is the emphasis on data classification, which requires that government data be managed according to its sensitivity and criticality. This classification plays a vital role in determining the conditions under which data can be stored, processed, and transferred, particularly imposing stricter security measures on sensitive data and placing restrictions on cross-border transfers to ensure the protection of personal and sensitive information.

Additionally, the circular reinforces the principle of data sovereignty, asserting that Philippine laws govern any government-owned or processed data, regardless of where it is stored. This principle necessitates compliance with local regulations, influencing cross-border data transfer conditions even when data is handled by foreign entities. Agencies are required to conduct thorough assessments of CSPs to verify that they meet established security and compliance standards, ensuring the reliability of external cloud services and directly impacting conditions for data flows.

Moreover, the circular provides detailed guidelines for managing data within cloud environments, emphasizing the need for protective measures and ensuring that data transfers comply with existing laws, which is crucial for maintaining the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of government data.

indicators.question_description:
Conditional flow regimes
Exception: Not score data localization measure applied to government data.
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 10173 - Data Privacy Act of 2012;

Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of the Data Privacy Act of 2012 of 2016
indicators.impact:
In the Philippines, the transfer of personal data is governed by specific criteria outlined in the Data Privacy Act (DPA) and its implementing rules. Under Section 12, personal information can only be processed when at least one lawful basis is satisfied, such as obtaining consent from the data subject, fulfilling a contractual obligation, complying with legal requirements, or protecting the vital interests of the data subject. For sensitive personal information, Section 13 imposes stricter conditions, allowing processing only under specific circumstances, including consent, compliance with laws that safeguard such information, or in cases of medical treatment.

Moreover, Sections 14 and 15 address subcontracting and privileged communication, emphasizing the responsibility of personal information controllers to ensure that safeguards are in place when subcontracting data processing tasks. The controller must also adhere to the DPA's requirements and ensure confidentiality. Overall, the conditions for lawful processing and the emphasis on consent and protection of sensitive data illustrate the careful approach taken by the Philippine regulatory framework regarding data transfer and processing.

indicators.impact:
BSP Circular No. 899 outlines essential provisions for banks in the Philippines regarding data management in outsourcing arrangements. The circular emphasizes that while banks may outsource services, they must implement appropriate processes and information systems to monitor and mitigate operational risks associated with outsourced activities. This includes safeguarding customer and bank data, ensuring its confidentiality, integrity, and availability throughout the outsourcing process (BSP Circular No. 899, Section X162).

Risk assessments are crucial, as highlighted in Subsection X162.4, which requires banks to evaluate the implications of outsourcing on data management, considering operational, compliance, and reputational risks. The documentation mandated in Subsection X162.5 ensures that banks have a clear record of their due diligence in selecting service providers, further solidifying their commitment to data protection and regulatory compliance. Additionally, when outsourcing within a business group, confidentiality must be preserved, as specified in Subsection X162.6, thereby ensuring sensitive information remains protected.

The circular also addresses offshore outsourcing in Subsection X162.7, stipulating that banks can only engage service providers located in jurisdictions that maintain adequate data confidentiality. This necessitates ongoing monitoring of external conditions to ensure compliance with Philippine laws regarding data protection. Finally, the BSP reserves the right to take enforcement actions in cases of non-compliance, as noted in Subsection X162.9, reinforcing the importance of effectively managing outsourcing arrangements to protect customer data and maintain operational integrity.

The RCEP involves 15 countries: the 10 ASEAN member states (Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Veit Nam) and five of ASEAN's free trade partners (Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and the Republic of Korea). indicators.impact:
Appointing a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is a legal requirement for personal information controllers (PICs) and personal information processors (PIPs) in the Philippines set by the RA 10173. This requirement applies to any natural or juridical person or any other body in the government or private sector engaged in the processing of personal data of individuals living within and outside the Philippines. The Data Privacy Act of 2012 mandates the appointment of a DPO to ensure compliance with data protection rules:

"The personal information controller and personal information processor shall designate an individual or individuals who shall function as data protection officers... to ensure compliance with applicable laws and regulations for the protection of data privacy and security" (Data Privacy Act, Section 26). It is also regulated under Section 4.a) of the National Privacy Commission (NPC) Circular No. 16-03.

The DPO is responsible for monitoring the PIC's or PIP's compliance with the Data Privacy Act, its implementing rules and regulations, issuances by the National Privacy Commission (NPC), and other applicable laws. The DPO must be a full-time or organic employee of the government agency or private entity.

Furthermore, under National Privacy Commission (NPC) Circular No.16-03, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is required: "A privacy impact assessment shall be conducted prior to the implementation of any program, project, or activity involving the processing of personal data, especially those likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects." (Section 5).

indicators.impact:
In the Philippines, the National Privacy Commission issued Advisory Opinion No. 2017-65 clarifying that the government cannot compel access to personal data because the Bill of Rights (Art. III), Sec. 3(1) of the 1987 Philippine Constitution upholds that “the privacy of communication and correspondence shall be inviolable, except under lawful order of the court or when public safety or order requires otherwise.”

The Philippine Constitution guarantees the right against unreasonable searches and seizure, as well as the right to privacy of communication and correspondence. The Constitution also mandates the judiciary to determine issues of grave abuse of discretion and to settle actual controversies involving rights that are legally demandable and enforceable. These principles sets a comprehensive legalframe work, that effectively protects the right to privacy.

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.impact:
A basic legal framework on intermediary liability is absent in Philippine law and jurisprudence. Arguably, safe harbor clauses are present in the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 (RA 8792) and the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175), but these laws’ definition of an intermediary limits its capacity to provide a safe harbor. Particularly, RA 8792’s scope is limited to electronic documents, while RA 10175 is limited to cybercrimes defined under the law. This makes safe harbors in Philippine law sectoral or content-specific.

Under the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10175), Section 9 establishes that intermediaries must comply with takedown orders when the Department of Justice (DOJ) issues a directive to restrict or block access to illegal computer data. Failure to do so can result in liability. Additionally, Section 5 states that intermediaries can be held liable if they "willfully aid or abet" in the commission of cybercrimes. However, liability is not automatic for all content transmitted through their platforms, indicating a limit to their responsibility.

Similarly, the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8792), in Section 30, provides that intermediaries are not liable "merely for providing access to or for operating facilities for the transmission, routing, or storage of an electronic data message or electronic document." However, this immunity is conditional: intermediaries must not have knowledge of the illegal activity or content and must act to remove or block access when notified by authorities.

In conclusion, RA 8792 and RA 10175 contain some safe harbor provisions for intermediaries, these are limited in scope and effectiveness. The narrow definition of intermediaries and the specific content areas (electronic documents and cybercrimes) reduce the broader applicability of these laws in today’s internet landscape, leaving gaps in protection and practical enforcement, especially regarding intellectual property and other non-cybercrime issues. 

The Rules on Voluntary Administrative Site Blocking issued by the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) also directly relate to safe harbor provisions for copyright infringements. The safe harbor provision is outlined in Section 11 of the IPOPHL Rules on Voluntary Administrative Site Blocking provides protection for Internet Service Providers (ISPs) regarding copyright infringement. This provision states that no administrative, criminal, or civil proceedings can be brought against ISPs for actions taken in good faith while performing their duties, provided that they do not have actual knowledge of the unlawful nature of the content they are hosting or transmitting. Furthermore, ISPs must not receive any financial benefit directly attributable to the unlawful activity. This framework effectively allows ISPs to operate without fear of liability for copyright infringement as long as they act responsibly and do not facilitate or knowingly engage in infringing activities​

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 8792 - Electronic Commerce Act of 2000;

The Republic Act No. 10175 - Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012
indicators.impact:
In the Electronic Commerce Act of 2000 (RA 8792), Section 30 provides a limited safe harbor for intermediaries who act as mere conduits for the transmission or storage of electronic data messages or electronic documents. This protection applies as long as the intermediary does not have "actual knowledge" of the unlawfulness of the content being transmitted. However, the scope of this provision is narrowly confined to cases involving electronic documents, making it inapplicable to other types of online illegal activities, such as defamation, fraud, or trafficking. Therefore, while intermediaries are shielded from liability in these specific instances, they remain exposed in cases involving other forms of illicit activity that do not directly pertain to electronic document handling or e-commerce transactions.

The Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175) similarly offers safe harbor, but only in the context of cybercrimes, which are clearly defined in the law as offenses such as hacking, cybersex, identity theft, and online child pornography. Under Section 9, intermediaries are required to comply with takedown orders issued by law enforcement following the acquisition of a court order. Failure to comply may result in liability, but intermediaries are protected if they act according to the legal process. Nonetheless, this safe harbor is also sector-specific, applying only to cybercrime offenses, leaving intermediaries without explicit protections for involvement in other illegal activities—such as online fraud or terrorism—that fall outside the scope of cybercrimes defined in the law.

indicators.question_description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
indicators.source_legislation: The Joint Administrative Order No. 22-01 - Guidelines for Online Businesses Reinterating the Law and Regulations Applicable to Online Businesses and Consumers Series of 2022
indicators.impact:
Order 22-01 issued by the Philippine Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) provides guidelines for online businesses and emphasizes the legal framework under which they operate. Section 13 stipulates liability of e-commerce platforms and e-marketplaces. E-commerce platforms, e-marketplaces and the like shall be treated and shall be held liable in the same manner as online sellers, merchants, and e-retailers when the latter commits any violation of the laws implemented by these rules. Morever, the platforms shall verify if the goods sold by online sellers, or merchants, and e-retailers in their respective platforms are regulated, prohibited, original, genuine, licensed or unexpired (Section 13.1). 

In case of a prima facie violation commited in an online post by the online seller, merchant, e-retailer, e-commerce platform, e-marketplace, and the link, the concerned authorized agency shall issue a notice giving the violator a maximum period of 3 calendar days to take down such post. E-commerce platforms, e-marketplaces and the like may appeal the take down notice in their reasonble determination, there is no violation of any law. 

Additionally, delivery platforms shall be liable in the same manner as online sellers, merchants, and e-retailers only upon notice that they are carrying or deliverying restricted, prohibited or infringing items (Section 13.5).

indicators.question_description: User identify requirements
indicators.source_legislation: The Republic Act No. 11934 - Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) Registration Act of 2022
indicators.impact:
The user identity requirement for SIM registration in the Philippines is governed by Republic Act No. 11934, known as the SIM Card Registration Act. Enacted to enhance security measures and combat crimes involving mobile communications—such as text scams, cyberbullying, and other illegal activities—the law mandates that all public telecommunications entities (PTEs) register all SIM card users. Specifically, Section 4 of the Act states, "All subscribers of mobile phone services must register their SIM cards with their respective public telecommunications entities." This requirement applies to both prepaid and postpaid subscribers, ensuring that all users are accounted for within the telecommunications network.

To facilitate this registration, Section 5 requires subscribers to provide valid identification when registering their SIM cards. The law specifies that the registration process shall necessitate the presentation of a government-issued identification card, which must include a photo of the subscriber and other relevant information. This step is crucial in ensuring that the identity of SIM card users can be verified effectively. Furthermore, the Act emphasizes the importance of data privacy in Section 9, stating that the information collected during the registration must be treated confidentially. It explicitly mentions, "The information gathered in the registration shall be kept confidential and shall not be disclosed to third parties without the consent of the subscriber, unless authorized by law." This provision aims to protect the privacy of individuals while still allowing authorities to access necessary information in cases of crime or security threats.

Finally, Section 12 of the Act outlines penalties for non-compliance with the registration requirements, indicating that telecommunications companies that fail to adhere to the mandate may face fines and other sanctions.

indicators.question_description: Monitoring requirements
indicators.impact:
There is no specific mention in the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173) that requires digital service providers to actively monitor or take down illegal content. 

Under the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10175), whose Section 12 establishes "Real-Time Collection of Traffic Data". It allows law enforcement to monitor traffic data in real-time for the purpose of investigating cybercrimes. The section grants authorities the ability to collect or record traffic data, provided they secure a court warrant, highlighting the legal framework under which monitoring is permitted for cybercrime investigations​.

However, according to the case Disini v. Secretary of Justice (G.R. No. 203335) by the Supreme Court of the Philippines, which addresses the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 10175, also known as the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, Section 12 lacked sufficient safeguards and was "too sweeping," as the phrase "with due cause" too vague. the Supreme Court ultimately declared Section 12 unconstitutional.
As a result of this ruling, Philippine law enforcement cannot collect real-time traffic data under this specific provision without a court-issued warrant, as it violates the right to privacy and the protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.

It is important to note that the Internet Transactions Act (ITA) empowers the Department of Trade and Industry to issue subpoenas, compliance orders, and takedown orders but in relation to the sale/transaction of goods and services, not particularly on content itself.

indicators.question_description:
Blocking or filtering commercial web content
Exception: Not score political content, criminal content (e.g., child pornography), aged-restricted content, defamation and other non-commercial content.
indicators.impact:
Philippine regulations block or filter illegal content, such as child pornography in accordance to the Anti-Child Pornography Act of 2009 (RA 9775).

The Philippine National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) ordered access to the independent news websites Bulatlat and Pinoy Weekly to be blocked on accusations they publish “misinformation” and support local terrorist organizations.

The NTC’s order was based on the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020, officially designated as Republic Act No. 114794. This law is intended to prevent, prohibit, and penalize terrorism in the Philippines. Section 9 of the Act criminalizes incitement to commit terrorism "by means of speeches, proclamations, writings, emblems, banners or other representations tending to the same end". However, Bulatlat and other organizations affected by this order have condemned it as a form of internet censorship and a violation of press freedom. They argue that the accusations are false and that authorities have failed to provide any evidence to justify the blockages.

the "Revised Rules of Procedure on Administrative Enforcement of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR), otherwise known as the Rules on Voluntary Administrative Site Blocking" of 2024
indicators.impact:
The Philippine framework includes specific provisions for blocking websites that infringe on intellectual property rights. Under the Rules on Voluntary Administrative Site Blocking by the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL), ISPs are required to block access to identified piracy websites upon receiving a request from IPOPHL.

The rules established by IPOPHL explicitly provide for the blocking of websites that infringe on intellectual property rights, particularly those hosting pirated content. Section 6 of the Rules states: "Upon the denial of the protest or after the lapse of the period to file the protest, the Supervising Director or the Deputy Director General shall, within twenty-four (24) hours, issue a request to the ISP/s and/or NTC to block or disable access to the pirate website." 

According to Section 7, once an ISP receives a blocking request, they are required to implement the blocking within forty-eight (48) hours.

In terms of specific industry restrictions, the advertising of alcohol and tobacco products is tightly regulated under the Consumer Act of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 7394), particularly to protect minors and public health. indicators.question_description: Other import restrictions on ICT goods and online services
indicators.impact:
Under An Act Preventing the Proliference of Weapons of Mass Destruction by Managing the Trade in Strategic Goods 2015, the Provision of Related Services and for Other Purposes (known as the Strategic Trade Management Act (STMA)), any person who engages or intends to engage in the export, import, and re-export of strategic goods or provide related services shall register directly with the Strategic Trade Management Office (Section 13). The NSGL shall comprise three (3) annexes: Military Goods (Annex 1), Dual Use Goods (Annex 2), and Nationally Controlled Goods (Annex 3) (Section 4 The National Strategic Goods List).

In 2017, the Philippines' government has promulgated a list of dual use strategic goods that are highly regulated, both for exports and for imports, due to national security concerns. Some examples of these dual use goods are electronics and computers that reach a specified technical standard that qualify it to be fit for military use.

In 2020, the Philippines added a third Annex to the Republic Act No. 10697 providing a list of a strategic goods list placed under unilateral controls for reasons of national security, foreign policy, anti-terrorism, crime control, and public safety. This implements sanctioned items for export, import, transit and transshipment to and from specific countries. This list contains a full category about Electronics (Category 3), but also one about Telecommunication (Category 5)

Most recently, the Strategic Trade Management Office (STMO) issued guidelines in November 2021 pursuant to Section 8 of Republic Act No.10697 concerning the registration process for individuals and entities involved in the export and import of strategic goods. It mandates the registration of entities engaged in strategic goods trade within 30 days of starting their activities. As per Section 4, applicants must submit corporate documents and descriptions of goods, while Section 6 outlines the STMO’s authority to review and request further information.

In 2020, the Philippines added a third Annex to the Republic Act No. 10697 providing a list of a strategic goods list placed under unilateral controls for reasons of national security, foreign policy, anti-terrorism, crime control, and public safety. This implements sanctioned items for export, import, transit and transshipment to and from specific countries. This list contains a full category about Electronics (Category 3), but also one about Telecommunication (Category 5)

Most recently, the Strategic Trade Management Office (STMO) issued guidelines in November 2021 pursuant to Section 8 of Republic Act No.10697 concerning the registration process for individuals and entities involved in the export and import of strategic goods. It mandates the registration of entities engaged in strategic goods trade within 30 days of starting their activities. As per Section 4, applicants must submit corporate documents and descriptions of goods, while Section 6 outlines the STMO’s authority to review and request further information.

indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 4109 - Standards Law of 1964;

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), Bureau of Philippine Standards - Standards Development
indicators.impact:
The Philippines does not implment a measure that doesn't allow foreign businesses to participate in the standard setting process. There were no reports of any lack of transparency in the stardards requirements either.

Under Republic Act No. 4109 (Standards Law), which governs the Bureau of Philippine Standards (BPS), technical committees are formed to create national standards, including for ICT goods. The law emphasizes the importance of technical expertise in these committees but does not specify citizenship or residency requirements for committee members (Section 2). The law allows for the participation of industry experts, which can include foreigners, regardless of whether they are residents of the Philippines. This is further supported by the fact that the BPS collaborates with international bodies such as the ISO, and in doing so, regularly works with foreign experts who may not be residents of the country. Thus, no provision restricts foreigners or non-residents from being involved in the standard-setting process.

Moreover, the DTI-BPS serves as the Philippines’ National Enquiry Point (NEP) and National Notification Authority (NNA), ensuring transparency in compliance with the WTO-TBT Agreement. As NEP, it disseminates draft technical regulations and collects stakeholder feedback, while as NNA, it acts as the sole notifier to the WTO on these regulations. The DTI-BPS also reports to the Technical Committee on WTO Matters, aligning the country’s positions with its WTO commitments.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.impact:
The Bureau of Philippine Standards (BPS) establishes as series of products that, whether locally manufactured or imported, must be certified and are not allowed to be distributed in the Philippine market without the necessary PS or ICC marks. Some of the products included on this list are TVs, CD/VCD/DVD/Blu-ray disc players, or Electric Vehicle Charging Equipment.

Articles 7 and 8 of the Consumer Act of the Philippines (RA 7394) provide the legislative foundation for these requirements:

Article 7: Directs the establishment of quality and safety standards for consumer products. These standards cover various aspects, such as performance, construction, packaging, and safety labeling. It also calls for collaboration among stakeholders (government, business, and consumer sectors) in developing these standards and aligning them with international benchmarks when applicable. This article justifies the BPS mandate to standardize and certify products to ensure public safety and market consistency.

Article 8: Requires the dissemination of these standards through publication and information campaigns. This ensures that all stakeholders, including manufacturers, importers, and consumers, are aware of the applicable regulations and standards for consumer products.

There are two Mandatory Product Certification Schemes: 1) the Philippine Standard (PS) Quality and/or Safety Certification Mark Licensing Scheme and 2) the Import Commodity Clearance (ICC) Certification Scheme. The PS License is granted to either local or foreign manufacturer whose factory and product/s have successfully complied with the requirements of the PNS ISO 9001 and the relevant product standard/s.

The ICC Certificate is issued to an importer whose imported products have shown conformance to relevant standards through inspection, verification, and product testing by the BPS and its recognized testing laboratories for electrical, electronic, chemical, mechanical, and consumer products. 

Among the recognized testing laboratories, companies from all over the world can be found, such as Spanish, Chinese or Vietnamese organizations, so it can be concluded that third party-certification is allowed in the Philippines.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation: ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangement for Electrical and Electronic Equipment of 2002
indicators.impact:
Self-certification is not allowed for telecommunications, wireless and radio equipment. Certification of some equipment types requires testing at the incumbent telecom carrier laboratories, while for other categories approval is based on review of foreign standard test reports. The Philippines' National Telecommunication Commission also issues certification of telecom equipment to be connected to public network services.

However, based on the ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangement for Electrical and Electronic Equipment, Article 3, a member state shall accept or recognize the test reports and certifications issued by the testing laboratories and certification bodies of other parties, which implies that there should be no exceptions in the domestic law of the Philippines.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation:
ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) of 1998;

Asia-Pacific Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation (APLAC) of 2019
indicators.impact: The ASEAN Sectoral Mutual Recognition Arrangements (MRA) allows the Philippines to recognize test reports and certifications from Conformity Assessment Bodies (CABs) in other ASEAN countries. Certifications must meet standards like ISO/IEC 17025 for testing labs and ISO/IEC Guide 65 for certification bodies. While focused on ASEAN, the Philippines also accepts certifications from non-ASEAN countries if they adhere to international standards or are recognized through agreements like APLAC.

indicators.question_description: Product screening and testing requirements
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 4109 - Standards Law of 1964;

The Republic Act 7394 - The Consumer Act of the Philippines 1993
indicators.impact:
The Consumer Act of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 7394) establishes stringent requirements for the certification and screening of consumer products, particularly imports. Article 14 mandates that consumer products must be certified for compliance with quality and safety standards by the Bureau of Philippine Standards, which grants the Philippine Standard Certification Mark (PS Mark) following inspection. Article 15 outlines that imported products can be refused admission if they do not meet safety standards, allowing for a hearing and an opportunity for modification if necessary, and prohibits the importation of banned products. Furthermore, non-admitted products must be exported or destroyed at the owner's expense. Article 16 exempts products intended solely for export from these safety provisions, provided they are properly labeled, thus facilitating trade without imposing local regulatory burdens.

Article 17 makes provisions for third-party certification. Specifically:
Article 17(f): It allows the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) and other concerned departments to accredit independent, competent non-government bodies to assist in monitoring the market for the presence of hazardous or uncertified products. These bodies can also aid in the enforcement of product standards, particularly where government resources are limited.
Article 17(g): The law also provides for the accreditation of independent competent testing laboratories to expand the capacity for testing and certification of consumer products​

As mentioned in Pillar 11, section 2, among the recognized testing laboratories, companies from all over the world can be found, such as Spanish, Chinese or Vietnamese organizations, so it can be concluded that third party-certification is allowed in the Philippines.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.impact:
Foreign equity participation in e-commerce businesses operating in the Philippines is primarily governed by Republic Act No. 7042, or the Foreign Investments Act (FIA) of 1991, as amended by Republic Act No. 11647. Under Section 7 of the FIA, foreign nationals may own up to 100% of a domestic market enterprise, including those engaged in e-commerce, provided that the enterprise does not engage in activities listed in the Foreign Investment Negative List (FINL), which is updated periodically through Executive Orders, such as EO No. 175 (12th FINL).

Pursuant to Section 8 of the same law, List A of the FINL enumerates areas of investment reserved for Philippine nationals either by constitutional mandate or existing statutes, such as: Mass media, Small-scale retail trade, Enterprises with paid-in capital below the statutory threshold of US$200,000, subject to specific exemptions.

In accordance with Republic Act No. 11659, which amended the Public Service Act, telecommunications services are no longer classified as public utilities. This legislative change permits up to 100% foreign ownership in businesses providing internet and related services. This is particularly significant for e-commerce operators that rely on robust telecommunications infrastructure, as it eliminates prior ownership restrictions in this supporting sector.

Nevertheless, e-commerce platforms must ensure that their operations do not fall within the scope of constitutionally restricted sectors, such as mass media, which is limited to ownership by Filipino citizens under Article XVI, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution.

Moreover, enterprises classified as micro or small, with paid-in capital below US$200,000, remain subject to foreign ownership limitations of up to 40%, unless they meet exemption criteria under the FIA, such as:
 • Exporting at least 60% of their output, or
 • Employing advanced technology.

Retail enterprises with a minimum paid-in capital below Php 25 million are also subject to full foreign equity restrictions pursuant to the Retail Trade Liberalization Act, and these restrictions are reinforced under the FINL.

Overall, while the legal framework allows large e-commerce platforms to be fully foreign-owned, foreign investment in smaller-scale or retail-focused digital ventures remains regulated and conditional.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.source_legislation:
The Republic Act No. 8762 - Retail Trade Liberalization Act of 2000;

The Republic Act No. 11595 - Amendment to the Retail Trade Liberalization Act of 2000
indicators.impact:
Foreign participation in the retail sector, including e-commerce businesses engaged in the direct sale of goods to consumers, is governed by Republic Act No. 8762, or the Retail Trade Liberalization Act of 2000, as amended by Republic Act No. 11595. Under this legal framework, foreign investors may own 100% of a retail enterprise in the Philippines provided that the business has a minimum paid-up capital of at least Twenty-Five Million Pesos (Php 25,000,000). For foreign retailers intending to operate more than one physical store, each additional store must involve a minimum investment of at least Ten Million Pesos (Php 10,000,000), unless the investor was already engaged in retail trade prior to the enactment of the amendment. This minimum capitalization must be maintained at all times unless the investor formally notifies the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) or the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of its intention to cease operations and repatriate its investment.

Additionally, only foreign retailers whose home countries allow Filipino retailers to operate under reciprocal terms may be granted entry. Retail enterprises with capital below the Php 25 million threshold remain reserved exclusively for Filipino citizens or corporations with at least 60% Filipino ownership. In the context of digital commerce, e-commerce platforms engaged in direct B2C retail sales are considered within the scope of the Retail Trade Liberalization Act (RTLA), whereas pure marketplace platforms may be classified differently depending on the nature of their business model. This structure, in coordination with Republic Act No. 11967 or the Internet Transactions Act of 2023, provides a balanced environment that encourages foreign investment in large-scale online and offline retail while ensuring continued protection for Filipino-owned small and micro retail enterprises.
