indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in telecom sector
indicators.source_legislation:
Foreign Business Act B.E.2542 (พระราชบัญญัติการประกอบธุรกิจของคนต่างด้าว พ.ศ. 2542);

Telecommunications Business Act B.E.2544 (พระราชบัญญัติ การประกอบกิจการโทรคมนาคม พ.ศ. 2544)
indicators.impact:
Foreign businesses in telecom sector are subject to the Foreign Business Act (FBA) B.E.2542 and Telecommunications Business Act B.E.2544. If there is a conflict between a provision of sectoral rules and general rules, the rules that impose a stricter standard will apply. The general rule FBA prescribes that foreign business must obtain a foreign business license from the Ministry of Commerce. Foreign equity cap is applied on the business sectors listed in the Annex Lists of the FBA, including telecommunications. 

Regarding the sectoral law, the Telecommunications Business Act, the foreign equity cap in telecommunications sector is varied depending on the type of telecom license (Section 7 and Section 8):
(1) Type 1 license (Telecommunications operators who provide telecommunications service without operating their telecommunications network): no foreign equity restrictions.
(2) Type 2 license (Telecommunications operators who provide services to a specific group of customers with or without operating their own telecommunications network): Foreign equity cap at 49% of the total shares.
(3) Type 3 (Telecommunications operators who provide their own telecommunications network, for the use of the general public): Foreign equity cap at 49% of the total shares.

Therefore, if there is a conflict between a provision of sectoral rules and general rules, the rules that impose a stricter standard will apply. Therefore, in this case, foreigners are allowed to acquire shares in telecoms companies not exceeding 49% in 2 of those categories: 
(1) Type 1 licence: no ownership restrictions apply; thus, foreign operators with a Type 1 license are subject to the Telecommunications Business Act B.E.2544 and the Foreign Business Act B.E. 2542, and are also required to obtain a foreign business licence;
(2) Type 2 licence: the applicant for Type 2 license shall not be “a foreigner” under the Foreign Business Act B.E.2542; and
(3) Type 3 licence: the applicant for Type 3 license shall not be “a foreigner” under the Foreign Business Act B.E.2542.

“Foreigners” under the Foreign Business Act B.E.2542 refers to a juristic person having foreign shareholding at least 50% or more.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.impact:
Under the Telecommunications Business Act, any person who wishes to operate a telecommunications business in the country is required to obtain a license issued by the National Broadcasting and Telecommunications Commission (NBTC) (Section 7). Determination of the telecom license applicant qualification shall be in accordance with the prescribed criteria in the Telecommunications Business Act (Section 8). 

Moreover, the NBTC Notification in 2020 provides specific requirements for obtaining a license, including the applicant's qualification, procedures to grant the license and conditions. A Type 1 and Type 2 telecommunications business license shall remain valid for the duration of the approved service period (Section 9.1). A Type 3 telecommunications business license shall have a minimum validity period of no less than fifteen years and a maximum of not more than twenty-five years. The NBTC may consider revising the minimum and maximum duration framework for which the telecommunications business license is granted (Section 9.2). 
The criteria to obtain telecom business license covers foreign equity cap and commercial presence requirement. Specifically, telecoms service providers qualifications must include being a juristic person under Thai law, i.e., establish companies in Thailand, and has the main objective for operating telecommunications business (Clause 6.1).

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.impact:
Previously, satellite businesses have been operated under concession contracts. In 2020, Thailand opened its satellite telecommunications services to foreign-owned satellites. Anyone who wants to provide satellite telecommunications services must apply to the National Broadcasting and Telecommunications Commission (NBTC) for a telecommunication services license. Regarding the NBTC Notification, any persons who wish to orbit their satellites in the country must apply for a license and comply with the requirements. 

The Notification regarding License Foreign Satellite to Provide Domestic Services prescribes that the applicant who wishes to operate satellite must be: (1) a limited company or public limited company established as a juristic person under Thai law with an establishment in Thailand, and also (2) a representative of a foreign satellite operator who meets the qualifications prescribe state policy (Clause 5.1).

Moreover, the Notification regarding Criteria and Procedures for Licensing and the Right to Orbit Satellites B.E.2563 prescribes that individuals seeking to secure Thailand’s or a government agency’s right to use satellite orbital slots must obtain authorization based on a first-come, first-served principle (Clause 4). The rights are categorized into preliminary rights and full rights. Authorization for planned orbital use or existing but unused satellite networks will follow criteria set by the NBTC (Clause 5). Those intending to use the rights for commercial services must obtain full rights and a Type 3 telecommunications business license. 
- For commercial services: Applicants must be a limited or public company established under Thai law, have a business presence in Thailand, and not qualify as a foreign entity under the Foreign Business Act (Clause 7)
- For government missions or specific non-commercial use: Applicants must be a government agency, state enterprise, or a Thai-incorporated legal entity that is not classified as a foreign entity (Clause 8).

The Credit Information Business Act 2002 specifically covers the collection and processing of credit information. Chapter 2 states that only a credit information company has the right to operate the credit information business (section 9). Section 12 states that No credit information company or information controller or information processor carrying on or operating the business in the Kingdom shall operate, control or process information outside the Kingdom. Specifically, the credit information refers to facts that consumer applying for credit, including qualifications of the customers and history of application for and approval of credit (Section 3).

(1) Facts that identify clients applying for credits: (a) In case of an individual, this subparagraph means client’s name, address, date of birth, marital status, occupation, official identification card number or government employee’s identification card or passport, and tax payer number (if any); (b) In case of a juristic person, this subparagraph means address, corporate registration
number, or tax payer number. (2) Record of credit application and approval and payment of credit transaction of client
who applies for credit including record of payments of goods or services by credit card.

indicators.impact:
Thailand's Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) published a subordinate regulation regarding cross-border transfer of personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act. The Notification concerns about the binding corporate rules (BCRs) and appropriate safeguards to transfer data in exemption of Section 28 of the PDPA. 

Part 1 of the Notification focuses on BCR. Personal data can be transferred to affiliated business or group undertaking if they have issued BCR which have been reviewed and certified by the PDPC (Clause 5) The BCR must be submitted for review and approval, and must meet the following criteria (Clause 7):
(1) A legally binding privacy policy for all parties involved (e.g., processors, senders, receivers, employees) that complies with data protection laws.
(2) A guarantee for data protection, data subject rights, and a proper complaint mechanism for cross-border transfers.
(3) Security measures that meet the minimum standards set by Thailand’s data protection laws.

Part 2 focuses on Approprite Safeguards provides that the sender or transferer must implement Appropriate Safeguards to protect data subjects' rights and ensure effective legal remedies (Clause 8). These safeguards must be legally binding and can take several forms:
(1) Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC): Contracts must include key provisions such as compliance with data protection laws, robust security measures, and specific obligations for data processors and controllers (e.g., following instructions, notifying breaches, and handling data upon contract termination). They must also guarantee effective legal remedies for data subjects, aligning with recognized models like the ASEAN or EU GDPR clauses.
(2) Certification: This involves meeting PDPC-established standards for cross-border transfers, ensuring the safeguards are legally enforceable.
(3) Code of Conduct: Used for transfers between government agencies, this must also provide binding and enforceable data protection measures.
In essence, Part 2 ensures that all methods of safeguarding data in cross-border transfers are legally robust, protect personal data, uphold data subject rights, and allow for effective complaint and remediation mechanisms.

indicators.impact:
Thailand has signed 18 PTAs. Of these agreements, 12 PTAs include e-commerce provisions: (1) the ASEAN Economic Community (Upgrade), (2) the ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand (Upgrade) Free Trade Agreement, (3) the ASEAN-China Free Trade Agreement (Upgrade), (4) ASEAN-Hong Kong, China Free Trade Agreement, (5) the ASEAN-India Free Trade Agreement (Upgrade), (6) the ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, (7) Australia-Thailand Free Trade Agreement, (8) the India-Thailand Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, (9) the Japan-Thailand Economic Partnership Agreement. Furthermore, (10) New Zealand-Thailand Closer Economic Partnership, (11) Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), as well as (12) Thailand-Chile Free Trade Agreement.

Among these agreements, RCEP's Article 12.15(2) on "Cross-border Transfer of Information by Electronic Means" contains a binding commitment, stipulating that a Party shall not prevent cross-border transfers of information by electronic means when conducted for the business activities of a covered person.

Moreover, the Customs Department has implemented cross-border data transfer under the ASEAN Framework Agreement and the Japan-Thailand Economic Partnership Agreement (JTEPA). The ASEAN Economic Community (Upgrade) has already established data connectivity for the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) e-Form D and the ASEAN Customs Declaration Document (ACDD), while the Japan-Thailand Economic Partnership Agreement is currently in the testing phase of data exchange.

indicators.source_legislation: Personal Data Protection Act B.E.2562 (พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล พ.ศ. 2562)
indicators.impact:
The Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of Thailand was published in the Government Gazette on 27 May 2019 and fully entry into force on 1 June 2022. Thai PDPA, a general rule on data protection, was drafted based on EU Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR) and governs how personal data is processed, collected, used, disclosed, and transferred. For example, Section 19 states that the Data Controller shall not collect, use, or disclose personal data unless the data subject has given explicit consent, which can be in the written statement or via electronic means. 

The PDPA will join a suite with other legislations related to the digital economy: cybersecurity, consumer protection, etc. Those who violate or fail to comply with the PDPA will incur penalties, including civil, criminal, and administrative liabilities (Chapter VII Penalties). However, the PDPA shall not apply to operations of data undertaken by a credit bureau company (Section 4.6). Therefore, the details of a particular issue are in the Credit Information Business Operation Act. 

Moreover, before PDPA, data protection is regulated under specific laws, including the National Health Act (personal health information), Credit Information Business Operation Act (credit information), Telecommunications Business Act (personal information under the telecom sector), Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act (computer data, computer traffic data), and the Cyber Security Maintenance Act (computer data, computer system).

According to Section 3 of the Credit Information Business Operation Act 2002, 'information' means facts of credit information or credit mark, through any means and forms: document, diagram, sound recording, etc. The 'credit information' is defined as (1) Facts concerning a customer applying for credit: (a.) Natural person: name, address, date of birth, status, identification card number, passport number, and taxpayer identification number, (b.) juristic person: name, location, registration number or taxpayer-identification number; or (2) History of credit application, including the history of payment for goods or services by credit card.

Regarding rights and duties of a credit information company, Section 20 provides that a credit information company shall disclose or provide credit information to its member or the service user who wishes to use the information for credit analysis and issuance of the credit card. Prior consent must be obtained from the information subject every time before disclosing or providing the information. Without consent, the disclosure can be done only by court order, the letter requested from the official, or the letter requested from the governmental agencies. The penalty, including fines or imprisonment, or both shall be applied to each committed offense.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.impact:
Section 50 Chapter 5: Rights of the Service User of the Telecommunications Business Act 2001 states that the Commission shall establish the measures for user protection concerning personal data, right to privacy, and freedom to communicate through telecommunications. The licensee shall have to comply with the prescribed measures. If there is a person who breaches the right of a service user, the licensee or the Commission shall take action to terminate such breach and inform the user promptly. 

Regarding Section 64, if a licensee has violated or not complied with the measures related to personal data protection, then the Secretary-General shall order the licensee to refrain from such action or carry out rectification and perform the action correctly within a specific period. In addition, Section 66 provides that if the licensee fails to perform under section 64 and the warning notice, then the licensee is subjected to the administrative procedure to pay not less than 20,000 Thai Baht (pprximately 600 USD) per day.

Under the Notification, a telecom licensee must collect users' personal data directly from the users only as necessary and in accordance with lawful purposes (Clause 6). The users must be informed before or at the time of collection, except in the following cases (Clause 10): 
(1) The user has given consent for the licensee to collect their personal data from other sources. In such cases, the licensee must inform the user of the collection from other sources without delay, but no later than 30 days from the date of collection, and must comply with the criteria set forth in the personal data protection law.
(2) The collection of users' personal data falls under an exemption from requiring consent. The licensee must provide users with a means to update their personal data to keep it current, ensuring a secure identity verification and authentication system.

(ประกาศกสทช. เรื่องมาตรการคุ้มครองสิทธิของผู้ใช้บริการโทรคมนาคมเกี่ยวกับข้อมูลส่วนบุคคลสิทธิในความเป็นส่วนตัวและเสรีภาพในการสื่อสารถึงกันโดยทางโทรคมนาคม พ.ศ. 2566)
indicators.impact:
The Notification regarding Telecommunications Service Users' Rights Concerning Personal Information Rights to Privacy and Freedom of Communication B.E.2566 (2023) repealed the Notification regarding Telecommunications Service Users' Rights Concerning Personal Information Rights to Privacy and Freedom of Communication B.E.2549 (2006) (Clause 2). 

Regarding the data retention requirement, Clause 11 provides that a licensee must retain users' personal data related to their service usage for at least 90 days throughout the period of service usage. However, if a user files a complaint regarding telecommunications service usage, requiring personal data to verify the accuracy of service usage, billing, or service quality assessment, the licensee must retain the data only as necessary for resolving the complaint. This retention period must not exceed two years from the date the complaint is filed.

In cases where telecommunications services are terminated, the licensee must retain the users' personal data for at least 90 days from the contract termination date. However, if necessary, or if there are outstanding payments, the licensee must retain the data but not beyond two years from the contract termination date, unless another law requires a different retention period.

Computer-Related Crime Act
B.E.2550 (พระราชบัญญัติ ว่าด้วยการกระทำความผิดเกี่ยวกับคอมพิวเตอร์ พ.ศ.2550)
indicators.impact:
Section 26 of the Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act 2007 (so-called Computer Crimes Act 2007) defines 'Computer Traffic Data' as data in relation to the communication of computer system or the origin, time, duration, type of service, or else related to the computer system. The Act requires a service provider to retain computer traffic data for not less than 90 days from the date when the data was entered into the computer system. If necessary, the competent official may order any service provider to retain computer traffic data for a period exceeding 90 days but not exceeding 2 years as a matter of an individually exceptional case and on an ad hoc basis. The service provider shall maintain client data which is necessary for identifying the client since his or her first use of service and shall maintain such data for not less than 90 days as from the ending date of service. Those who fail to comply with this measure shall be liable to a fine not exceeding 500,000 Thai Baht (around 16,599 USD).

(**Remark: The Ministry of Information and Communications Technology (ICT) currently is the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES).)

indicators.source_legislation: Notification of the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology Regarding Computer Traffic Data Retention Criterias of Service Providers B.E.2564
indicators.impact:
The Notification of the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology B.E.2564 repealed the existing Notification B.E.2550 (Clause 3). Clause 5 provides that Certain service providers must retain computer traffic data in accordance with the specifications in Annex B, including telecom and broadcast carriers, access service providers, host service providers, internet cafe providers, online application store providers, social media service providers, content and application service providers, cloud computing service providers and digital service providers (Clause 6 and Clause 7). In general cases, service providers must retain computer traffic data for at least 90 days from the date it enters the system (Clause 12.1). If there is reason to suspect a violation of this Act or crimes related to national security, terrorism, transnational crime, or public order, officials may order service providers to retain specific user traffic data for up to six months per extension, but not exceeding two years in total (Clause 12.2). 

The service providers must securely store traffic data with integrity and access control, prevent unauthorized modifications, appoint a liaison for legal compliance, and ensure user identification, even for proxy or Wi-Fi services. Specifically, the service provider shall ensure that traffic data retention enables the identification and authentication of individual users. This includes logging services such as Proxy Servers, Network Address Translation (NAT), Proxy Cache, Cache Engine, or Free services (Clause 9).

Note: Annex A lists down types and examples of service providers, such as VOIP, mobile service providers, Internet data center, Game online, App store, Google play, Chatbot, Telegram, Facebook, Youtube, Linkedin, Instagram, Line, MSN Messenger, Whatsapp, Web board, Blog, Internet Banking, and E-commerce service providers. Service providers must retain traffic data from the effective date of this notification. However, Internet cafés must comply within 1 year, and digital service providers within 180 days of its entry into force (Clause 13).

indicators.impact:
The Credit Information Business Operation Act 2002 stipulates the requirements for controlling and processing credit information. Section 13 states that the credit information company, information controller, or processor are not allowed to process the information that is older than that prescribed in the Notification of the Credit Information Protection Committee. Similarly, the processing period shall not exceed 3 years after receiving the credit information (Clause 3 of the Notification in 2014).

In addition, section 17(6) of the Credit Information Act requires that a credit information company or a person assigned to process information shall set up at least a system of recording and reporting the result of every access to the credit information. The information recording must keep for at least 2 years from the date of access to the information.

indicators.impact:
The appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) is a mandatory condition under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). Section 41 of the Act specifies that the data controller and data processor shall designate a data protection officer in the following circumstances: the activities such as collection, use, or disclosure of the personal data. 

The duty of the DPO, including: advise the data controller and data processor, investigate the performance of the data controller and data processor, coordinate and cooperate with the Office or the Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) when there are problems and keep confidentiality of the personal data (Section 42).

indicators.source_legislation:
Computer-Related Crime Act
B.E.2550 (พระราชบัญญัติ ว่าด้วยการกระทำความผิดเกี่ยวกับคอมพิวเตอร์ พ.ศ.2550)
indicators.impact:
Section 18 of the Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act (so-called Computer Crimes Acts) provides that, when there is reasonable ground to believe that there is a violation of the Act, competent officials have the power to do:
(1) to address written inquiry or issue a summons on a person connected with the offender;
(2) to summon computer traffic data from providers of services;
(3) to order a service provider to hand over to the competent official data concerning users;
(4) to make a copy of computer data, or computer traffic data from the computer system
(5) to hand over such computer data from a person having in possession or custody
(6) to inspect and access a computer system, computer data, computer traffic data, or equipment used for retaining computer data 
(7) to decryption computer data 
(8) to seize or attach a computer system as necessary for identifying details of the offense

The person receiving a request from the competent official shall take action in response to the request without delay. Moreover, section 19 of the Act provides that the officials have the authority to access the computer data, computer traffic data from a computer system without filing a court petition. Only the power according to Section 18(4), (5), (6), (7), and (8) requires to apply motion to the court. 

The Act applies to Computer data, computer traffic data/ Telecommunication and Broadcast carrier, Access Service Provider, Host Service Provider, Content Service provider, and Application Service Providers. 

(*Remark: Sections 18 and 19 of the Commission of Computer-Related Offences Act 2007 is repealed and replaced by the information in Section 13 of Thailand's Computer-Related Crimes Act (No.2) 2017.)

indicators.impact: The National Intelligence Act B.E.2562 gives the power to the National Intelligence Agency to perform duties related to activities on intelligence operations, civil security safeguard and monitoring the situations which affect the national security (Section 5). The National Intelligence Agency may request public agencies or any person to submit information or documents relevant to national security within a specified period (Section 6). In cases where it is necessary to obtain such information, the Agency is authorized to undertake any necessary actions by adopting electronic, scientific, telecommunication devices, or other technology tools to obtain such information. Regulations, means and requirements of the proceeding shall be in accordance with rules set by the Director with the approval of the Prime Minister. The proceedings under this section, if performing duties or acting in good faith, reasonably and for the benefit of the national security or the public safety, are considered legitimate.

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.source_legislation:
Copyright Act B.E.2537
(พระราชบัญญัติ ลิขสิทธิ์ พ.ศ. 253);

Copyright Act (No.5) B.E.2565
(พระราชบัญญัติลิขสิทธิ์ (ฉบับที่ 5) พ.ศ. 2565)
indicators.impact:
Copyright “safe harbor” protection for intermediaries (service providers) is contained in the 2015 amendments to copyright laws (Copyright Act No.2 and No.3). The provisions exempt Internet intermediaries from liability in broad circumstances, provided that they did not control, initiate, or order the infringement. Section 32(3) provides that a copyright work of another person which does not conflict with normal exploitation of the copyright work by the owner fo copyright and does not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate rights of the copyright owner shall not be deemed an infringement. Specifically, comment, critisim or introduction of word with an acknowledgement of the ownership of copyright in such work shall not be considered as an infringement. 

Copyright Act (No.5) 2022 has added provisions to enhance protection to internet service providers and against online copyright infingement. For example, timely suspension of online copyright infringement is provided (Section 43).

Note: Section 32 (3) is one example of the copyright infringement exceptions provided in section 32, however, it is considered as a general exception and does not specifically address online or digital copyright infringement.

indicators.impact:
The Notification of the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES) in 2017 introduces the 'Notice and Take Down' procedure to remove the offenses content and the intermediary's liability. However, the 2017 Notification has been amended since 2022, which no longer allows the content owner to submit an appeal complaint. The service providers shall remove the claimed content within 24 hours after received the Notification. 

This Notification also grants an authority to the official to submit the notices. Moreover, if the service providers do not remove certain content within the specified period or appeal, they shall be determined as internationally supports under the Act (Sections 14 or 15). Specifically, the Notification divided into offenses under Section 14 (1) that must be removed within 7 days, offenses under Section 14 (2) and (3) that must be removed within 24 hours, and offenses under Section 14 (4) that must be removed within 3 days, but If it is child pornography must be removed within 24 hours.

indicators.question_description:
Blocking or filtering commercial web content
Exception: Not score political content, criminal content (e.g., child pornography), aged-restricted content, defamation and other non-commercial content.
indicators.impact:
The Constitution of the Kingdom of Thailand B.E.2560 states that all notifications, orders, and performances of the National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO) shall be considered constitutional, lawful, and effective under this Constitution (Section 279). Thailand’s government was formally transferred from the military’s NCPO to the National Assembly in July 2019. The NCPO Notifications and Orders have been repealed, including 66 revoked in 2019 and 24 more in 2024. However, the government still retains several NCPO notifications and related laws that are reported to restrict freedom of expression, for example, the NCPO Notifications No. 18/2557 and No. 26/2557. 

Specifically, according to the NCPO Notification No.18/2557(2014) regarding Public Information Dissemination, all types of media services, including both public and private, must prohibit from broadcasting or disseminating the following information: (3) A criticism of the performance of the NCPO and related persons; (4) A confidential information of the state agency; (5) An information that creates misunderstanding and inciting conflicts in the Kingdom; and (7) Threatening to harm to any person that could create fear among the public.

The NCPO Notification No.26/2557 regarding Supervision and Surveillance of the Online Social Media provides that the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES) has the power to designate a competent officer to access/ investigate the computer traffic data and online content within the scope of inciting violence and to oppose the performance of NCPO (Clause 1). If the online content is under the scope of Clause 1, then the officer shall block/suspend certain information and access to the block/suspend the dissemination of the website, social media content, text, images, and audio clip, if certain content has the following nature, such as incite violence, against the law, or oppose the performance of NCPO (Clause 2).

The number of URLs blocked by court orders is not available. However, the MDES's Statistics on blocking illegal and counterfeit social media pages and URLs reported that from October 2023 to September 2024 has intensified efforts to combat online crime, particularly by blocking illegal social media pages and URLs. Notification of Electronic Transactions Development Agency No.3/2567 Regarding Guidelines for Advertising on Digital Platforms B.E.2567
(ประกาศสำนักงานพัฒนาธุรกรรมทางอิเล็กทรอนิกส์ที่ธพด.32567เรื่องคู่มือการดูแลโฆษณาบนบริการแพลตฟอร์มดิจิทัล พ.ศ. 2567)
indicators.impact:
This guideline, issued by the Electronic Transactions Development Agency (ETDA), aims to support digital platform service providers in implementing effective self-regulation mechanisms under Section 32 of the Royal Decree on Digital Platform Services B.E. 2565. The purpose of the Notification of Electronic Transactions Development Agency No.3/2567 regarding Guidelines for Advertising on Digital Platforms B.E.2567 is to serve as a guideline for digital platform service business operators and is not legally binding.

It provides best practices for overseeing advertisements to enhance credibility and accountability while addressing issues such as investment scams, impersonation, counterfeit goods, misinformation, and illegal activities. However, compliance with this guideline does not exempt businesses from legal responsibilities under other applicable laws, and it remains a non-legally binding reference that should be adapted as appropriate for each platform (Clause 1 Objectives). 

Digital platform operators shall have the following obligations:
- Verify advertisers (Clauses 5 and 6)
- Securely store data into machine-readable format, including watchlists for high-risk advertisers, blacklists for those with past violations, and whitelists for trusted advertisers. Data retention periods should be appropriately set, considering advertiser quality assessments (Clause 7).
- Review ads before publication (Clause 8)
- Establish Ads library (Clause 9)

Moreover, the digital platform operators shall monitor published ads using automated systems or personnel. They must provide reporting channels for flagged content, prioritize serious violations, and oversee advertiser accounts for compliance (Clauses 10-12).
references: The purpose of the Notification of Electronic Transactions Development Agency No.3/2567 regarding Guidelines for Advertising on Digital Platforms B.E.2567 is to serve as a guideline for digital platform service business operators and is not legally binding.

Royal Decree on the Operation of Digital Platform Services Businesses that are Subject to Prior Notification B.E.2565 
(พระราชกฤษฎีกา การประกอบธุรกิจบริการแพลตฟอร์มดิจิทัลที่ต้องแจ้งให้ทราบ พ.ศ.2565)
indicators.impact:
According to the Royal Decree, issued under the Electronic Transaction Act, digital service platforms are required to notify before operating their business (Sections 8 and 12). The royal decree defines "Digital Platform Service" as "the provision of intermediary services that connect business users, consumers, or users for the purpose of generating electronic transactions, with or without remuneration but does not include digital platform service, which is for the offering of goods or services of a single operator of a digital platform service or its affiliate acting as its representative, with or without remuneration." (Section 3).

Companies operating online platform services that have a gross income of more than THB 50,000,000 per year or have more than 5,000 monthly active users in Thailand must comply with the full-form notification requirement .Online platform service providers that do not meet the previous criteria, including e-service platforms containing web-boards hyperlinks/banners, are subject to the short-form notification. Both full-form and short-form notification information are required to be updated annually. 

The Royal Decree also applies to the offshore operator that meet the prescribed criteria (e.g.,using .th domain name, using the Thai language or currency on the platform) (Sections 9 and 10). Note that for full-form notification, platforms are required to notify the ETDA by 18 November 2023, and for short-form notification, platforms are required to notify the ETDA by 20 August 2024.

indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.impact:
Standards and technical requirements regulations, as well as conformity assessment and accreditation are regulated under the National Standardization Act and Industrial Products Standards Act. The Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) is established by the Ministry of Industry, the national standards body in Thailand. For industrial promotion, the foreign or international standard shall be referred to as any industrial standard. The Ministry may refer to certain foreign or international standards which their documents are available in the foreign language (Section 15 amended by the Industrial Product Standard Act (No.7) in 2015). Therefore, the country has implemented the TISI TIS standards on various products.

In addition, the country has adopted several international standards: WTO Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT), International Organization for Standardization (ISO), and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), as well as participated in international and regional standardization: WTO Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) and the regional standard of ASEAN Consultative Committee for Standards and Quality (ACCSQ).

This Notification provides detailed procedures and format of the establishment of the Thai Conformity Assessment Standards (TCAS). The process for developing TCAS mainly involves the National Standards Body (NSB), the Standards Development Organization (SDO), and the Conformity Assessment Standards Development Committee.

The requirements for public participation in the standards development process are available under Clause 5 and 6 (Public Input in Drafting and Adopting

These Clauses ensure public participation in drafting and adopting standards by allowing stakeholders to submit proposals and provide feedback on translations and relevance before approval. The telecommunication and telecommunication equipment application are categorized into three groups: Class A (requires registration), Class B (requires certification), and Supplier's Declaration of Conformity (requires a test report or equipment certification). However, it is important to note that Class A and Class B telecommunication products are not subject to SDoC. 

Specifically, Chapter 4 focuses on suppliers declaration conformity. The suppliers are responsible to submit a written confirmation that telecommunications equipement and devices comply with technical standards or technical requirements must use the Supplier’s Declaration of Conformity (SDoC) as specified in Clause 10 and followed the format in Annex B (Clause 19). Operators must retain copies of the self-declaration form along with supporting documentation: product information, specifications or technical characteristics and test data verifying compliance with technical standards or technical requirements (Clause 19). Additionally, the NBTC has not entered into any Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) with other countries at this time.

Additionally, in 2019, the NBTC Notification Regarding Electromagnetic Compatibility of the Telecommunication and Telecommunication Equipment requires that the telecommunication and telecommunication terminal equipment, including telephone set, facsimile equipment, key telephone system, modem, data terminal equipment, PABX, xDSL equipment, must follow the Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) technical standard. Therefore, an applicant of such telecommunication equipment shall submit sDoC as the specifications laid down in the NBTC Notification issued in 2019.

indicators.impact:
Thailand does not implement restrictions on e-commerce purchase. Products and services offered through online or e-commerce channel are subject to regulations by various government bodies and regulators, such as the Office of the Consumer Protection Board. 

Moreover, Thailand’s Electronic Transactions Act B.E. 2544 (2001) provides legal recognition for electronic data, signatures, and contracts, ensuring they have the same effect as paper-based documents. indicators.question_description:
Licensing scheme for e-commerce providers (B2B and B2C)
Exception: Licenses pertiaining to other aspects of e-commerce businesses, such as license to operate online payment services and delivery are not captured.
indicators.impact:
The objective of electronic commercial registration is to improve reliability and confirm the existence of entrepreneurs. Under the Business Registration Act, the objective is to store business registration statistics. Section 10 provides that registration shall be made at the Business Registration Office in the area where the principal office of the operator of a business is located. If the principal office is located in a foreign country and the business is carried out in Thailand, registration shall be made at the Business Registration Office in the area where the principal branch office is located. The operator of a business shall file an application for registration of the business within 30 days from the date of commencement of such business (Section 11). The information to be submitted in the application, such as name, age, ethic origin, the amount of capital regularly used in the operation, and type of the businesses (for full details, please see Section 12). 

The Notification of the Ministry of Commerce Regarding Requirements for the Business Operators to Register their Businesses (No.11) B.E.2553 is issued under the Business Registration Act. Clause 5(4) provides that website that includes the transaction of goods and services must register the 'E-Commercial Registration' under the Commercial Registration Act 1956. Therefore, the electronic business operating in the internet system, service providers, web hosting, e-Marketplace or platform (for example, Lazada, Shopee, etc.), require to register to the Department of Business Development (DBD). In addition, the DBD registration is valid for 5 years. Ordinary persons and juristic persons engaged in E-commerce businesses without commercial registration are considered to be in violation and shall subject to a fine penalty as stipulated. Also, foreign companies require to submit additional documents for registration: 
(1) A copy of company registration; and
(2) An appointment of operation in Thailand: work permits and a foreign business license or document certificate (if any).

Additionally, the Notification of the Ministry of Commerce Regarding Requiring Business Operators to Register Businesses and Prescribing Businesses Not Falling Under the Applicability of the Business Registration Act, B.E. 2499, B.E. 2567 (2024), is issued under the Business Registration Act B.E. 2499 (1956). Clause 5(5) requires that business operators who are individuals or general partnerships engaged in online trading of goods or services — such as a clothing store operating through marketplace platforms like Lazada or Shopee — must register their business. Failure to register results in the imposition of regulatory fines under Section 19(1) of the Business Registration Act and the Act on the Imposition of Regulatory Fines, B.E. 2565 (2022). 

Moreover, Clause 6 provides that registration shall be made at the Business Registration Office in the area where the principal office of the operator of the business is located. The information to be submitted in the application includes: name, age, nationality, type of business, amount of capital regularly used in the operation of business, and addresses of the principal office (for full details, please see Section 12).

(พระราชกฤษฎีกา การประกอบธุรกิจบริการแพลตฟอร์มดิจิทัลที่ต้องแจ้งให้ทราบ พ.ศ.2565)
indicators.impact:
Under the Royal Decree on the Operation of Digital Platform Services Business, issued under the Electronic Transaction Act, digital service platforms are required to notify before operating their business (Sections 8 and 12). The royal decree defines "Digital Platform Service" as "the provision of intermediary services that connect business users, consumers, or users for the purpose of generating electronic transactions, with or without remuneration but does not include digital platform service, which is for the offering of goods or services of a single operator of a digital platform service or its affiliate acting as its representative, with or without remuneration." (Section 3). 

The Royal Decree also applies to the offshore operator that meet the prescribed criteria (e.g.,using .th domain name, using the Thai language or currency on the platform). Companies operating online platform services that have a gross income of more than THB 50,000,000 per year or have more than 5,000 monthly active users in Thailand must comply with the full-form notification requirement .Online platform service providers that do not meet the previous criteria, including e-service platforms containing web-boards hyperlinks/banners, are subject to the short-form notification. Both full-form and short-form notification information are required to be updated annually.

Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act, B.E.2545
(พระราชบัญญัติขายตรงและตลาดแบบตรง พ.ศ.2545);
indicators.impact:
The Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act under the supervision of the Office of the Consumer Protection Board requires the business involving direct sales/marketing to register to the Office of the Consumer Protection Board (OCPB). Since the enactment of the Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act (No.3), the definition of 'direct marketing' is amended and will cover the e-commerce transaction. Any business operators who do not register as required shall be liable to a fine penalty, or imprisonment, or both. 

The requirements for Direct Marketing Registration:
1. Individuals or juristic persons both in Thai and abroad who wish to sell products by means of electronic commerce in Thailand.
2. The persons in item 1 whose income from selling products or services through electronic commerce exceeds 1.8 million Baht
per year.

Exemption from Direct Marketing Registration: in order to stimulate e-commerce by retail entrepreneurs, small and medium enterprises ("SME"), and community enterprises, a Ministerial Regulation on sales of goods or services through e-commerce which are not considered direct marketing was published in the Royal Gazette on 20 November 2018. As a result, the following types of sales and services through e-commerce are not considered direct marketing, and entities conducting these businesses no longer need to register with the OCPB as direct marketing business operators before commencing the business:
1. Sales of goods or provisions of services by an individual who is not registered as an entrepreneur performing direct marketing, and who derives income of no more than THB 1.8 million a year by selling goods or providing services through e-commerce.
2. Sales of goods or provisions of services by a SME that registered under the laws on SMEs.
3. Sales of goods or provisions of services by a community enterprise registered under the Community Enterprise
Incentives laws.
4. Sales of goods or provisions of services by a cooperative and group of farmers registered under the laws on cooperatives.

indicators.impact:
The Payment Systems Act B.E.2560 regulates electronic money services, acquiring services, payment facilitating services, electronic money transfer services, and services for the receipt of payment on behalf of sellers, service providers, or creditors. These services are subject to obtain E-Payment license from the Minister of Finance by recommendation of the Bank of Thailand (BOT) prior to the operation of such services. To be eligible to apply for an E-Payment License for Undersigned Payment Services, business providers must meet the minimum requirements specified below (Section 13, Section 14 of the Act and Clause 4.2 of the Bank of Thailand Notification):

(2) Company directors must meet the requirements of the BOT notification issued under the PSA and must not have prohibited characteristics, for example, being a bankrupt person; an incompetent person; and having been discharged from being a director or an executive of a public limited company due to lacking of appropriateness in respect of trustworthiness in managing business. 
(3) At least one director of a company must be a Thai national residing in Thailand.
(4) The paid-up capital requirements shall be in accordance with the prescribed threshold.
 For example, not less than 100 million thai baht for debit card, credit card or ATM card and for e-money.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.source_legislation:
Royal Decree on the Operation of Digital Platform Services Businesses that are Subject to Prior Notification B.E.2565 
(พระราชกฤษฎีกา การประกอบธุรกิจบริการแพลตฟอร์มดิจิทัลที่ต้องแจ้งให้ทราบ พ.ศ.2565)
indicators.impact:
Section 11 of the Royal Decree , issued under the Electronic Transaction Act, prescribes that the offshore digital platform providers shall appoint, in writing, a point of contact to perform duties to coordinate with the Agency in the Kingdom. The point of contact must be located within the Kingdom and must not carry out business operation under the law on foreign business operations. A contact person shall perform relevant duties, such as, filing annual reports or notifying any change to the terms and conditions. Notably, the Royal Decree solely establishes a point of contact for the purpose of notifying business operations and ensuring compliance with the regulations outlined in the Royal Decree. The point of contact mentioned in Section 11 does not require companies to have a representative office, local agent, legal representative, or a postbox within the economy to provide their services. Furthermore, the point of contact and the Digital Platform Services
Business Operator may be the same or separate entities. For example, a Digital Platform Services Business Operator (A) may designate a local entity in Thailand (B) to serve as the point of contact responsible for submitting documents and communicating with ETDA as the first-level liaison.

Moreover, the large-scale digital platform services shall be required to appoint a compliance officer along with implement a risk management system, conduct external audit, and comply with other obligations prescribed (Sections 19,20, 21). The large-scale digital platform services refer to digital platform services with revenue (before subtracting expenses) exceeding THB 300,000,000 per annum for each type of service or exceeding THB 1,000,000,000 per annum for all types of service, or with users in Thailand exceeding 10% of the country’s total population (Section 18). The compliance officer does not impose any local presence requirement.

https://www.etda.or.th/getattachment/Regulator/DigitalPlatform/law/Clean-Royal-Decree-on-DP-Corrected-1.pdf.aspx?lang=th-TH

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.source_legislation: Notification of the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology Regarding Computer Traffic Data Retention Criterias of Service Providers B.E.2564
indicators.impact:
The Notification of the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology B.E.2564 repealed the existing Notification B.E.2550 (Clause 3). Clause 5 provides that Certain service providers must retain computer traffic data in accordance with the specifications in Annex B, including telecom and broadcast carriers, access service providers, host service providers, internet cafe providers, online application store providers, social media service providers, content and application service providers, cloud computing service providers and digital service providers (Clause 6 and Clause 7). 

The service providers must securely store traffic data and appoint a personnel responsible for coordinating and providing information to authorized officers under the Computer-Related Crime Act B.E. 2550 (2007) and its amendments to ensure prompt data delivery (Clause 9.3).

Note: Annex A lists down types and examples of service providers, such as VOIP, mobile service providers, Internet data center, Game online, App store, Google play, Chatbot, Telegram, Facebook, Youtube, Linkedin, Instagram, Line, MSN Messenger, Whatsapp, Web board, Blog, Internet Banking, and E-commerce service providers. Service providers must retain traffic data from the effective date of this notification. However, Internet cafés must comply within 1 year, and digital service providers within 180 days of its entry into force (Clause 13).

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.source_legislation:
Consumer Protection Act B.E.2522
(พระราชบัญญัติคุ้มครองผู้บริโภค พ.ศ. 2522)
indicators.impact:
The scope of the Consumer Protection Amendment Act or the (No.2) Act B.E.2541 (1998) provides protection for online consumers in an electronic transaction. A contract between the traders and the consumers must include necessary contract terms which not cause unreasonably disadvantage and unfair contract terms to the consumers (Section 35 bis). Additionally, advertising is considered as a part of the contract. Therefore, business operators must provide products or services to consumers exactly as offered through advertising. The conditions for advertising are in accordance with Section 22. Any businessman who fails to deliver the contract having the contract terms as required in Section 35 bis shall be liable to fine or imprisonment, or both (Section 57). 

Note that the Consumer Protection Act was amended by Consumer Protection Act (No.4) B.E.2562.

indicators.question_description: Imposing trade defence measures (anti-dumping, countervailing duties and safeguards) on ICT-related products imported by other Asia-Pacific economies
indicators.source_legislation: Anti dumping measure and Anti-circumvention duty
indicators.impact:
There are no explicit trade defense measures (anti-dumping, countervailing duties, or safeguards) specifically targeting ICT-related products (e.g., telecommunications equipment, semiconductors, or electronic devices) in Türkiye.

The measures identified primarily focus on:
- Textiles (e.g., woven fabrics, polyester staple fiber, blankets),
- Construction materials (e.g., glass fiber reinforcement materials),
- Industrial products (e.g., stainless steel tubes and pipes).

While some of these products (e.g., stainless steel tubes or glass fiber materials) may have indirect applications in ICT infrastructure (e.g., telecom towers or fiber optics), there are no direct measures targeting core ICT products like electronics, semiconductors, or telecommunications equipment.

By including products with indirect applications in ICT infrastructure, the updated list of active measures in Türkiye highlights the importance of stainless steel tubes and glass fiber materials in supporting telecom and ICT-related industries. However, there are still no direct measures targeting core ICT products like semiconductors, telecommunications equipment, or electronic devices.

1. Welded Stainless Steel Tubes, Pipes, and Profiles
Product: Welded stainless steel tubes, pipes, and profiles.
Countries: Viet Nam, China, Taiwan Province of China, Malaysia.
Measure: Definitive anti-dumping duties.
Duty Rates: Ranging from 19.64% to 25% for Vietnam and varying rates for other countries.
Sector: Industrial and telecom infrastructure (e.g., telecom towers, structural components).
Status: Active since July 10, 2021.

2. Glass Fiber Reinforcement Materials

Country: China.
Measure: Anti-dumping duty.
HS Codes: 7019.11, 7019.12, 7019.19, 7019.31, 7019.90.
Duty Rates: Specific rates applied to imports.
Sector: Construction and industrial applications, with potential use in fiber optic cables and telecom infrastructure.
Status: Active since December 31, 2010.

3. Anti-Circumvention Measures on Glass Fiber Reinforcement Materials
Product: Glass fiber reinforcement materials.
Country: Thailand.
Measure: Anti-circumvention duty.
HS Codes: 7019.11, 7019.12, 7019.19, 7019.31, 7019.90.

indicators.question_description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
indicators.source_legislation: The Public Procurement Law (PPL) No. 4734, Amended by Law No. 7257 of December 2020
indicators.impact:
The Public Procurement Law, specifically Article 63, allows contracting authorities to exclude foreign firms from public procurement under certain circumstances. These circumstances are tied to the estimated cost of the procurement. If the estimated cost falls below specific thresholds (detailed in Article 8), the contracting authority may exclude foreign bidders. This is not an absolute exclusion under all circumstances, but it does allow for exclusion based on a specific criterion (cost).

If the estimated cost of a tender is below the thresholds, the contracting authority may close the tender to foreign companies. For example:
- Goods and services procurement by central government units: 1,073,525 TL (approximately 300,000 USD).
- Goods and services procurement by other government units: 1,789,213 TL (approximately 500,000 USD).
- Works procurement: 39,362,920 TL (approximately 11 million USD).

If the estimated cost of a tender is equal to or above the thresholds, the contracting authority must open the tender to foreign companies. However, even in such cases, a price advantage of up to 15% may be applied in favor of domestic suppliers. Additionally, If a foreign company is part of a joint venture, the entire joint venture is considered foreign unless all partners are domestic.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Since January 2003, last amended in December 2020

indicators.question_description: Specific requirements on source codes, encryption and trade secrets
indicators.source_legislation:
The Public Procurement Law (PPL) No. 4734, Amended by Law No. 7257 of December 2020;

Public Procurement Contracts Law No. 4735 2002
indicators.impact:
There are no explicit requirements in Turkish public procurement law for tenderers to surrender patents, source codes, or trade secrets, there are provisions that protect the confidentiality of such information. The laws emphasize the importance of not disclosing proprietary information and ensuring that technical specifications do not unfairly restrict competition. Therefore, tenderers can generally expect that their proprietary information will be protected during the procurement process.

Public Procurement Law No. 4734:
- Article 29 of the Public Procurement Law No. 4734: "Persons in charge of implementing this Law and those who offer consulting services shall not disclose any confidential information or documents pertaining to contractor’s business or transactions or their technical or financial structures and shall not use them for their own or any third parties’ benefit."
- Article 12 of the Public Procurement Law No. 4734 requires that technical specifications must not include elements that impede competition. While this does not explicitly mention patents or trade secrets, it suggests that specifications should be designed to allow for fair competition without requiring proprietary information.
- Article 24 outlines the contents of procurement notices, which must include the criteria for participation and the required documents. While it does not specify the surrender of patents or trade secrets, it does require transparency in the procurement process.

Public Procurement Contracts Law No. 4735
- Article 29 of the Public Procurement Contracts Law No. 4735 states that persons in charge of implementing the law and those who offer consulting services must not disclose any confidential information or documents pertaining to a contractor’s business or transactions, including technical or financial structures. This implies a level of protection for proprietary information, including patents and trade secrets.

indicators.question_description: Limitations in procurement bidding
indicators.impact:
Public Procurement Law No. 4734 and the relevant amendments, there are no explicit legal measures that ban participation in public procurement based on nationality. However, measures that can effectively ban participation in public procurement unless certain local content requirements are met. 

- Article 63 explicitly allows for the exclusion of foreign suppliers from public procurement procedures under specific conditions, particularly when the estimated cost is below certain thresholds. It also provides for a price advantage for domestic tenderers. Contracting authorities can stipulate that only domestic tenderers may participate in procurement procedures when the estimated cost is below the threshold. A price advantage of up to 15% may be provided in favor of domestic tenderers in the procurement of services and works. This effectively creates a preference for local suppliers.
- Article 9 allows for procurement to be limited to suppliers offering domestically produced goods or goods produced in specific regions as part of regional development programs. Procurement may be conducted as being open only to participation of tenderers offering domestically produced goods or goods produced in the cities where regional development programs are implemented.
A price advantage may be applied in favor of tenderers offering goods produced in provinces where regional development programs are implemented.
- Article 12 requires that technical specifications must not consist of elements that impede competition. However, it allows for local content requirements to be included in the specifications if they are justified.
- Article 11 outlines the conditions under which individuals or entities may be prohibited from participating in tenders. While it does not explicitly mention local content, it establishes a framework for disqualification based on non-compliance with procurement regulations.

indicators.impact:
Türkiye does not have any blocking or discouraging mechanisms for foreign investments or mergers and acquisitions in sectors related to digital trade under the Foreign Direct Investment Law. indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Industrial Property Code Law No. 6769 (2016)
indicators.impact:
Industrial Property Code No. 6769

Civil and Administrative Procedures
Article 136: Infringement of Rights Conferred by a Patent. Defines acts that constitute infringement, including:
- Imitating a patented product without consent.
- Selling, distributing, or using patented products without permission.
- Using patented processes without authorization.
The patent holder has the right to take legal action against infringers.

Article 137: Legal Proceedings. The patent holder may appeal to the court for:
- Cessation of infringing acts.
- Compensation for material and moral damages.
- Confiscation of infringing products and means used in infringement.
- Precautionary measures to prevent continued infringement.

Article 138: Infringers are liable to remedy the unlawful situation and compensate damages caused by their actions.
Compensation includes both actual losses and lost profits due to infringement.

Article 139: Documents Evidencing Infringement
The patent holder can request documents from the infringing party to evaluate damages suffered due to infringement.

Article 149: Patent owners whose rights are infringed can file lawsuits.

Article 158: Exclusive licensees can independently file lawsuits for infringement. Non-exclusive licensees must notify the patent owner and wait three months before filing a lawsuit if the owner does not act.

Criminal Penalties 
Article 73/A of Imprisonment terms:
- 1-2 years for false declarations
- 2-3 years for unauthorized rights transfer
- 2-4 years for patent infringement
- Monetary fines ranging from 300 million to 1 billion liras
- Business closure for minimum one year
- Ban on commercial activities

Provisional Measures
Article 151: Parties intending to institute proceedings can request the court to order precautionary measures to secure the effectiveness of the main action. Precautionary measures may include:
- Cessation of infringing acts.
- Seizure of infringing goods.
- Placement of security for damages to be compensated.

Article 152: Nature of Precautionary Measures. The court can order measures to prevent continued infringement, including:
- Modifying the shapes of infringing products.
- Destruction of infringing products if necessary.

Objections and Appeals
Article 99: Objection to Granting of Patent. Third parties can object to the granting of a patent within six months of publication, citing non-compliance with patentability conditions. The objection must be evaluated by the Board, and the patentee has the right to respond.

Article 100: Objection to Decisions of the Office. The patent applicant, patentee, or related third parties can object to decisions made by the Office within two months of notification.

indicators.question_description: Lack of copyright framework and exceptions
indicators.source_legislation: The Law on Intellectual and Artistic Works Law No 5846 as amended by Law No. 5728
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has a comprehensive copyright framework established under the Law on Intellectual and Artistic Works (Law No. 5846), which has been amended multiple times to align with international standards and treaties. Türkiye's copyright law includes several exceptions and limitations to balance the rights of authors with public interest. These exceptions are consistent with international norms, such as those outlined in the Berne Convention and the TRIPS Agreement.

Articles 30–37 of Public Order and Public Interest:
- Works can be used as evidence in court or for public security purposes.
- Reproduction of laws, regulations, and court decisions is permitted.
- Speeches made in public assemblies or courts can be reproduced for news purposes.
- Educational and Research Use (Articles 33–34):
- Published works can be performed in educational institutions for face-to-face teaching without profit.
- Selected or collected works can be created for educational purposes, provided they do not conflict with the normal exploitation of the work.

Article 35 of Freedom of Quotation:
- Quotations from published works are allowed for purposes such as criticism, review, or scientific research, provided the source is cited.

Article 38 of Personal Use:
- Individuals can reproduce works for personal use without profit, as long as it does not conflict with the normal exploitation of the work or harm the rights holder's legitimate interests.

Article 40 - Use of Works in Public Spaces:
- Works of fine art permanently located in public spaces can be reproduced through photography or similar means.

Additional Article 11 of Special Provisions for Disabled Persons:
- Reproduction of works in formats such as Braille or audio for personal use by disabled persons is permitted.

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures

Law on Intellectual and Artistic Works (Law No. 5846)
Article 66 of Action for Cessation of Infringement allows any person whose moral and economic rights have been infringed to bring an action against the infringer to cease the infringement.
Article 68 of the Compensation for Infringement: Right holders can claim compensation for unauthorized adaptations, reproductions, performances, or communications of their works, with compensation potentially up to three times the amount that could have been demanded if the right had been granted by contract.
Article 69 of Action for Prevention of Infringement: Authors can bring an action to prevent probable infringements, especially if the infringement is likely to continue or recur.
Article 70 of Action for Damages: Individuals whose moral rights have been infringed can claim moral damages, and economic rights infringements allow for claims for compensation, including profits gained by the infringing party.
Article 77 of Precautionary Measures: Individuals can request precautionary measures to secure the effectiveness of their main action, such as cessation of infringing acts or seizure of infringing goods.

Industrial Property Code No. 6769
Article 146: Establishes specialized courts to handle actions and claims related to copyright and intellectual property rights.
Article 137 of Confiscation of Infringing Goods: The proprietor of a patent or copyright can request the confiscation of products manufactured or imported in infringement of their rights.
Article 163 of Seizure and Destruction of Infringing Goods: If infringing goods cannot be preserved, they may be destroyed after taking sufficient samples, with the destruction performed under judicial oversight.

indicators.impact:
Trade secrets are protected under several Turkish regulations, including the Turkish Commercial Code No. 6102, which states that disclosing manufacturing and business secrets that belong to others unlawfully constitutes unfair competition. Employees are obliged not to disclose their employers' business and manufacturing secrets to third parties and not to utilize them for their own benefit. Trade secrets, such as technical production secrets, production methods, and research and development plans, are also protected. There is no mandatory disclosure of trade secrets in Türkiye, and there is no regulatory requirement to be an escrow agent.

Article 55: Defines acts of unfair competition, including the unlawful disclosure of manufacturing and business secrets belonging to others. "Disclosing manufacturing and business secrets that belong to others unlawfully or using them for one's own benefit constitutes unfair competition." This provision explicitly protects trade secrets and prohibits their unauthorized disclosure or use.
Article 396: Obligates employees to maintain confidentiality regarding their employers' business and manufacturing secrets.

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing

indicators.impact:
Passive sharing is mandated and is effective in both the mobile and fixed sectors. The Authority may impose obligations on operators to provide any kind of collocation including physical collocation for the equipments of other operators within their own facilities in return for a cost-based charge (Article 17(2)). 

Electronic Communications Law No. 5809
Article 12(2)(c) explicitly grants the Authority the power to impose obligations related to co-location and facility sharing, ensuring that operators comply with such requirements.
Article 16(5) reinforces the principle of non-discrimination and fair access, which is essential for effective passive sharing in both mobile and fixed sectors.
Article 17(1) emphasizes the Authority's power to mandate facility sharing in the public interest, ensuring efficient use of resources and promoting competition.
Article 17(2) explicitly mandates passive sharing by allowing the Authority to impose obligations on operators to share facilities and provide collocation services, ensuring that charges are cost-based.
Article 24(1) highlights the priority of facility sharing in cases where existing infrastructure is available, further supporting the effectiveness of passive sharing.

indicators.question_description: Lack of functional/accounting separation
indicators.source_legislation: The Electronic Communications Law No. 5809 (2008)
indicators.impact:
Under Article 21 of the Electronic Communications Law (Law No. 5809) Only accounting separation is mandated for operators with Significant Market Power (SMP). However, functional separation is not explicitly mandated.

Article 20 – Obligations for Operators with Significant Market Power (SMP)
"The Authority may impose obligations on operators with significant market power, including obligations related to transparency, non-discrimination, accounting separation, access, and price control." This article establishes the legal basis for imposing functional separation and other obligations on SMP operators to ensure fair competition.

Article 21 – Accounting Separation Obligations: "The Authority may impose obligations on operators with significant market power to keep separate accounts for their activities related to electronic communications services and networks, including the preparation of financial reports for each service provided." This article explicitly empowers the ICTA to require accounting separation from operators with SMP to ensure transparency and prevent cross-subsidization between competitive and non-competitive services.

indicators.question_description: Licensing requirements in telecom sector for operators
indicators.source_legislation: The Electronic Communications Law No. 5809 (2008)
indicators.impact:
The Electronic Communications Law No. 5809 (2008)
Companies providing electronic communication services must obtain authorization from the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA). This often involves establishing a local entity or representative.
Article 6 of Competencies of the Authority: This provision grants the ICTA the authority to regulate competition in the electronic communications sector, including imposing obligations on SMP operators and addressing issues such as mergers and acquisitions that may affect competition.

Article 9 states that telecom operators must obtain authorization to provide electronic communications services or operate networks. Authorization is based on:
- Notification: For services that do not require scarce resources (e.g., frequency, numbering, or satellite positions).
- Right of Use: For services requiring scarce resources, such as spectrum or numbering.
Article 9(9) allows the ICTA to reject applications for authorization or impose additional conditions based on national security, public order, or public health. While this could indirectly affect foreign operators, it is not explicitly discriminatory and applies to all operators.

Articles 20 and 21 - Operators with SMP are subject to additional obligations to ensure fair competition:
- Access and Interconnection: SMP operators must provide access and interconnection to other operators on a non-discriminatory and cost-oriented basis.
- Accounting Separation: SMP operators may be required to maintain separate accounts for different services to prevent anti-competitive practices (Article 21).
- Tariff Regulation: SMP operators may be subject to tariff approval, price ceilings, or cost-based pricing to prevent anti-competitive behavior (Article 20).

Article 8 of Authorization Requirement: Companies intending to provide electronic communications services or construct and operate electronic communications networks or infrastructure must obtain authorization from the Authority.
Article 9 of Notification or Rights of Use: Authorization is issued based on:
- Notification: For services that do not require the assignment of scarce resources (e.g., frequency, number, satellite position).
- Rights of Use: For services that require the assignment of scarce resources.
Steps for Authorization:
- Notification: Companies must notify the Authority of their intention to provide electronic communications services or operate networks/infrastructure before starting their activities. This notification must comply with the Authority’s regulations.
- Rights of Use: If the service requires scarce resources (e.g., frequency, number, satellite position), the company must apply for and obtain the right of use from the Authority.
- Timeframe for Authorization: The Authority must issue the right of use within 30 days of a valid application if the number of rights of use is not limited. If the number of rights of use is limited, the Authority may conduct a tender process to allocate the rights.
- Grounds for Rejection: The Authority may reject applications for rights of use due to: Insufficient resources. Failure to meet qualification requirements. Concerns related to national security, public order, public health, or similar public interests.

Article 10 of Trial Permissions: The Authority may issue provisional permissions for trial or demonstration purposes to companies applying to provide electronic communications services or operate networks/infrastructure.

indicators.question_description: Lack of independent telecom authority
indicators.source_legislation:
The Electronic Communications Law No. 5809;

Law on the Establishment of the Information and Communication Technologies Authority Law No.2813
indicators.impact:
Law No. 5809 establishes that Türkiye has an independent telecommunications authority, the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA). The ICTA is responsible for supervising and administering services in the telecommunications sector and making impartial decisions (Article 6). 

- ICTA is defined as a public legal entity with administrative and financial autonomy under Article 5 of Law No. 2813.
It has its own budget and income sources, including administrative fees, fines, and other revenues, as outlined in Article 5 of Law No. 2813 and Article 11 of Law No. 5809.

- ICTA operates independently in performing its duties, and no organ, authority, institution, or person can give orders or instructions to the Authority (Article 5 of Law No. 2813). The Information and Communication Technologies Board, the decision-making body of ICTA, is composed of seven members, including a chairman, who are appointed for fixed terms and cannot be arbitrarily dismissed.

- ICTA has broad regulatory powers, including licensing, spectrum management, tariff regulation, competition oversight, and consumer protection, as outlined in Articles 6 and 7 of Law No. 5809. It can impose obligations on operators with Significant Market Power (SMP) to ensure fair competition and prevent anti-competitive practices (Article 6 of Law No. 5809).

- ICTA's decisions are subject to judicial review by the Council of State, ensuring accountability while maintaining its independence (Article 62 of Law No. 5809).

The ICTA is legally independent and has the necessary regulatory powers to oversee the telecommunications sector. However, practical concerns, such as its association with the Ministry of Transport and the government's ownership in major telecom operators, may raise questions about the full extent of its operational independence.

indicators.source_legislation:
The Regulation on Processing of Personal Data and the Protection of Privacy in the Electronic Communication Sector;

Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK), as amended in August 2024 by Law 7499
indicators.impact:
Article 5(2) of the Regulation on Processing of Personal Data and the Protection of Privacy in the Electronic Communication Sector said that it is essential that traffic and location data are not exported abroad for national security reasons. However, Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 further clarifies that data can be transferred abroad if consent is sought or third party countries have the same level of data protection as the one in Türkiye.

Türkiye has specific bans and local processing requirements for personal data, as outlined in Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK) and its amendments.

Local Processing Requirements
Article 16 of KVKK establishes the Registry of Data Controllers (VERBIS), which requires data controllers to register and disclose:
- Whether personal data will be transferred abroad.
- Measures taken to ensure data security.
Article 12 of KVKK mandates that data controllers take technical and administrative measures to ensure data security, including preventing unauthorized access and ensuring compliance with local laws.

Article 9(5) of KVKK prohibits the transfer of personal data abroad if it would seriously harm the interests of Türkiye or the data subject. This includes cases where:
- National security or public order is at risk.
- The transfer conflicts with Türkiye's international agreements.
Key Clause: Article 9(5) states: "In cases where the interest of Türkiye or the data subject will be seriously harmed, personal data may only be transferred abroad upon the permission of the Board after receiving the opinions of related public institutions and organizations."

Article 18 of KVKK imposes administrative fines for violations of cross-border data transfer rules:
- Fines range from 20,000 to 1,000,000 TL for failing to comply with Article 9.
- Additional penalties may apply under the Turkish Penal Code (Article 138) for failing to erase or anonymize personal data.
