indicators.impact:
Presidential Circular No. 2019/12 mandates that critical data, such as population, health, communication records, genetic, and biometric data, must be stored domestically within Türkiye. This is not explicitly a restriction on cross-border data transfers but is interpreted as a requirement to maintain a backup of such data within Türkiye for accessibility and security purposes.

Article 1 of the Presidential Circular No. 2019/12 "Critical information and data such as population, health, and communication records, and genetic and biometric data shall be securely stored domestically." This provision mandates that critical data must be stored within Türkiye to ensure its confidentiality, integrity, and accessibility. While not explicitly prohibiting cross-border transfers, it requires a domestic backup for accessibility and security purposes.

Article 2 of the Presidential Circular No. 2019/12"Critical data in public institutions and organizations shall be kept in a secure network in an offline and physically secure medium, access to the devices to be used in such network shall be controlled, and the logs shall be preserved under precautions against modification." This applies to public institutions and critical infrastructure enterprises, ensuring that their critical data is stored securely within Türkiye.

The decision also states that all data should be kept within Turkish borders. Moreover, where the devices manufactured to be used in Türkiye or imported to the country have remotely programmable SIM (eUICC, eSIM/embedded SIM, etc.) technologies, their relevant modules are expected to be programmable only by local mobile operators and only local mobile operator profiles may be installed.

indicators.impact:
Banking Law No. 5411 (only available in Turkish) foresees specific rules for cross-border transfers of customer data. Conditions regarding the cross-border transfer of customer data set forth under the Banking Law should take precedence over conditions set forth under the Data Protection Law. The Banking Law stipulates that even if the explicit consent of the customer is obtained pursuant to the Data Protection Law for cross-border transfers or transfers of customer data to third parties located in Türkiye, the customer data should not be shared with and transferred to third parties located in Türkiye or outside Türkiye without the customers' instructions or requests.

Furthermore, under the Banking Law, the Banking Regulation and Supervision Authority is authorised to prohibit the sharing or transfer of customer data or bank secrets with third parties located outside Türkiye, as well as to make decisions regarding keeping information systems used by banks and their backups locally due to evaluations regarding economic security.

indicators.question_description:
Conditional flow regimes

indicators.source_legislation: Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK), as amended in August 2024 by Law 7499
indicators.impact:
According to the article 9 of the Personal Data Protection Law, data cannot be processed or transferred abroad without the individual's explicit consent. Consent will not be required if the transfer is necessary to exercise a right or is required by law, and either: 
- Sufficient protection exists in the transferee country, or
- if the data controller gives a written security undertaking and Türkiye’s Data Protection Board grants permission.

It is reported that these conditions are very restrictive, so that, in some cases, data controllers have made their own assessment of whether personal data will be adequately protected based on the criteria used by the Turkish Personal Data Protection Authority to assess adequacy. 

Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK)

Article 9: This is the primary article regulating cross-border data transfers. Key provisions include:
- Adequacy Decision: Data can be transferred to countries deemed to provide an adequate level of protection by the Personal Data Protection Board (DPA).
- Appropriate Safeguards: If no adequacy decision exists, data can be transferred if the data controller provides appropriate safeguards (e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)), subject to DPA approval.
- Explicit Consent: In the absence of adequacy or safeguards, data can only be transferred abroad with the explicit consent of the data subject.
Exceptional Transfers: Data may be transferred without consent in specific cases, such as:
- Protection of life or physical integrity.
- Performance of a contract.
- Establishment, exercise, or protection of legal claims.
- Legitimate interests of the data controller, provided it does not harm the data subject's rights.

Article 8: Regulates the domestic transfer of personal data but also applies to cross-border transfers indirectly. Requires compliance with general data processing principles and the data subject's explicit consent, unless an exception applies.

Article 18: Specifies penalties for non-compliance with cross-border data transfer rules, including:
- Administrative fines ranging from 15,000 to 1,000,000 TL.
- Suspension of data processing activities.

indicators.question_description: Not in an agreement with binding commitments on data transfer.
indicators.source_legislation: Lack of participation in agreements with binding commitments on data flows
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has not joined any agreement with binding commitments to open transfers of data across borders.

Türkiye has not fully committed to binding international agreements on data flows, such as those under the EU GDPR framework. While Türkiye has introduced mechanisms like Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) and Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) for cross-border data transfers, these are implemented domestically under the Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK) and are subject to approval by the Personal Data Protection Authority (DPA).

Türkiye has not formally committed to or joined binding international agreements on data flows, such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) or the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement (DEPA).

Türkiye's data localization policies and conditional data flow regimes create challenges for aligning with international agreements like the CPTPP, DEPA, or similar frameworks. Key domestic policies include:

- Presidential Circular No. 2019/12: Mandates domestic storage of critical data, such as health, population, and communication records.
- Sector-Specific Regulations: Banking, healthcare, and telecommunications sectors impose strict localization requirements.
- KVKK (Article 9): Allows cross-border data transfers only under specific conditions, such as adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards, or explicit consent.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.source_legislation: Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK), as amended in August 2024 by Law 7499
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has adopted a comprehensive data protection legal framework that applies to personal data across sectors. In April 2016, Türkiye enacted the Law on Protection of Personal Data No. 6698, which regulates the processing of personal data in Türkiye. The law includes stricter provisions for special categories of personal data, such as sensitive personal data relating to race, ethnic origin, political opinions, philosophical beliefs, religion, sect or other beliefs, clothing, membership of associations, foundations, or trade unions, health data, information related to sexual life, previous criminal convictions and security measures, and biometric and genetic data. The law is primarily based on EU Directive 95/46/EC and includes provisions similar to those of the GDPR. The law also allows the Personal Data Protection Authority to prohibit the cross-border transfer of data even if explicit consent of the data subject is obtained if it deems necessary

Türkiye has a dedicated data protection law, the Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK), which was enacted in 2016. It provides a legal framework for the protection of personal data and includes:

- General Principles: Articles 4 and 5 outline principles such as lawfulness, accuracy, purpose limitation, and data minimization.
- Data Subject Rights: Article 11 grants individuals rights such as access, rectification, erasure, and objection to data processing.
- Obligations for Data Controllers: Articles 10 and 12 impose obligations on data controllers to inform data subjects and ensure data security.
- Cross-Border Data Transfers: Article 9 regulates the transfer of personal data abroad, requiring either explicit consent or sufficient protection in the recipient country.
- Sensitive Data: Article 6 provides additional safeguards for sensitive data, such as health and biometric data.

indicators.source_legislation: Regulation on the Registry of Data Controllers
indicators.impact:
According to Article 11 of the Regulation on the Registry of Data Controllers, a contact person must be appointed if the data controller is a legal entity located in Türkiye and is not exempt from registration with the Turkish Personal Data Protection Authority. Additionally, if the data controller is not located in Türkiye, it must appoint a representative who must be either a Turkish legal entity or Turkish citizen.

The data controller’s contact person or representative is responsible for managing communications with the Turkish Personal Data Protection Authority and data subjects. Data controllers remain liable for compliance with the Protection of Personal Data Law regardless of the appointment of a contact person or a representative.

indicators.question_description: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) or Data Protection Officer (DPO) requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK), as amended in August 2024 by Law 7499
indicators.impact:
Accord to the law, companies are required to appoint a "data controller" who will be responsible for compliance under the Protection of Personal Data Law. If a data controller is located in Türkiye, a contact person for the data controller must be appointed. However, if a data controller is located outside Türkiye, a national representative, either a natural or juristic person, must be appointed.

While the Law does not directly require companies to appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO), it does regulate the obligation to take all necessary technical and administrative measures to provide a sufficient level of security in order to prevent unlawful processing of personal data.

KVKK does not explicitly require a DPO. However, organizations must designate a contact person (referred to as "İrtibat Kişisi") for communication with the Personal Data Protection Authority (KVKK Board) if they are registered in the Data Controllers Registry (VERBIS).
Contact Person (İrtibat Kişisi):
- This person is responsible for ensuring communication between the organization and the KVKK Board.
- The contact person does not have the same responsibilities as a GDPR DPO but serves as a point of contact for compliance-related matters.
- For foreign data controllers, a representative must be appointed in Türkiye.

KVKK does not explicitly require a DPIA as defined under GDPR. However, there are obligations that indirectly align with the objectives of a DPIA:
- Under Article 12 of KVKK, data controllers are required to take technical and administrative measures to ensure the security of personal data and prevent unlawful processing, access, or loss. This includes conducting internal assessments to identify risks and implement appropriate safeguards.
- For sensitive data (e.g., health, biometric, or genetic data), Article 6 requires the implementation of adequate measures determined by the KVKK Board. These measures may involve risk assessments similar to a DPIA to ensure compliance.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698 (KVKK), as amended in August 2024 by Law 7499
indicators.impact:
Article 28 of the Personal Data Protection Law outlines situations where personal data can be shared without the consent of the user. These include:
-Personal data used for official statistics, research, planning, and statistics after anonymization.
-Personal data used for artistic, historical, literary, or scientific purposes, as long as it doesn't violate various national interests or personal rights.
-Personal data processed for national defense, security, public order, or economic security by authorized public institutions.
-Personal data processed by judicial or execution authorities during investigations or legal proceedings.

Additionally, certain provisions of the law related to informing data subjects, their rights (excluding compensation claims), and data controller registration do not apply when personal data processing is necessary for:
- Crime prevention or investigation.
- Data voluntarily made public by the individual.
- Regulatory, supervisory, or disciplinary activities conducted by authorized public institutions or professional organizations.
- Protection of the State's economic and financial interests regarding budget, tax, and financial matters.

The provisions in Article 28(2) of the KVKK provide a legal basis for processing personal data without consent in specific scenarios, such as crime prevention, regulatory activities, or protecting the State's financial interests.

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.source_legislation:
Law No. 5651 on Regulating Broadcasting in the Internet and Fighting Against Crimes Committed through Internet Broadcasting as amended by the Amending Law of July 31 2020;

Regulation on Electronic Commerce Intermediary Service Providers and Electronic Commerce Service Providers No. 32058
indicators.impact:
Article 4 and 6 of the Law No. 5651 regulates the liability of Internet intermediaries and service providers and provide a safe harbor to both. However, Article 6 also states that, if informed by the government, the access providers should prevent access to the content that considered illegal in accordance with the provisions of the law.

Türkiye has a framework in place that limits liability for intermediaries under Internet Law No. 5651. This law outlines the responsibilities and obligations of intermediaries, such as content providers, hosting providers, and access providers, while also limiting their liability under certain conditions.

Article 4: Content providers are responsible for the content they create, amend, or provide on the internet.They are not liable for links to third-party content unless it is clear that they endorse or intend to make the linked content accessible.

Article 5: Hosting providers are not obligated to monitor the content they host or investigate its legality. They are required to remove illegal content only if notified in accordance with Articles 8 and 9 of the law.

Article 6: Access providers are not responsible for the content accessed through their services. They are required to block access to illegal content only if notified in accordance with the law.

Article 6/A: The association is responsible for implementing decisions to block access or remove content. Notifications to the association are considered sufficient for compliance by access providers.

Intermediaries (content, hosting, and access providers) are not held liable for illegal content unless they fail to act after being notified of a legal decision to remove or block access to the content.

indicators.source_legislation: The Regulation on the Process of Identity Authentication of Applicants in the Electronic Communications Sector of the Information Technologies and Communication Authority No.31523
indicators.impact:
This Regulation establishes procedures and principles for authenticating identity during the creation of electronic documents for subscription contracts and applications in the electronic communications sector.

The Regulation introduces four different methods for identity authentication in the electronic communications sector:
- Authentication through the e-Government System.
- Authentication through artificial intelligence compliant with the ICAO 9303 standard.
- Authentication through the Turkish Republic Identity Card (TCKK) by Enhanced PDF Electronic Signature compliant with the TSI EN 319 142 standard.
- Authentication through video recording in face-to-face applications.

indicators.question_description: Monitoring requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Law No. 5651 on Regulating Broadcasting in the Internet and Fighting Against Crimes Committed through Internet Broadcasting as amended by the Amending Law of July 31 2020
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has monitoring requirements under its legal framework, particularly through Internet Law No. 5651 and related regulations. These requirements include obligations for monitoring users' activities and removing or blocking content under specific circumstances.

Article 7: Mass use providers (e.g., internet cafes, public Wi-Fi providers) are required to:
- Restrict access to illegal content.
- Keep access records of users' activities.
- Take measures to protect minors and prevent crimes.
These obligations effectively require monitoring of users' activities in public internet access points.

Article 8: Content and access providers must comply with decisions to remove content or block access to illegal content, such as:
Child sexual abuse,
Terrorism, Public misinformation, Crimes against national security.
These decisions can be issued by a judge, public prosecutor, or the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA).

Social Media Law No. 7253 (2020)

Article 5: Individuals can request the removal of content that violates their personal rights. Providers must act on such requests and remove or block access to the content within 24 hours of receiving a judicial decision.
New Clause (10): Courts may decide that the applicant's name should not be associated with the content in search engines, effectively requiring monitoring of search engine results.

indicators.question_description:
Blocking or filtering commercial web content
Exception: Not score political content, criminal content (e.g., child pornography), aged-restricted content, defamation and other non-commercial content.
indicators.source_legislation:
Law No. 5651 on Regulating Broadcasting in the Internet and Fighting Against Crimes Committed through Internet Broadcasting as amended by the Amending Law of July 31 2020；

Social Media Law No. 7253 (2020)
indicators.impact:
Internet Law No. 5651 provides the legal basis for blocking and filtering online content, including commercial websites, under certain conditions. The law allows for the removal of content and blocking access to websites that violate Turkish laws, including those related to:
- National security,
- Public order,
- Protection of minors,
- Prevention of crimes such as obscenity, gambling, and terrorism.

Law No. 7253, which amended Internet Law No. 5651, expanded the government's authority to block or filter content, including commercial web content.
- Article 8: Allows blocking of content related to specific crimes (e.g., obscenity, gambling, terrorism) without prior judicial approval in urgent cases.
- Article 9: Permits individuals to request content removal or access blocking for violations of personal rights.
- Article 8/A allows the President of Türkiye or relevant ministries to issue urgent decisions to block access to content or websites without prior judicial approval in cases involving national security, public health, or public order.
- Article 9 allows individuals to request the removal of content that violates their personal rights, including commercial disputes, through court orders.

Social network providers with more than 1 million daily users in Türkiye are required to:
- Remove or block content deemed illegal within 24 hours of notification.
- Respond to user complaints about content removal within 48 hours.
- Failure to comply can result in administrative fines, advertising bans, or bandwidth throttling.
If they fail to comply, the following penalties are applied in stages:
- First Stage: An administrative fine of 10 million Turkish Liras.
- Second Stage: An additional fine of 30 million Turkish Liras if the obligation is not fulfilled within 30 days of the first fine.
- Third Stage: A ban on advertising for the social network provider if the obligation is not fulfilled within 30 days of the second fine.
Bandwidth Reduction Policy: A bandwidth reduction policy is explicitly mentioned in Additional Article 4, Paragraph 2 of Law No. 7253, which amends Law No. 5651
- If the obligation is still not fulfilled within three months of the advertising ban, the President of the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK) may apply to a criminal court of peace to reduce the social network provider's internet traffic bandwidth by 50%.
- If the obligation remains unfulfilled within 30 days of the 50% bandwidth reduction, the President may request a further reduction of up to 90%.
- The judge may decide on a lower percentage (not less than 50%) based on the nature of the service provided.
- The bandwidth reduction decision is sent to access providers, who must implement it immediately and within four hours of notification.

This provides a legal basis for export restrictions on ICT goods if they are deemed sensitive or critical to national interests.

indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.source_legislation: Law No. 7223 on Product Safety and Technical Regulations
indicators.impact:
There isn't any measure that prohibits foreign business to participate in standard-setting bodies and there were no reports that standard requirements are not transparent.

Article 3, Item j: The Turkish Standards Institute (TSE) is identified as the primary audit unit for conformity assessments. TSE collaborates with international organizations (e.g., ISO), but participation in its standard-setting processes is generally limited to domestic stakeholders.

Article 4, Item 3 Technical regulations must be:
- Clear, proportionate, and feasible.
- Prepared in a way that does not prevent competition.
- Open to opinions from the Ministry and all related parties during the draft stage.
- Notified to relevant international parties as required by legislation and international obligations.
Article 4, Item 3b: The competent body must open technical regulations to opinions from all related parties, but there is no explicit mention of foreign stakeholders or their ability to participate in the standard-setting process.

Article 6, Item 6: Products imported for use as inputs in branded products must comply with TSE standards. This indirectly promotes local content and limits foreign influence in standard-setting.

Article 8, Item 2: Risk analysis criteria for inspections are determined by the Ministry, with input from other parties if deemed necessary. The criteria for risk analysis and the decision-making process are not disclosed, making it difficult for foreign companies to predict outcomes.
Article 8, Item 9: If a product fails to meet the relevant standard, the importer can request re-inspection or object to the test result. However, the process for resolving disputes is not fully transparent.

Article 9, Item 3 Actual inspections can be based on:
- International standards (e.g., ISO, IEC, CEN, CENELEC, ETSI).
- Criteria determined by international agreements.
While international standards are referenced, the criteria for their application and the decision-making process are not always clear.

Article 24, Item 1: Procedures and principles for preparing technical regulations must align with European Union technical legislation.
Coordination between authorized organizations is provided by the Ministry, but the process for foreign participation is not explicitly mentioned.

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation: Law No. 7223 on Product Safety and Technical Regulations
indicators.impact:
Product Safety and Technical Regulations Law No. 7223
Article 13: Products must comply with technical regulations and undergo conformity assessment procedures before being placed on the market. The law does not explicitly allow or prohibit SDoC but emphasizes compliance with technical regulations.
Article 14: Conformity assessment bodies (CABs) may be employed for technical regulations, and their activities must be independent, impartial, and transparent. 

Radio Equipment Regulation (2014/53/EU):
Türkiye has adopted the Radio Equipment Regulation (2014/53/EU), which allows for SDoC in the EU for certain low-risk products. However, it does not explicitly confirm whether Türkiye permits SDoC for radio equipment or EMC/EMI products. 

TAREKS System (Risk-Based Control System):
Products subject to import inspections (e.g., radio equipment, EMC/EMI products) must be registered in the TAREKS system. The system requires documentation such as:
- EU Declaration of Conformity (if applicable).
- Test reports from accredited laboratories.
- Other compliance documents.
The TAREKS system does not explicitly allow SDoC for foreign businesses. Instead, it emphasizes third-party certification and conformity assessment.

Article 9 of the Radio Equipment Import Inspection Communique (2025/8):
Conformity assessment reports from CABs accredited by TURKAK (Turkish Accreditation Agency) or equivalent bodies in the European Union are accepted. This indicates that Türkiye recognizes third-party certifications from CABs in countries with Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) or equivalent accreditation systems.
Article 12 of the Radio Equipment Import Inspection Communique (2025/8):
Importers are responsible for ensuring that products comply with all relevant legislation, including the Radio Equipment Regulation (2014/53/EU).

Article 9 of the Import Conformity with Standards Audit Communique (2025/1):
For certain tests (e.g., raw material tests, long-term performance tests), reports from CABs accredited by TURKAK or EU-accredited bodies are sufficient. Türkiye accepts third-party certifications from CABs in countries with established agreements or equivalence.
Article 12 of the Import Conformity with Standards Audit Communique (2025/1):
Importers must ensure that products comply with Turkish standards and provide accurate documentation. The TAREKS reference number does not guarantee product safety or compliance, indicating that additional verification may be required.

Mutual Recognition in the Unregulated Area Regulation (2021):
Products imported under A.TR certificates (within the EU-Türkiye Customs Union) may benefit from mutual recognition. However, the Ministry reserves the right to evaluate whether the product meets Türkiye's protection levels and may impose additional requirements.

indicators.question_description: Product screening and testing requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Communiqué no. 2011/53 on the Risk-Based Trade Control System (TAREKS) launched at the end of 2010
indicators.impact:
The TAREKS system conducts real-time risk assessment and makes a determination regarding whether the shipment should proceed for physical examination. In cases where the system identifies a high level of risk, both the exporter and the Head of Inspectors are promptly notified of the necessity for a physical inspection. The Head of Inspectors utilizes the TAREKS system to assign a Product Inspector to conduct the physical checks and shares all relevant information provided by the exporter about the shipment, including its type, variety, and quality classification, with the assigned Product Inspector.

Subsequently, the designated Product Inspector arrives at the inspection location to carry out a thorough physical examination and collect samples for laboratory analysis, if deemed necessary. It is essential that the consignment is appropriately packaged, labeled, and prepared for transportation prior to the inspection. Following the physical inspection, if the Product Inspector determines that the shipment complies with the quality and labeling standards outlined in the applicable regulations, they grant approval through TAREKS using their electronic signature.

Article 8 of Import Conformity with Standards Audit:
- Risk analysis determines whether products are directed to actual inspection.
- Criteria for risk analysis include past inspection results, product type, origin, and other relevant factors.
Article 9 of Radio Equipment Import Inspection:
- Products directed to actual inspection must provide all required documents within 20 working days.

indicators.question_description: Product screening and testing requirements
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has robust screening and testing requirements for imported products, particularly for high-risk items. The TAREKS system plays a central role in identifying products that require additional scrutiny, including laboratory testing. While third-party testing results are accepted under specific conditions, importers remain responsible for ensuring compliance with Turkish technical regulations and safety standards.

Product Safety and Technical Regulations Law (Law No. 7223)
Article 4 (Technical Regulations):
- Products must comply with technical regulations before being placed on the market.
- Non-compliant products cannot be supplied, placed on the market, or put into service.
- Screening and testing are required to ensure compliance with technical regulations, particularly for safety, health, and environmental protection.
Article 5 (Product Safety):
- Products must be safe and comply with technical regulations or general product safety legislation.
- In the absence of specific technical regulations, products are evaluated under general product safety legislation.
Article 7 (Manufacturer's Obligations) Manufacturers must:
- Perform conformity assessments.
- Maintain technical files for at least 10 years.
- Take corrective measures for non-compliant products.
This implies that products may undergo screening and testing to verify compliance.

Article 9(4) of Import Conformity with Standards Audit (2025/1):
Third-party testing results are accepted if:
- The testing is conducted by a conformity assessment body (CAB) accredited by TURKAK (Turkish Accreditation Agency) or equivalent bodies in the EU.
- The tests cannot be performed domestically or require specific conditions (e.g., long-term performance tests, raw material tests).

Article 9(4) of Radio Equipment Import Inspection (2025/8):
Third-party testing results are accepted for:
- Long-term performance tests.
- Tests conducted at the production stage.
- Tests on raw materials.

Product Safety and Control: 2025/1) Import Conformity with Standards Audit
Article 4 (TAREKS System):
- All transactions related to the audit of products are conducted via the TAREKS system (Risk-Based Control System).
- Products are screened based on risk analysis, which determines whether they are directed to actual inspection.
Article 8 (Risk Analysis): Risk analysis considers factors such as:
- Past inspection results.
- Product type, origin, and manufacturer.
- Market surveillance data.
- Products flagged as high-risk are directed to actual inspection, which may include laboratory testing.
Article 9 (Actual Inspection) Products directed to actual inspection must provide:
- Test reports.
- Conformity certificates.
- Other relevant documents.
Laboratory testing may be required for certain products, especially if there are concerns about compliance with technical standards.
Article 12 (Importer Responsibility):
- Importers are responsible for ensuring that products comply with all relevant legislation and are safe.
- The issuance of a TAREKS reference number does not guarantee product safety, and additional testing may be required.

Product Safety and Control: 2025/8 - Radio Equipment Import Inspection
Article 4 (TAREKS System):
- All transactions related to the import inspection of radio equipment are conducted via TAREKS.
- Products are screened based on risk analysis, and high-risk products are directed to actual inspection.
Article 9 (Actual Inspection) Products directed to actual inspection must provide:
- EU Declaration of Conformity.
- Test reports or other documents requested by the audit unit.
Laboratory testing may be required for:
- Long-term performance tests.
- Tests on raw materials.
- Tests conducted after assembly.
Article 12 (Importer Responsibility):
- Importers must ensure compliance with the Radio Equipment Regulation (2014/53/EU).
- Devices with electronic identity information (e.g., IMEI numbers) must be registered with the Information Technologies and Communication Authority.

Product Safety and Control: 2025/12 - Consumer Product Import Inspection
Article 4 (TAREKS System):
- All transactions related to the audit of consumer products are conducted via TAREKS.
- Products are screened based on risk analysis, and high-risk products are directed to actual inspection.
Article 9 (Actual Inspection) Products directed to actual inspection must provide:
- Test reports.
- Conformity certificates.
- Other relevant documents.
Laboratory testing may be required for certain products, especially if there are concerns about compliance with safety standards.

indicators.question_description: Foreign equity limits in e-commerce sector
indicators.impact:
According to Art. 3 (a) of the Foreign Direct Investment Law, 100% foreign equity share is allowed. Foreign investors are free to make investments and shall be subject to equal treatment as domestic investors. This law also applies to the E-commerce sector.

Foreign Direct Investment Law (Law No. 4875):
Article 3(a): Foreign investors are free to make investments in Türkiye and are subject to equal treatment with domestic investors.
There are no specific provisions in this law imposing foreign equity limits in the e-commerce sector.

The e-commerce sector in Türkiye is primarily regulated by the E-Commerce Law (Law No. 6563), which does not impose any foreign equity restrictions. Foreign investors can fully own e-commerce companies in Türkiye, provided they comply with general regulatory requirements, such as registration with the E-Commerce Information System (ETBIS).

indicators.question_description:
Online purchases and delivery limitations
Exception: Not score limitations on online purchases and delivery applied specifically to products related to consumer protection, notably restrictions on alcoholic beverages, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals.
indicators.source_legislation: Decision on the Amendment of Certain Articles of the Customs Law No. 4458, as amended in August 2024
indicators.impact:
The Turkish government aims to reduce competition from international e-commerce platforms like AliExpress, Temu, and Amazon, which have been undercutting local retailers. These measures are part of a broader effort to address the budget deficit and increase customs revenues. By limiting the number of items and imposing stricter customs procedures, the government seeks to curb bulk imports and resale activities.

Decision No. 5303 amending certain articles of Customs Law No. 4458 - New Duty-Free Shopping Limits:
- As of August 21, 2024, the Turkish government reduced the duty-free shopping limit for international online purchases to €30 (including shipping costs), down from the previous limit of €150.
- The number of items allowed per shipment has been reduced to 500 items, down from 2,000 items, for non-commercial imports. This is intended to prevent bulk purchases and resale activities.
- A flat €3 shipping fee is now applied to all international purchases, even for items that previously included free shipping. If the shipping cost is not documented, this fee is automatically added during customs processing.
- For items exceeding the €30 limit but valued below €1,500, buyers must complete customs declarations and follow additional procedures. This applies to goods that are not in commercial quantities.
- Goods purchased from the European Union are now subject to a 30% customs duty, up from 18%.
- Goods purchased from non-EU countries (e.g., China) are subject to a 60% customs duty, up from 30%.
- An additional 20% tax is applied to certain luxury items, such as electronics and fashion accessories.

Initially, these were the limit that were changed as per summary above:
Article 62: New Tax Rates for Goods Delivered via Post or Express Cargo
Goods valued up to €150 (non-commercial) are subject to:
- 18% tax if originating from EU countries.
- 30% tax if originating from non-EU countries.
- An additional 20% tax for goods listed under the Special Consumption Tax Law (Law No. 4760).
Books and printed materials for personal use valued up to €1,500 are exempt from taxes.
Goods for legal entities valued up to €22 are taxed at the same rates as above.
Goods must not exceed 30 kilograms in weight to qualify for these provisions.

Article 62, Paragraph 5 - Restrictions on Commercial Quantities
Goods imported via post or express cargo must not be in commercial quantities or exceed the specified value and weight limits.
Article 62, Paragraph 6 - Exemptions for Diplomatic and Special Goods
Diplomatic goods and passenger goods under Article 58 are exempt from the value and weight limits.

Article 126 - Customs Procedures for Specific Goods
Simplified customs declarations are allowed for:
- Goods under €150 for personal use.
- Goods valued between €150 and €1,500 (non-commercial).
- Goods for export valued up to €1,500 and weighing up to 30 kilograms.
- Express cargo companies are authorized as indirect representatives for customs procedures, provided they employ customs brokers.

Article 127 - Prohibition of Additional Fees by Cargo Companies
- Express cargo companies are prohibited from charging additional fees (e.g., customs brokerage, terminal fees) for customs services.
- No storage fees can be charged for the first three days after notifying the recipient of the arrival of goods.

Article 91 - Exemptions for Research and Medical Materials
Exemptions are granted for:
- Goods imported for research, analysis, or testing purposes.
- Biological materials sent for medical testing, provided they are sent to licensed medical laboratories or genetic evaluation centers.
Article 67 - Restrictions on Sale of Certain Imported Vehicles
Vehicles imported under Article 67 cannot be sold for 10 years without paying customs duties. After 10 years, they can be sold without customs duties.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Since September 2009, as amended in August 2024

indicators.question_description:
Licensing scheme for e-commerce providers (B2B and B2C)
Exception: Licenses pertiaining to other aspects of e-commerce businesses, such as license to operate online payment services and delivery are not captured.
indicators.source_legislation: Law on the Regulation of Electronic Commerce No.6563 as amended by the Law on the Amendments to the Law on the Regulation of Electronic Commerce No.6563
indicators.impact:
E-commerce intermediary service providers with a net transaction volume of over 10 billion Turkish Lira and over 100,000 transactions, excluding cancellations and returns in a calendar year, will be required to obtain a license since 2014. The Amendment of the Regulation said that Electronic commerce intermediary service providers with a net transaction volume over ten billion and number of transactions over 100,000 excluding cancellations and returns in a calendar year shall obtain a license from the Ministry and renew such license to continue its activities. The provisions regarding the obligation to obtain a license will enter into force on 1 January 2025

Internet Law No. 5651
Article 7 (Liabilities of Mass Use Providers)
Licensing Requirement: Mass use providers (e.g., internet cafes or public internet access points) operating in a commercial manner are required to obtain a permission document from the local district official. The local district official must notify the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK) within 30 days of issuing the permit.
Penalties - Violations of these obligations may result in:
- A warning.
- An administrative fine ranging from 1,000 to 15,000 Turkish Liras.
- Suspension of commercial activities for up to three days.

Disinformation Law (Amendments to Internet Law No. 5651)
Additional Article 4 - Representative Requirement for Social Network Providers: Social network providers with over one million daily accesses from Türkiye must appoint a local representative in Türkiye.
The representative must:
- Be a Turkish citizen and a resident of Türkiye (if an individual).
- Be a branch of the social network provider (if a legal entity).
The representative is responsible for ensuring compliance with Turkish laws, including responding to requests for content removal, access blocking, and user data disclosure.
Penalties for Non-Compliance such as failure to appoint a representative:
- First fine: 10 million Turkish Liras.
- Second fine: 30 million Turkish Liras.
- Advertisement ban: Taxpayers in Türkiye are prohibited from advertising with the provider.
- Bandwidth throttling: Internet traffic bandwidth may be reduced by 50%, and eventually by 90% if non-compliance persists.

Technical Regulations and Product Safety Law
Article 4 (Technical Regulations) - Licensing for Products in E-Commerce:
- Products offered in the market (including through e-commerce) must comply with technical regulations and general product safety legislation.
- Non-compliant products cannot be supplied, placed on the market, or put into service.
Article 5 (Product Safety) - Obligations for E-Commerce Providers:
- E-commerce providers must ensure that the products they sell are safe and comply with technical regulations.
- Products are considered safe if they meet the requirements of the relevant technical regulations or general product safety legislation.
Article 20 (Administrative Fines) - Penalties for Non-Compliance:
Violations of technical regulations or product safety legislation:
- Fines ranging from 50,000 to 500,000 Turkish Liras.
- Violations of other provisions:
- Fines ranging from 20,000 to 200,000 Turkish Liras.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Law on Payment 6493 

Article 66, Paragraph 3 - Restrictions on Cross-Border Payments: Payment transactions where both parties are located in Türkiye must be conducted in Turkish Lira and through local payment service providers. This effectively mandates the use of local bank accounts for such transactions.

Article 11, Paragraph 2 Licensing and Operational Requirements: Companies applying for a license to provide payment services or issue electronic money in Türkiye must meet minimum capital requirements and establish operations locally, which includes maintaining a local bank account.

Article 60, Paragraph 2 Payment Account Accessibility: Payment service providers must ensure secure communication and access to payment accounts for authorized payment initiation services. This requires the accounts to be maintained within Türkiye to comply with technical and operational requirements.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Law on Payment 6493

Article 66(1): For payments where one of the parties is located abroad, the transaction can be conducted in the currency agreed upon by the parties, provided it complies with the Turkish Currency Protection Law (Decree No. 32).

Article 66(3) Mandate for Local Currency (Turkish Lira) in Domestic Transactions:
If both parties to the transaction are located in Türkiye and use local payment service providers, the payment must be conducted in Turkish Lira (TRY).
:
Article 66(4) Restrictions on Foreign Currency Accounts:
Payment service providers are prohibited from opening foreign currency payment accounts for residents in Türkiye. Additionally, foreign currency cannot be deposited or held in such accounts unless the transaction involves a party located abroad.

Article 66(4) Time Limits for Foreign Currency Transfers:
For payments involving foreign currency:
- Foreign currency deposited domestically for transfer abroad must be sent by the end of the next business day.
- Foreign currency received from abroad must be credited to the recipient's account within one month.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has national standards for payment security that, in some cases, deviate from international standards. These deviations are primarily driven by the country's regulatory framework, which emphasizes data localization, consumer protection, and financial stability. 

- Data Localization Requirements: Turkish regulations mandate that sensitive payment data and customer information must be stored within Türkiye. This is stricter than many international standards, such as PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard), which do not impose geographic restrictions on data storage.
Law on Payment 6493 Article 66, Paragraph 3: Sensitive customer data related to payment services must be stored within Türkiye.
Electronic Money Regulation (Article 62, Paragraph 3): Payment service providers must ensure that sensitive customer data is stored domestically.

- Strong Authentication Requirements: Türkiye enforces strong customer authentication (SCA) for all electronic payment transactions, including financial and non-financial transactions. This includes multi-factor authentication (MFA) and specific requirements for biometric data and PINs. While international standards like PSD2 (in the EU) also require SCA, Türkiye's implementation is more prescriptive in certain areas.

- Shared Payment Regulation Article 10, Paragraph 8: Strong authentication is mandatory for all financial and non-financial transactions unless explicitly exempted.
- Law on Payment 6493 (Article 64): Strong authentication must include unique, tamper-proof elements such as PINs or biometric data.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
To offer electronic money and electronic payment services in Türkiye, companies must obtain a license from the Central Bank of Türkiye. Starting in June 2015, companies that meet specific criteria, including having a physical business presence in Türkiye in the form of a joint-stock company, are eligible for this license. It's important to highlight that these licensed entities are restricted from participating in any other commercial activities aside from providing payment services. Additionally, they are prohibited from offering certain financial services such as accepting deposits or extending credit.

Banking and Payment Services (Law No. 6493)
- Payment service providers and electronic money institutions must obtain licenses from the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BRSA) to operate in Türkiye. This law explicitly requires a commercial presence (e.g., a local subsidiary or branch) for foreign companies offering payment services or digital financial solutions.

Law on Payment 6493, Article 11: Any entity providing payment services or issuing electronic money in Türkiye must obtain a license from the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT). Payment service providers and electronic money institutions must apply for a license and meet specific conditions to operate legally in Türkiye.
Article 11(1): Applicants must pay a licensing fee of 500,000 TRY and provide proof of payment during the application process.
Article 11(2): Minimum Capital Requirements: Companies must meet minimum paid-in capital requirements, which vary depending on the type of service:
- 1 million TRY for basic payment services.
- 2 million TRY for other payment services.
- 5 million TRY for electronic money issuance.
Article 11(3): Payment service providers and electronic money institutions must establish a local entity in Türkiye to apply for a license. The licensing process includes an intelligence review and a final approval stage, requiring the applicant to have a local presence.
Article 16: Payment service providers and electronic money institutions are prohibited from offering credit or engaging in activities that create the impression of credit issuance.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
There are ceilings on the maximum amount that can be paid using electronic payment methods in Türkiye, as outlined in Law on Payment 6493 and related regulations.

Article 16(3): Payments facilitated by telecommunication or electronic communication operators (e.g., for utility bills) are subject to a ceiling of 1,000 TRY per transaction and 2,750 TRY per month for all accounts linked to a single customer.

Article 58: Anonymous prepaid cards or payment instruments that are not linked to a payment account are subject to stricter ceilings. These instruments cannot exceed 2,750 TRY in stored value or spending limits.

Article 73: For payment instruments with a spending limit of 2,750 TRY or less, or those containing funds not exceeding 2,750 TRY at any time, specific rules and ceilings apply.
- Payment instruments with these limits are subject to simplified information and reporting requirements.
- These instruments cannot be used for payments exceeding their defined limits.
Article 73(4): The Central Bank of Türkiye has the authority to increase or decrease these ceilings by up to five times or reduce them to one-fifth of the defined limits, depending on economic conditions or regulatory needs.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Türkiye has specific requirements mandating the use of certain intermediaries for online payments.

Law on Payment 6493:
Article 66(3): Payment transactions involving Turkish residents must be processed through local payment service providers authorized by the CBRT.
Article 3(l): The Bankalararası Kart Merkezi (BKM), or Interbank Card Center, is a key intermediary for payment systems in Türkiye. It provides infrastructure for card payments, clearing, and settlement. Payment service providers must integrate with BKM for certain services, such as card payments and open banking APIs. The BKM-API Gateway is a mandatory intermediary for open banking services, ensuring compliance with security and data-sharing standards.

indicators.question_description: Restrictions on online payment
indicators.impact:
Law on Payment 6493:

Article 19: Entities offering digital wallet services must apply for a license by April 7, 2025, to continue operations legally.
Digital wallet providers must comply with the new 4/A article of the regulation, which includes stricter operational and security requirements.

Transition Periods for Compliance:
Existing payment service providers and electronic money institutions must comply with new regulations by specific deadlines, such as:
- March 31, 2025, for certain technical requirements.
- December 31, 2025, for direct online access to customer accounts.

Regulation on the Non-Use of Crypto Assets in Payments
Article 3 and 4: Crypto assets cannot be used directly or indirectly for payments in Türkiye. Payment service providers and electronic money institutions are prohibited from:
- Using crypto assets in payment services or electronic money issuance.
- Facilitating the transfer of funds to or from platforms offering crypto-related services.

indicators.question_description: Low De Minimis
indicators.source_legislation: The Decree on Amendments of Certain Articles of Customs Law No. 4458
indicators.impact: The Decree of 2019 removed the exemption threshold for certain imported goods. The Council of Ministers Resolution No. 15481, published in 2009, established the exemption threshold for imported products whose price did not exceed €150, which was then reduced to €75 in 2011, to €30 at the beginning of 2017, to €22 in April 2018 and finally to zero on 15 May 2019. There is now no more de minimis threshold in Türkiye. Therefore, there is no value below which goods are exempted from taxes and duties collected by customs. It's important to note that the exemption threshold still applies to books or relevant publications whose price does not exceed €150.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.source_legislation: E-Commerce Law (Law No. 6563)
indicators.impact:
E-Commerce Law (Law No. 6563)
Service providers and intermediary service providers engaged in e-commerce must register with the E-Commerce Information System (ETBIS) before initiating operations in Türkiye.
Implication: While this does not explicitly mandate a physical presence, compliance with local registration and reporting requirements can act as a de facto commercial presence obligation for foreign companies.

Article 3 – Obligations of Service Providers and Intermediary Service Providers:
Service providers and intermediary service providers engaged in e-commerce must comply with the obligations set forth in the law, including transparency, information disclosure, and consumer protection requirements.

Article 11 – E-Commerce Information System (ETBIS):
Companies engaged in e-commerce activities are required to register with the E-Commerce Information System (ETBIS), which is managed by the Ministry of Trade. The registration includes providing detailed information about the company, its activities, and its compliance with Turkish e-commerce regulations.

ETBIS Registration Requirements. To register with ETBIS, companies must:
- Provide their tax identification number (which typically requires a local tax registration).
- Submit information about their e-commerce activities, including:
- The website or platform used for e-commerce.
- Types of goods or services offered.
- Payment methods and delivery processes.
- Comply with Turkish consumer protection laws, data protection laws, and other relevant regulations.

indicators.question_description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
indicators.impact:
Law on Payment 6493:

Article 14: Online service providers offering payment services or electronic money issuance must establish a local presence in Türkiye to obtain a license from the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT).
This includes:
- Registering as a legal entity in Türkiye.
- Maintaining a physical office or operational base within the country.

Article 19: Foreign entities providing payment services in Türkiye must collaborate with a local representative or establish a local subsidiary to comply with Turkish regulations. The local representative is responsible for ensuring compliance with Turkish laws and regulations.
Article 19(1): Foreign service providers can only offer services in Türkiye through partnerships with locally licensed entities. These partnerships must comply with Turkish laws and are limited to cross-border transactions where one party is located outside Türkiye.

Article 64: Online service providers must submit to audits and inspections by Turkish authorities, including the CBRT. This requires maintaining local systems and records accessible to regulators.

Article 21(1): Payment service providers must ensure that their primary and secondary systems, as well as data backup centers, are located within Türkiye. This applies to all information systems used for payment transactions involving Turkish residents.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.impact:
The general consumer protection law was updated in 2013 in order to be harmonized with the EU framework. The law covers all consumer transactions. For financial services (banking, private pensions, insurance, investment and payment services) sold on distance sales, consumers have the right to withdraw from the agreement within a period of 14 days. There are no barriers found related to the consumer protection practices in Türkiye. The Law on Consumer Protection has been amended in 2022 to include provisions on distance contracts, which are contracts concluded without the physical presence of the parties. 

Another relevant legal framework is the Regulation on Distance contracts. It includes the regulation of the performance methods and principles of distance contracts, the delivery processes, prior information of consumers, right of withdrawal and the liabilities of the parties. The supplier or seller has to perform the order within 30 days, and the consumer has the right to withdraw from the distance contract within 14 days, starting from the date of delivery for goods.

In Türkiye, e-signature is regulated by Law No. 5070 on Electronic Signature.

Consumer Protection Law No. 6502

Article 48 regulates contracts concluded without the simultaneous physical presence of the consumer and the seller (e.g., online shopping). It mandates that sellers provide clear and accurate information about the product or service, including:
- Price,
- Delivery terms,
- Right of withdrawal.
- Consumers have the right to withdraw from the contract within 14 days without providing a reason.
Article 11 - Consumer Rights for Defective Goods
Consumers can demand:
- Free repair,
- Replacement,
- Price reduction,
- Full refund for defective goods purchased online.
Article 68 - Consumer Arbitration Committees
Consumers can file complaints about disputes under a certain monetary threshold with Consumer Arbitration Committees, which provide a cost-effective resolution mechanism.

Right of Withdrawal (Article 9): Consumers can cancel the contract within 14 days of receiving the product without incurring any penalties.
Obligations of the Seller (Article 12): Sellers must refund payments within 14 days of receiving the returned product. Delivery must occur within the agreed timeframe, and delays can result in contract termination.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.impact:
Law on Payment 6493:

Article 3 - Information Obligations for E-commerce platforms must provide clear and accessible information about:
- The seller's identity,
- Contact details,
- Terms of sale,
- Payment methods.
Article 5 - Commercial Communication: Prohibits misleading advertisements and requires explicit consumer consent for promotional messages.
Article 11 - Data Protection: Aligns with the Personal Data Protection Law (KVKK) to ensure consumer data privacy in online transactions.

Article 49 Irrevocability of Payment Orders: A payment order cannot be revoked by the sender after it has been received by the payment service provider unless otherwise agreed between the parties.

Article 55 Liability for Non-Execution or Incorrect Execution of Payment Transactions: The sender's payment service provider is responsible for the correct execution of the payment transaction. If the transaction is not executed or executed incorrectly, the provider must promptly refund the sender for the unexecuted or incorrectly executed portion

Article 73 Low-Value Payment Instruments and Electronic Money: he payment service provider is obligated to inform the customer about the basic features of the payment service, including the method of use, responsibilities, fees, and other important information.

Article 74: Payment service providers must respond to complaints and objections related to payment services within 20 days of the application date, using the same method as the customer's application, in a verifiable and justified manner.

indicators.question_description: Patent application issues
indicators.source_legislation: Patents Act No.2 of 2003
indicators.impact: Part 4 of the Act prescribes the application for patents and Part 5 prescribes procedure for granting patent. A person shall filling an application with the Registrar of Patents (Section 12). If the Registrar determines the application does not comply with this Act, the Registrar must inform the applicant and ask to amend the application (Section 16). There is no restrictions related to the application process for patents.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Patents Act No.2 2003
indicators.impact: Patent enforcement involves both civil and administrative procedures. The patent owner can initiate court proceedings for any alleged infringement (Section 42.1), including an injunction restraining the defendant from any alleged act of infringement (Section 42.2a). Administratively, the Registrar manages the submission, examination, and publication of patent applications, resolves disputes between applicants (Section 21), and has the authority to revoke patents on specific grounds (Section 39). Remedies include injunctions, damages, destruction of infringing products, and declarations of validity and infringement.

indicators.question_description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
indicators.source_legislation: Patents Act No.2 of 2003
indicators.impact:
According to Part 11 of the Act, patent infringement and proceedings are regulated. If a person infringes a patent invention, the owner of a patent may bring proceedings in court for any act alleged to infringe the patent (Section 41). The remedies cover an injunction, damages for the infringement, an account of the profits derived by the defendant from infringement, etc. (Section 42).

There is no restriction or report related to the enforcement of patents.

indicators.source_legislation: Copyright and Related Rights Act No. 42 of 2000
indicators.impact:
Under the Copyright and Related Rights Act of 2000, Part 3 Acts Not Constituting Infringement of Copyright in Works, certain acts are not considered an infringement of copyright. The exceptions include fair dealing for purposes of research or private study, legal advise, criticism or review (Sections 10 -18). 

In particular, certain acts that not considered as an infringement are:
1. Private reproduction for personal purposes
2. Temporary reproduction
3. Quotation
4. Reproduction for educational or legal purposes
5. Reproduction by libraries and archives
6. Reproduction, broadcasting and other communication to the public for information purposes
7. Reproduction and adaptation of computer programs
8. Importation for personal purposes
9. Display of works
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator: Assented December 2000, commencement February 2011, last amended in November 2021

indicators.question_description: Online copyright enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies; and provisional measures
indicators.source_legislation: Copyright and Related Rights Act No. 42 of 2000
indicators.impact: Under Part 6 enforcement of rights and protection requirements, the Supreme Court has jurisdiction in respect of civil and criminal matters arising under the Copyright Act (Sections 34 and 35). A person who intentionally and for profit making purposes infringes a right protected under this Act is guilty of an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding 2,000,000 Vatu or imprisonment for not more than 2 years, or both (Section 35.2). The Court is also authorized to grant injunctions to prohibit the infringement. There have not been recent complaints related to online piracy.

indicators.question_description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
indicators.source_legislation: Trade Secrets Act of 2000 No.52 of 2000
indicators.impact:
A person who is the owner of a trade secret has the right to that secret remaining undisclosed (Section 2). 

If a trade secret is acquired, used or disclosed by a person without the authority of the owner of the trade secret, the owner has the right to apply to the Supreme Court for a declaration that the trade secret has been acquired, used or disclosed without authority (Section 3). The Supreme Court may grant an injunction and award damages to the owner.

indicators.question_description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
indicators.source_legislation: Trade Secrets Act of 2000 No.52 of 2000
indicators.impact:
The Trade Secrets Act defines a trade secret as any information that is (Section 1):
(a) not generally known among, or readily accessible to, persons who
normally deal with information of that kind; or
(b) about a person’s business or professional affairs and disclosure would, or could reasonably be expected to, unreasonably affect that person adversely in respect of his or her lawful business or professional affairs; and that has commercial value because of this. 

If a trade secret is acquired, used or disclosed by a person without the authority of the owner of the trade secret, the owner has the right to apply to the Supreme Court for a declaration that the trade secret has been acquired, used or disclosed without authority. The Court may: grant an injunction preventing anyone from dealing with, or otherwise using, the secret in a commercial way; and if it is satisfied that the owner has suffered damage because of the unauthorised disclosure—award damages to the owner (Section 3).

indicators.question_description: Absence of passive infrastructure sharing
indicators.source_legislation: Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulation Act No. 30 of 2009
indicators.impact:
Passive infrastructure sharing is not mandated. 
However, on the Island of Akam, South Malekula, TRBR was entrusted with the task of enhancing mobile coverage on the area of Akam Island and its adjacent mainland area. In collaboration with the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer (OGCIO), TRBR has decided to initiate a pilot project centered around 'Shared Infrastructure' to optimize resources to deliver services to the consumers. This approach entails that the Government will assume ownership of the tower, which will then be leased by the Telcos for using the tower and power.

The Universal Access and infrastructure sharing report 2024 is due to come out soon, and will have further information as to how infrastucture sharing is conducted.

indicators.question_description: Lack of comprehensive legal framework for data protection
indicators.impact:
Comprehensive data protection laws are currently before parliament. Data protection laws can be found in sectoral laws, such as the Electronic Transaction Act (Section 25), the Cybercrime Act, and Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulation Act (Section 40). 

Specifically, the Telecommunications Act provides that a service provider must not, without the consent of the end user, divulge any personal end user information to any other person who is not an agent or employee of the service provider, unless required by law or authorised by warrant or by the Regulator (Section 40(1)). A service provider must not, without the consent of the end user, collect any personal end user information not reasonably necessary for the provision of any telecommunications service to the end user, unless required by law or authorised by warrant or by the Regulator (Section 40(2)).

indicators.question_description:

Exception: Not score requirement applied to government data.
indicators.impact: There is no minimum period of data retention requirement implemented.

indicators.source_legislation: E-Business Act [Cap 264] of 2000
indicators.impact: According to Part 4, Section 15(2) of the E-Business Act, companies carrying any electronic business must appoint a data protection officer who is responsible for ensuring the company complies with such approved codes of conduct or standards.

indicators.question_description: Requirements to allow government access to personal data
indicators.source_legislation: Cybercrime Act No.22 of 2021
indicators.impact:
A service provider who receives an order from the Supreme Court relating to a criminal investigation shall disclose the information (Section 15, Disclosure of information of an investigation). The Commissioner of Police must apply to the Court to grant an interception warrant, the renewal of such warrant, or an urgent interception warrant (Sections 27 and 28).

However, the Commissioner of Police is authorized to request a service provider in writing to disclosure subscriber data, or traffic data, if the disclosure is necessary for law enforcement purposes or a foreign serious offence. A service provider must comply as soon as practical after receiving the request unless shall committed to offence and liable to fine (Sections 21 and 22). Moreover, the Commissioner can request a service provider in writing to access to traffic data in real time for up to 90 days for the enforcement of punishable offence or foreign serious offence (Section 23).

indicators.question_description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
indicators.source_legislation: Electronic Transactions Act No.24 of 2000
indicators.impact:
Intermediaries and e-commerce service providers are not civilly or criminally liable for the content of a message if the intermediary was not the creator of the message, and: (1) the intermediary did not know that dissemination of the message would be grounds for liability; or (2) the intermediary did not know any related facts or circumstances which would have made it reasonable to suspect there was liability; or if the intermediary has complied with Article 27 of the Electronic Transactions Act procedure if the intermediary has become aware of the existence of a civil or criminal penalty, or became aware of facts or circumstances which should have led the intermediary to conclude there was a reasonable likelihood of liability.

Specifically, under this Act, "e-commerce service provider" means a person who uses electronic means in providing goods, services or information, and "intermediary", in relation to an electronic record, means a person who, on behalf of another person, sends, receives or stores that electronic record or provides other services with respect to that electronic record.

indicators.question_description: Lack of transparent technical standards
indicators.source_legislation:
Bureau of Standards Act No.14 of 2016;

Telecommunications, Radiocommunications and Broadcasting Type Approval and Conformity to Technical Standards Order No.191 of 2018
indicators.impact:
There are no complaints about lack of foreign participation in standard-setting bodies for telecom products or of non-transparent standards. Vanuatu Standard is based on international best practises and harmonised with relevant international or regional standards (Section 16.2). A draft standard shall be published as a notice in a local newspaper and by other means to notify the public (Section 16.5). A person within 60 days may submit a written objection (Section 16.6).

In particular, the Order No.191 states that the radiocommunications device manufactured domestically or imported into the country must conform to the applicable technical standards (Section 3).
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Assented December 2016, commenced April 2017;

Since November 2018

indicators.question_description: Self-certification limitations for product safety (radio transmissions, EMC/EMI)
indicators.source_legislation: Telecommunications, Radiocommunications and Broadcasting Type Approval and Conformity to Technical Standards Order No.191 of 2018
indicators.impact:
SDoC is not implemented in Vanuatu. However, Vanuatu recognizes the 3rd party-certification (Section 15 of the 2018 Order). The list of the recognized certification bodies (CABs) can be found in Schedule 2, including Australia, China, European Union, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, the Republic of Korea, the United States, Hong Kong; China, and Taiwan Province of China.

Local importers need to obtain type approval import permits from the Telecommunications, Radiocommunications & Broadcasting Regulator for the approval of importation, use and for sale of any ICT equipment each time a consignment of relevant equipment is imported to Vanuatu.

indicators.question_description: Product screening and testing requirements
indicators.source_legislation: Telecommunications, Radiocommunications and Broadcasting Type Approval and Conformity to Technical Standards Order No.191 of 2018
indicators.impact:
Vanuatu does not require local laboratory testing or screening. 

If the record does not provides sufficient evidence, the regulator may require the suppliers in writing to submit a test report from a conformity assessment body recognized by one of the recognized certification bodies stating that the device conforms with each applicable standards; or a written statement from a conformity assessment body (CAB) recognized by one of the recognized certification bodies certifying that the device conforms with one or more requirements in an applicable standard (Section 15(1). A supplier must submit the request within 30 days (Section 15(2)).

indicators.question_description: Deviation from international encryption standards (ISO, IEC, ITU, FIPS, AES, TDES, and ECC)
indicators.source_legislation:

Electronic Transactions Act No.24 of 2000
indicators.impact:
Vanuatu has yet implemented encryption standards and there is no report of restrictions. 

The Electronic Transactions Act allows the Minister to make regulations in relation to the use, import and export of encryption programmes and products, and to prohibit the export of encryption programmes and products (Section 24(1)). None, however, appear to have been made.

indicators.question_description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
indicators.impact:
Vanuatu does not have a general consumer protection law. The consumer protection can be found under sectoral laws, including the Telecommunications and Radiocommunications Regulation Act 2009, the Utilities Regulatory Authority Act 2007; the Food (Control) Act 1993; and the Weights Act. 

Specifically, the Telecommunication and Radiocommunications Regulation provides online consumer protection in the telecom market (Part 8 Consumer relations and protection). For example, a service provider must establish procedures to deal with disputes and complaints from end-users (Section 41). Moreover, the order subsequently issued in 2015 prescribes online consumer protection in detail, such as the authorized uses and disclosure of consumer information, and online advertising.
indicators.timeframe_for_indicator:
Since November 2009, last amended in 2018;

Since October 2015
